guides.title: Atoms, Elements & the Periodic Table
guides.summary: The structure of the atom, what makes an element, how electrons are arranged, and how the periodic table organizes all matter so its behavior becomes predictable.

sections.heading: First principles: what everything is made of
sections.body:
All ordinary matter is built from atoms, the smallest unit of an element that still carries that element's chemical identity. A typical atom measures about 0.1 to 0.5 nanometres across, where a nanometre is one billionth of a metre. To put that in reach: a line of about five million carbon atoms would span a single millimetre, and a copper coin the size of a thumbnail contains on the order of a hundred thousand billion billion of them. Every atom has the same two-part construction — a tiny, extremely dense nucleus at the centre, and a surrounding cloud of electrons.

Three particles matter for chemistry. The proton is a positively charged particle in the nucleus, carrying a charge of exactly plus one in units of the elementary charge, which is 1.602 times ten to the minus nineteen coulombs, and having a mass of about one atomic mass unit, where one unit is 1.6605 times ten to the minus twenty-seven kilograms. The neutron sits alongside it in the nucleus, carries no charge at all, and has a mass fractionally greater than a proton's. The electron occupies the space around the nucleus, carries a charge of minus one exactly balancing the proton's, and has a mass of roughly one eighteen-hundred-and-thirty-sixth of an atomic mass unit — about 0.00055 u. That ratio is the reason essentially all of an atom's mass sits in the nucleus while essentially all of its volume, and all of its chemistry, belongs to the electrons.

The scale difference between the two parts is easy to state and hard to picture. The nucleus is roughly one hundred-thousandth the diameter of the whole atom. If an atom were scaled up to a football stadium, the nucleus would be a pea on the centre spot and the electrons would be a faint haze filling the stands. Everything between is empty space in the ordinary sense — which raises the fair question of why a table feels solid. The answer is that solidity comes from electrical repulsion between electron clouds and from the quantum rule that forbids two electrons from occupying the same state, not from any physical filling of space.

A neutral atom holds exactly as many electrons as protons, so the positive and negative charges cancel to zero. This balance is fragile in a useful way: electrons at the outer edge can be pulled off or added by ordinary chemical energies of a few electronvolts, whereas disturbing the nucleus takes millions of times more. That single asymmetry is why chemistry and nuclear physics are separate subjects, and why an element's identity survives every reaction it ever undergoes. Burn a diamond, dissolve it, react it into a thousand compounds, and every carbon nucleus emerges from the process exactly as it went in, with six protons and no memory of the journey.

sections.heading: Atomic number, mass number, and isotopes
sections.body:
Two whole numbers pin down any atom completely. The atomic number, written Z, is the count of protons in the nucleus, and it alone determines which element the atom is. Hydrogen is Z equals 1, carbon 6, oxygen 8, iron 26, gold 79. This is a definition, not a tendency: an atom with 79 protons is gold regardless of what else it carries, and if you could add one proton it would become mercury. Alchemists spent centuries trying to change base metals into gold with chemical means, and the reason they could never succeed is that chemistry only ever rearranges electrons, never protons. Transmutation is real, but it requires nuclear energies — and gold has in fact been made in particle accelerators, at a cost per atom that makes the exercise purely academic.

The mass number, written A, is the total count of protons plus neutrons, collectively called nucleons. Electrons are omitted because they are too light to shift the total meaningfully. From these two numbers the neutron count follows immediately as A minus Z.

Isotopes are atoms of the same element, meaning the same Z, that differ in neutron count and therefore in A. Because chemical behaviour is governed by electrons, and electron count follows proton count, isotopes of an element behave almost identically in reactions. Almost, not exactly: the mass difference slightly changes reaction rates, an effect large enough in hydrogen that heavy water is measurably toxic to organisms at high concentration, and small enough in heavier elements to be a specialist concern. What isotopes differ in substantially is nuclear stability.

Carbon is the standard illustration. Carbon-12 has 6 protons and 6 neutrons, is stable, and makes up about 98.9 per cent of natural carbon; it is also the reference standard by which the atomic mass unit itself is defined. Carbon-13 has 7 neutrons, is stable, and supplies the remaining 1.1 per cent. Carbon-14 has 8 neutrons, is radioactive with a half-life of 5,730 years, and is the basis of radiocarbon dating.

This immediately explains something on every periodic table that puzzles newcomers. The atomic mass printed under carbon is 12.011, not 12, even though no carbon atom has a mass number of 12.011. That figure is the weighted average across the natural isotope mixture — mostly 12, a little 13 — and it is a property of terrestrial carbon in bulk, not of any individual atom. Chlorine's 35.45 is the starker case: it reflects roughly three parts chlorine-35 to one part chlorine-37, and no chlorine atom weighs 35.45 units. A mass spectrometer resolves this directly, separating the two by their differing deflection in a magnetic field and displaying them as two distinct peaks in a three-to-one ratio rather than one peak at the average. Where isotope ratios vary geographically, the printed value carries a genuine caveat: standard atomic weights for a handful of elements, including hydrogen, carbon, oxygen and sulfur, are now published as intervals rather than single numbers precisely because the local mixture differs from place to place.

sections.heading: Electrons in shells: the key to chemistry
sections.body:
Chemistry is almost entirely about electrons, and specifically about the outermost ones. Electrons occupy energy levels, commonly called shells, arranged around the nucleus and labelled n equals 1, 2, 3 and so on outward. Each shell can hold a limited number of electrons, given approximately by two times n squared: the first shell holds 2, the second 8, the third 18. For the lighter elements the third shell behaves as though it holds 8, because the first eight of its places fill before the next shell begins, and the remaining ten are filled later out of sequence. This is the point at which the simple shell model starts to strain, and it is worth knowing that in advance rather than being ambushed by it at calcium.

Electrons fill from the inside outward, lowest energy first, because an electron closer to the positively charged nucleus sits in a deeper energy well. The outermost occupied shell is the valence shell, and its occupants, the valence electrons, do essentially all the chemistry — they are the ones shared, donated or captured when bonds form. Inner electrons are shielded and unavailable at ordinary chemical energies, which is why the enormous electron count of a heavy atom does not make it enormously more complicated to reason about.

Work a case through. Sodium has Z equals 11, so a neutral sodium atom has 11 electrons, filling as 2, then 8, then 1. Its valence shell holds a single electron, and that lone electron is both weakly held and an obstacle to a tidy configuration. Chlorine has Z equals 17, filling as 2, 8, 7. Its valence shell has seven electrons and needs exactly one more to be full. Put the two together and the mismatch resolves itself: sodium hands over its single outer electron, chlorine accepts it, and the resulting oppositely charged particles attract into sodium chloride, ordinary table salt. The violence of that reaction — sodium metal and chlorine gas combine with flame and heat — is the energy released by two atoms both reaching a stable arrangement at once.

The octet rule summarises the pattern: atoms tend toward eight electrons in the valence shell, or two for the tiny first shell, because that is the configuration of the noble gases, which are so unreactive that helium, neon and argon form essentially no ordinary compounds at all. The rule is a guide with real exceptions rather than a law. Boron is content with six, phosphorus and sulfur can accommodate ten or twelve, and any molecule with an odd electron count breaks it by arithmetic necessity. Used as a first approximation for the elements of the first three periods it is remarkably reliable; extended blindly to transition metals it fails.

sections.heading: How the periodic table is organized
sections.body:
Dmitri Mendeleev published his arrangement in 1869, and what makes it a scientific achievement rather than a filing system is that he left gaps. Ordering the known elements so that chemical behaviour repeated at regular intervals forced blank spaces into his table, and rather than fudging the arrangement he asserted that undiscovered elements must fill them — and predicted their properties. His eka-silicon was described in detail before anyone had seen it; germanium was isolated in 1886 with a density of 5.32 against his predicted 5.5 and an atomic mass of 72.6 against his 72. That is the difference between a classification and a theory.

The modern table orders all 118 known elements by increasing atomic number, wrapped into rows and columns so that chemically similar elements align vertically. Periods are the rows, numbered 1 to 7. Reading left to right along a period, each element has one more proton and one more electron than the one before, and a new period begins when a new electron shell starts filling. Period 2 runs lithium, beryllium, boron, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine, neon — the eight elements it takes to fill shell 2 — which is why that period has exactly eight members and period 1 has only two.

Groups are the columns, numbered 1 to 18, and they are the useful axis. Elements in a column share the same number of valence electrons and therefore behave alike. Group 1, the alkali metals, all have one valence electron, all form singly charged positive ions, and all react vigorously with water, increasingly so down the column. Group 17, the halogens, all have seven valence electrons and are aggressive nonmetals. Group 18, the noble gases, have full valence shells and are close to inert.

A rough left-to-right map holds across the whole table. Metals occupy the left and centre: shiny, malleable, good conductors, and inclined to lose electrons. Nonmetals occupy the upper right and supply the atoms of air, water and every biological molecule. Between them runs a diagonal staircase of metalloids — boron, silicon, germanium, arsenic, antimony, tellurium — with intermediate properties. Silicon's position there is not a curiosity: its conductivity sits between a metal's and an insulator's and can be tuned by adding trace impurities, which is precisely what makes transistors and therefore computers possible.

Two blocks are conventionally pulled out and printed beneath the main body. The lanthanides and actinides belong in periods 6 and 7 but would stretch the table impractically wide, so they are shown separately. This is a typographic decision, not a chemical one, and it regularly misleads readers into thinking those elements are somehow outside the system. They are not; they simply occupy the f-block, and the table is periodically redrawn in wide form to prove it.

sections.heading: Periodic trends: predicting behavior from position
sections.body:
An element's position predicts its properties, and three trends carry most of the predictive weight.

Atomic radius decreases from left to right across a period and increases down a group. Moving right, each step adds a proton to the nucleus and an electron to the same shell; the extra positive charge pulls that shell in tighter, so atoms get smaller even as they get heavier. Moving down, each new period adds an entire new shell, which more than offsets the added nuclear charge. The result is a diagonal gradient: caesium at the bottom left has a radius around 265 picometres, while fluorine at the top right is about 42. Chemists describe the balance with the idea of effective nuclear charge — the net pull an outer electron feels once inner electrons have screened part of the nucleus — and screening is what stops the trend down a group from reversing.

Ionisation energy, the energy needed to strip the outermost electron from a gaseous atom, runs the opposite way: it rises across a period and falls down a group, for the same reasons in mirror image. Caesium gives up an electron for about 376 kilojoules per mole; helium demands 2,372. Metals on the left have low ionisation energies, lose electrons readily and form positive ions, which is the whole reason sodium reacts so vigorously and gold does not. The trend is not perfectly smooth, and the wobbles are informative rather than noise: boron dips below beryllium, and oxygen below nitrogen, because a newly started subshell and a first electron pairing each cost a little stability.

Electronegativity measures how strongly an atom pulls on electrons it is sharing within a bond, and on Linus Pauling's scale it runs from about 0.7 to 3.98. It increases across a period and decreases down a group, peaking at fluorine on 3.98, with oxygen at 3.44, chlorine and nitrogen at about 3.16 and 3.04, and caesium and francium at the bottom near 0.7. Because it describes a tug-of-war rather than an isolated atom, it is only defined for elements that actually form bonds, and the noble gases are usually left blank.

Put the trends to work. Potassium sits in group 1, period 4 — large, low ionisation energy, one loosely held valence electron — so it should react with water even more violently than sodium, and it does, igniting the hydrogen it liberates. Fluorine, being the most electronegative element, should be the most aggressive electron-grabber, and it is, reacting with almost every element including some noble gases. The honest caveat is that trends predict tendencies, not rates: they tell you which direction a reaction favours, not how fast it goes or whether a kinetic barrier will stall it entirely.

sections.heading: Ions: charged atoms
sections.body:
When an atom gains or loses electrons its proton and electron counts stop balancing, so it carries a net electrical charge and becomes an ion. The nucleus is untouched by this — the element is unchanged, only its electron inventory has shifted.

Losing electrons leaves a surplus of positive charge and produces a cation. Metals do this, because their few valence electrons are weakly held. Sodium sheds one to become Na+, magnesium sheds two to become Mg2+, aluminium three to become Al3+. Gaining electrons produces an anion, and nonmetals do this: chlorine takes one to become Cl-, oxygen two to become O2-, nitrogen three to become N3-. A useful habit is to read the charge as an accounting statement rather than a property — the plus on Na+ means one fewer electron than protons, nothing more.

Atoms form ions because doing so reaches a full-octet, noble-gas configuration. Na+ ends up with neon's arrangement of 2 and 8; Cl- ends up with argon's 2, 8 and 8. Notice that the ions are chemically nothing like the noble gases they resemble electronically, because they still carry charge — sodium ion is a harmless component of blood plasma while sodium metal ignites on contact with water, and chloride ion is table salt while chlorine gas was used as a chemical weapon. Confusing an element with its ion is the single most consequential mistake a beginner can make about safety.

Size changes sharply on ionisation. Losing the whole outer shell makes Na+ dramatically smaller than sodium, about 102 picometres against 186. Gaining an electron increases repulsion within the outer shell and swells the anion, so Cl- at 181 picometres is markedly larger than neutral chlorine at 99. This is why ionic crystals pack the way they do, with small cations tucked into the gaps of a lattice built largely by the bigger anions.

Opposite charges attract, so cations and anions assemble into ionic compounds: Na+ with Cl- gives NaCl, Mg2+ with O2- gives MgO. Overall neutrality is mandatory, and it is the rule that generates chemical formulae without memorisation. Calcium chloride is CaCl2 because one Ca2+ needs two Cl- to cancel; aluminium oxide is Al2O3 because two 3+ ions balance three 2- ions at a total of six each. Magnesium oxide's doubled charges also explain a physical fact: its melting point is about 2,852 degrees Celsius against sodium chloride's 801, because the electrostatic attraction between 2+ and 2- is roughly four times as strong as between 1+ and 1-, and it takes correspondingly more heat to shake that lattice apart. The same reasoning predicts hardness, brittleness and solubility across the whole class of ionic solids, which is why magnesium oxide lines furnaces while sodium chloride dissolves in a glass of water.

sections.heading: Common mistakes, safety, and practical notes
sections.body:
Several errors recur so reliably that they are worth naming directly. The first is confusing mass number with atomic mass. Mass number is a whole-number count of nucleons in one specific isotope and is never a decimal; atomic mass, such as carbon's 12.011, is a weighted average across the natural isotope mixture and belongs to the element in bulk rather than to any atom. If a figure has a decimal point it is an average, and if it does not it is a count.

The second is believing the table is ordered by mass. It is ordered by atomic number, that is by proton count, and the two orderings very nearly but not exactly coincide. Tellurium has a greater atomic mass than iodine yet must precede it, because tellurium has 52 protons and iodine 53 — and chemically tellurium plainly belongs with selenium while iodine belongs with bromine. Mendeleev, working before protons were known, trusted chemical behaviour over measured mass and put them in what looked like the wrong order. Henry Moseley's X-ray work in 1913 vindicated him by measuring nuclear charge directly.

The third is muddling isotopes with elements. Changing the neutron count gives a different isotope of the same element; changing the proton count gives a different element entirely. No chemical process changes the second.

On safety, the reactivity trends have real consequences. Group 1 metals react with water to liberate hydrogen and enough heat to ignite it, and the vigour rises steeply down the group: lithium fizzes, sodium melts into a skittering ball, potassium ignites, caesium detonates on contact. They are stored under oil and are not materials for a domestic setting. Fluorine and chlorine gases are acutely toxic and corrosive, and chlorine is generated accidentally in homes every year by mixing bleach with acidic cleaners or ammonia — a genuinely common and occasionally fatal accident. Radioactive isotopes in old luminous watch dials and some vintage ceramics emit ionising radiation; intact and undisturbed they are usually a minor hazard, but grinding, sanding or breaking them creates inhalable dust, which is the dangerous form.

The practical payoff of all this structure is prediction. The table lets you infer an unfamiliar element's behaviour from a familiar neighbour, which is the single most powerful shortcut in chemistry. Knowing that every group 1 metal is soft, low-melting, reactive toward water and forms a singly charged positive ion tells you most of rubidium's chemistry before you have seen a sample. The limit is worth stating plainly: the trends predict thermodynamic tendency, not rate, and they are least reliable exactly where the electron structure gets complicated — the transition metals, the lanthanides, and the heaviest synthetic elements where relativistic effects on fast inner electrons distort the expected pattern.

sections.heading: Getting hands-on: equipment for exploring elements yourself
sections.body:
None of this needs a laboratory. Flame tests and simple spectroscopy are exactly how nineteenth-century chemists identified several elements, and the same observations can be repeated with items from a hardware shop, a grocery aisle and a craft store. Understanding why each item is on the list matters more than owning it.

The flame source works because heat promotes an atom's outer electrons into higher energy levels; when they fall back, they emit photons of precisely the energies the gaps allow, and those fixed energies appear as fixed colours. A gas flame is chosen over a candle because it burns hot and nearly colourless, so the element's emission is not buried under the yellow glow of incandescent soot.

The wire loop must be made of something that neither melts nor contributes its own colour. Nichrome and platinum both qualify; ordinary galvanised or copper wire does not, because zinc and copper have strong emissions of their own that will simply overwrite the sample. That is also why the acid rinse is essential rather than fussy: a trace of sodium left from a previous test emits so brightly that it swamps almost anything else, and sodium is present as contamination almost everywhere, including on fingertips.

The chosen salts are all chlorides for a reason. Chloride salts are relatively volatile and vaporise readily in the flame, delivering metal atoms into the hot zone efficiently; a carbonate or oxide of the same metal often gives a weak, grudging colour by comparison.

The compact disc is the heart of the spectroscope. Its data track is a spiral of pits spaced roughly 1.6 micrometres apart, close to the wavelength of visible light, so it acts as a genuine diffraction grating and fans white light into its component wavelengths. A DVD's finer 0.74-micrometre spacing spreads the spectrum wider still.

Safety goggles and gloves are not decoration. Hot metal loops, dilute acid and open flame are individually manageable and collectively a reason to work at arm's length over a sink.
ingredients: A periodic table poster or laminated reference card (any school-supply or bookstore) to keep in view while you work.
A butane lighter or kitchen gas stove for flame tests — an adult should supervise, and work outdoors or over a sink.
Nichrome or platinum flame-test wire loops (a cheap classroom set from a science-supply store), or improvise with a length of stainless-steel wire.

A small jar of dilute hydrochloric acid (sold as "muriatic acid" concentrate at hardware stores, diluted per the label) to clean the wire loop between tests, plus safety goggles and nitrile or rubber gloves.

Test salts for flame color: table salt (sodium), a potassium-chloride salt substitute (potassium), a calcium-chloride ice-melt pellet (calcium), and a copper-sulfate root-killer crystal from a hardware or garden store (copper).
An old music CD or DVD, a shoebox, a utility knife, and tape, to build a homemade diffraction-grating spectroscope.
A UV ("black light") flashlight from a hardware or novelty store, to see fluorescence in certain minerals and in tonic water (quinine).
Optional: a basic digital multimeter with a continuity setting, to compare how metals, nonmetals, and their compounds conduct electricity.

sections.heading: Step-by-step: flame tests and a homemade spectroscope
sections.body:
This two-part activity lets you see with your own eyes that different elements emit distinct, characteristic colours and lines of light — the actual evidence behind atomic emission spectra, and the reason the periodic table's structure could be inferred long before anyone understood quantum mechanics.

The mechanism behind every observation here is the same. Heat gives an outer electron enough energy to jump to a higher level, which it holds for only a few nanoseconds before falling back and emitting a photon whose energy exactly equals the gap it fell across. Because the gaps are fixed by the atom's structure, so are the wavelengths, and so are the colours. Sodium's dominant emission at 589 nanometres is the same yellow-orange that older sodium street lamps produced.

Two comparisons make the point. An incandescent bulb shows a continuous rainbow, because hot solid tungsten emits thermally across all wavelengths. A fluorescent tube shows discrete bright lines on a faint background, because the light originates in excited mercury atoms.

The cobalt-blue glass absorbs the yellow band almost completely, so the sodium contamination that ruins potassium tests disappears and the faint lilac beneath becomes visible.
steps: Put on safety goggles and gloves; work outdoors or over a sink with nothing flammable nearby, and tie back long hair.
Dissolve a pinch of each test salt separately in its own small cup with a few drops of water to make a thick paste.
Light the burner. Dip the wire loop into the dilute HCl, then hold it in the flame until it stops adding color — this cleans off contamination from the last test.
Dip the clean loop into the sodium-chloride paste and hold it at the edge of the flame; note the intense yellow-orange color, sodium's 589 nm emission line — the same color as most old streetlights.

Clean the loop in the HCl and flame again, then repeat with the potassium-chloride paste; if you have a piece of cobalt-blue glass, look through it — it filters out sodium contamination and reveals potassium's lilac color underneath.
Repeat the clean-and-test cycle for calcium chloride (brick-red/orange) and copper sulfate (blue-green).
Record each color next to its element on your periodic table — this is literally how 19th-century chemists discovered rubidium and cesium, named for the colors of their spectral lines.

To build the spectroscope, cut a narrow (about 1 mm) slit in one end of a shoebox and a small viewing hole in the other end, angled so a piece of the CD (shiny side up, acting as a diffraction grating) reflects light from the slit toward the hole; tape the CD piece in place at roughly a 30-degree angle.

Point the slit at a fluorescent light, then an incandescent bulb, and (briefly, never at the sun directly) a clear daytime sky, and look through the viewing hole — compare the continuous rainbow from the incandescent bulb to the discrete bright lines from the fluorescent tube.

Repeat the flame tests while looking through the spectroscope instead of with the naked eye; you'll resolve each flame's overall color into individual emission lines, which is how real emission spectroscopy identifies elements.

sections.heading: Electron configuration: beyond shells to subshells
sections.body:
The two-times-n-squared shell rule is a useful simplification for light elements, but the full picture organises electrons into subshells labelled s, p, d and f. These labels are historical abbreviations from spectroscopy — sharp, principal, diffuse, fundamental — and each subshell has a characteristic shape and capacity. An s subshell is spherical and holds 2 electrons; p is dumbbell-shaped, comes as three perpendicular orbitals and holds 6; d has five orbitals and holds 10; f has seven and holds 14. Which subshells exist depends on the shell: shell 1 has only 1s, shell 2 has 2s and 2p, shell 3 adds 3d, shell 4 adds 4f.

Three rules govern the filling. The Aufbau principle, from the German for building-up, says electrons occupy the lowest-energy subshell available. Because shell energies overlap once d subshells appear, the actual order is 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, 5s, 4d and onward — note that 4s fills before 3d, which surprises almost everyone and is the reason potassium and calcium are ordinary reactive metals rather than the first transition metals. The Pauli exclusion principle says no two electrons in an atom may share an identical set of quantum numbers, which caps any single orbital at exactly two electrons with opposite spin. Hund's rule says that within a subshell's set of equal-energy orbitals, electrons occupy them singly with parallel spins before any orbital takes a second, because two electrons sharing one orbital repel each other — much as bus passengers fill empty rows before sharing a seat.

Work iron through. Iron has Z equal to 26, so filling in Aufbau order gives 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d6, and the superscripts sum to 26 as a check. The partly filled 3d subshell, not the 4s, is what varies across the transition metals, and it is what gives iron its magnetism, its multiple oxidation states of plus two and plus three, and its catalytic usefulness. Hund's rule also explains why iron is magnetic at all: unpaired electrons in that 3d subshell each carry a magnetic moment that can align with its neighbours.

Two famous exceptions show that half-filled and completely filled subshells carry extra stability. Chromium is argon-core 4s1 3d5 rather than the predicted 4s2 3d4, and copper is 4s1 3d10 rather than 4s2 3d9. In both cases promoting one 4s electron buys a symmetrical d subshell and lowers the total energy. These are not the only exceptions — palladium, silver, gold and several others deviate too — and the honest summary is that the Aufbau order is an excellent bookkeeping device rather than a physical law. This subshell structure is also exactly what the table's block shapes encode: the s-block on the far left, the p-block on the right, the d-block of transition metals in the centre, and the f-block printed beneath.

sections.heading: Isotopes, radioactivity, and where you meet them every day
sections.body:
An unstable nucleus sheds energy through radioactive decay, converting itself into a different and more stable nucleus. Instability comes down to the balance between the strong nuclear force, which binds nucleons together but acts only over about a femtometre, and electrostatic repulsion between protons, which acts across the whole nucleus. Beyond bismuth, at 83 protons, no combination is stable at all.

Three classic modes cover most cases. Alpha decay ejects a helium nucleus of two protons and two neutrons, dropping the mass number by 4 and the atomic number by 2; alpha particles are stopped by a sheet of paper or the dead outer layer of skin, but are seriously damaging if the source is inhaled or swallowed, which is what made radium dial painting so lethal. Beta decay converts a neutron into a proton while emitting an electron, or the reverse while emitting a positron, shifting atomic number by one with no change in mass number; a few millimetres of aluminium or plastic stops it. Gamma decay releases a high-energy photon with no change in nucleon count at all, usually as a nucleus settles after an alpha or beta event, and needs dense shielding such as lead or thick concrete.

Decay is statistical, not scheduled: no individual nucleus ages, and each simply has a fixed probability of decaying per unit time. Over large numbers this produces an exponential law summarised by half-life, the time for half a sample to decay. After n half-lives the surviving fraction is one half raised to the power n. Carbon-14, with a half-life of 5,730 years, forms continuously in the upper atmosphere as cosmic-ray neutrons strike nitrogen, and living things take it up at the ambient ratio. Once an organism dies, uptake stops and the clock runs. A sample holding 25 per cent of the living ratio has passed two half-lives, giving an age near 11,460 years. The method's honest limits are worth stating: below about 5 per cent remaining, roughly 50,000 years, the signal is too faint, and results need calibration against tree-ring records because atmospheric carbon-14 has not been perfectly constant.

Radioactivity is unexotic. Household ionisation smoke detectors contain a microscopic americium-241 source whose alpha particles ionise air between two plates, letting a tiny current flow that smoke particles interrupt. Hospitals use iodine-131 to treat thyroid disease, exploiting the thyroid's own appetite for iodine, and technetium-99m with its six-hour half-life as an imaging tracer that has largely cleared within a day. Background exposure is constant and unavoidable, from cosmic rays, from radon seeping out of soil and rock, and from potassium-40 in bananas, potatoes and your own muscle tissue. The informal banana equivalent dose is about 0.1 microsieverts, against roughly 3,000 for a single chest CT scan and about 3,000 per year from natural background alone.

guides.title: Chemical Bonds & How Molecules Form
guides.summary: Why atoms stick together, the three main bond types (ionic, covalent, metallic), how to predict molecular shapes, and why bonding explains everything from why salt dissolves to why water is wet.

sections.heading: Why atoms bond at all
sections.body:
A chemical bond is a stable attractive force holding atoms together, and the reason it exists is simpler than the arithmetic that describes it. Atoms bond because the bonded arrangement has lower total energy than the separated atoms. Nature moves toward lower energy the way a ball rolls downhill, and the surplus energy is released — usually as heat, sometimes as light. That release is not a metaphor. Two hydrogen atoms joining into H2 shed about 436 kilojoules per mole, and the same accounting run in reverse says that pulling H2 apart again costs exactly that much.

The physics underneath is electrostatic and has two competing terms. As two atoms approach, each nucleus begins to attract the other's electrons, which lowers the energy. But the two positively charged nuclei also repel each other, and the electron clouds repel each other, which raises it. The two terms scale differently with distance, so there is one separation where the total is at a minimum. That distance is the bond length, and the depth of the minimum is the bond energy. Push the atoms closer than the minimum and they resist hard; pull them apart and they pull back. A bond is not glue — it is a balance point in a potential-energy well, which is why bonds behave like stiff springs and molecules genuinely vibrate.

The electrons doing this work are the outermost ones, called valence electrons. The octet rule captures what they are steering toward: most atoms are most stable holding eight valence electrons, the configuration of the noble gases, which almost never bond because they already have it. Hydrogen and helium are the exceptions, since their single first shell holds only two, so they aim for a duet instead. The rule is a reliable guide for the first two rows of the periodic table and a rougher one beyond it — boron is content with six electrons, sulfur and phosphorus routinely exceed eight, and any molecule with an odd number of electrons breaks the rule by arithmetic necessity.

Atoms reach a stable arrangement by three strategies, and those three strategies are the three bond types. Electrons can be transferred outright from one atom to another, giving an ionic bond. They can be shared between two atoms, giving a covalent bond. Or they can be pooled collectively among many atoms at once, giving a metallic bond. These are not sharp categories but the corners of a continuum, and most real bonds sit somewhere between two of them.

Bonds form and break in every chemical reaction — in a campfire, in a battery, and in every cell of your body at this moment. Understanding them is understanding why matter behaves as it does.

sections.heading: Ionic bonds: giving and taking electrons
sections.body:
An ionic bond forms when one atom transfers electrons to another outright, and the resulting oppositely charged ions attract. It happens between a metal, which has low electronegativity and gives up electrons readily, and a nonmetal, which has high electronegativity and takes them. A useful rule of thumb on the Pauling scale is that an electronegativity difference above about 1.7 gives a predominantly ionic bond, though the threshold is a convention rather than a natural boundary — bonding is a continuum, and even sodium chloride retains a few per cent of covalent character.

Sodium chloride is the standard worked case. Sodium has one valence electron, and shedding it leaves a full underlying shell, producing Na+. Chlorine has seven valence electrons, and gaining one completes its shell, producing Cl-. The two ions attract electrostatically, but they do not pair off. Each sodium ion surrounds itself with six chlorides and each chloride with six sodiums, building a rigid repeating three-dimensional lattice extending through the whole crystal. There is no such thing as an NaCl molecule in a salt grain; the formula states the simplest whole-number ratio, not a particle.

Every characteristic property follows from that lattice of charges. Melting points are high — sodium chloride melts at 801 degrees Celsius and boils at 1,465 — because melting requires breaking a vast network of electrostatic attractions at once, not just separating pairs. Charge magnitude matters more than any other variable here: magnesium oxide, built from 2+ and 2- ions, melts at 2,852 degrees because doubling both charges roughly quadruples the attraction, which is precisely why magnesium oxide lines furnaces.

Ionic solids are hard but brittle, and the brittleness is the more revealing property. Struck sharply, one plane of the lattice slides by one ion-width, which brings like charges into alignment; the crystal that a moment earlier was held together by attraction is now driven apart by repulsion, and it cleaves along a flat plane. This is why salt and quartz shatter along clean faces while copper merely dents.

Conduction is the diagnostic test. A solid ionic compound does not conduct electricity, because its ions are locked in place with no mobile charge carriers. Melt it, or dissolve it in water, and it conducts well, because the ions are then free to migrate toward opposite electrodes. Many ionic compounds dissolve readily in water because polar water molecules cluster around each ion, oxygen ends toward the cations and hydrogen ends toward the anions, and the energy released by that hydration pays for the energy needed to dismantle the lattice. When it does not pay — as for calcium carbonate or barium sulfate — the compound is essentially insoluble, which is why limestone survives rain and why barium sulfate is safe to swallow before an X-ray.

sections.heading: Covalent bonds: sharing electrons
sections.body:
A covalent bond forms when two atoms share a pair of electrons, each contributing one. It occurs between nonmetals with similar and generally high electronegativities: neither atom can take electrons outright from the other, so they compromise. The shared pair occupies the region between the two nuclei, and because both positively charged nuclei are attracted to the same concentration of negative charge, they are held together through it. This is why a covalent bond is directional in a way an ionic bond is not, and why covalent substances form discrete molecules with definite shapes rather than open-ended lattices.

Sharing can be multiplied. A single bond is one shared pair, two electrons, as in the H-H bond of hydrogen gas. A double bond is two shared pairs, four electrons, as in the O=O of oxygen gas; it is both stronger and shorter than a single bond, because more shared electron density between the nuclei pulls them closer. A triple bond is three shared pairs, six electrons, as in the N-to-N bond of nitrogen gas, and it is formidable: 941 kilojoules per mole, with the two atoms drawn to just 110 picometres apart. That single number explains why the atmosphere is 78 per cent nitrogen yet almost nothing can use it, why lightning and specialised bacteria are the natural routes to fixing it, and why the industrial Haber process needs roughly 450 degrees Celsius, 200 atmospheres and an iron catalyst to do the same job.

Water is the worked example. Oxygen has six valence electrons and needs two more. It shares one pair with each of two hydrogen atoms, which gives oxygen its octet and each hydrogen its duet. The product is a discrete molecule: a fixed, countable group of atoms held together internally by covalent bonds, existing as an individual particle in a way an ionic formula unit never does.

The properties follow. Molecular covalent substances usually melt and boil at low temperatures, because heating them does not break the covalent bonds at all — it only overcomes the much weaker attractions between separate molecules. Water boils at 100 degrees while its O-H bonds survive intact to well above 2,000. They rarely conduct electricity, having no free charges. And they span every state at room temperature, from gases such as carbon dioxide and oxygen to liquids such as water and ethanol to soft solids such as sugar and wax.

The important exception is the covalent network solid, where covalent bonds extend continuously through the entire sample instead of stopping at a molecular boundary. Diamond and quartz are the classic cases, and they are extraordinarily hard with melting points above 1,700 degrees, because melting them means breaking real covalent bonds by the mole.

sections.heading: Polar bonds and why water is special
sections.body:
When two atoms in a covalent bond have different electronegativities, the shared electrons spend more time near the greedier atom. That atom acquires a small negative charge, written delta minus, and its partner an equal small positive charge, delta plus. The symbol delta simply means a partial amount — a fraction of an electron's charge, not a whole one. Such a bond is polar covalent, and it has a dipole: a separation of charge along its length with a definite direction.

Water is the case worth knowing in detail. Oxygen's electronegativity is 3.44 and hydrogen's is 2.20, a difference of 1.24, so each O-H bond is distinctly polar with oxygen negative and hydrogen positive. Crucially, the water molecule is bent rather than straight, with an H-O-H angle near 104.5 degrees, so the two bond dipoles do not point in opposite directions and cannot cancel. They add to give the whole molecule a substantial net dipole. Molecular shape, not bond polarity alone, decides whether a molecule is polar — and carbon dioxide proves it, since its two strongly polar C=O bonds point exactly opposite along a straight line and cancel to nothing.

Two large consequences follow from water's polarity. The first is its power as a solvent. Like dissolves like: the negatively charged oxygen ends cluster around positive ions and the positive hydrogen ends around negative ions, wrapping each in a hydration shell and prising the crystal apart ion by ion. Water is called the universal solvent, which overstates it — it dissolves polar and ionic substances well and nonpolar ones hardly at all — but its range is genuinely exceptional.

The second is hydrogen bonding. The positive hydrogen of one water molecule is attracted to a lone pair on the negative oxygen of a neighbour. Each such link is weak, roughly 20 kilojoules per mole against about 460 for the covalent O-H bond, but each molecule can form up to four of them and their collective effect is enormous. Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius where comparable molecules of similar mass boil far below zero; hydrogen sulfide, chemically water's near-twin and heavier, boils at minus 60. Hydrogen bonding also gives water its high surface tension, strong enough to support a pond skater, and its high heat capacity, which moderates climates and body temperature alike. Most consequentially, it makes ice less dense than liquid water: freezing locks each molecule into four rigid, evenly spaced hydrogen bonds, forcing an open hexagonal lattice about 9 per cent less dense than the liquid. Ice therefore floats, lakes freeze from the top down, and life beneath survives the winter.

Where electronegativities match closely, as in O2 or a C-H bond, sharing is even and the bond is nonpolar — which is why oil and water refuse to mix.

sections.heading: Molecular shape: VSEPR theory
sections.body:
Molecules are three-dimensional objects, and shape controls behaviour at least as much as composition does. VSEPR theory — valence shell electron pair repulsion — predicts that shape from one idea: regions of electron density around a central atom repel one another and arrange themselves as far apart as geometry allows.

The counting rule is deliberately crude and works remarkably well. Count electron groups around the central atom, where every bond counts as one group regardless of whether it is single, double or triple, and every lone pair counts as one group as well. A double bond holds twice the electrons but occupies one direction in space, which is why bond order does not enter the count.

Two groups spread to 180 degrees, giving a linear molecule. Carbon dioxide is the example, drawn O=C=O in a straight line, and its geometry is why it is nonpolar overall despite two strongly polar bonds — the dipoles point in exactly opposite directions and sum to zero. Three groups spread to 120 degrees in a flat triangle, trigonal planar, as in boron trifluoride. Four groups cannot spread evenly in a plane; the maximum separation puts them at the corners of a tetrahedron, 109.5 degrees apart, which is methane's shape and the reason carbon chemistry is three-dimensional rather than flat.

Lone pairs are where the theory earns its keep. A lone pair is held by only one nucleus rather than shared between two, so its electron cloud is fatter and closer in, and it repels neighbouring groups more strongly than a bonding pair does. The electron groups still adopt the predicted arrangement, but the shape you can actually see — defined by the atomic positions — is squeezed. Water has four groups on oxygen, two bonds and two lone pairs, so the electron geometry is tetrahedral but the molecular shape is bent, with the H-O-H angle compressed from 109.5 to about 104.5 degrees. That compression is precisely why water's bond dipoles fail to cancel and why water is polar at all. Ammonia has three bonds and one lone pair, giving a trigonal pyramidal shape at about 107 degrees — one lone pair, one degree of compression less.

Same atoms differently arranged behave completely differently. Carbon dioxide, linear and nonpolar, is a gas you exhale; water, bent and polar, is the solvent of life. In biology the stakes rise further: enzymes recognise substrates by shape, and two molecules identical in formula but mirror-imaged in three dimensions can be a drug and a poison.

VSEPR's honest limits are worth stating. It predicts approximate geometry, not exact angles, ignores the size of the attached atoms, and gives no reliable account of transition-metal complexes, where partly filled d subshells impose their own preferences.

sections.heading: Metallic bonds and intermolecular forces
sections.body:
Metallic bonding explains metals with a single picture. Each atom releases its loosely held valence electrons into a shared sea of delocalised electrons that moves freely through a rigid array of fixed positive ions. No electron belongs to any particular atom, and the whole crystal is held together by the attraction between the positive lattice and the negative sea.

Every classic metal property drops out of that model. Electrical conductivity follows because mobile electrons carry charge the instant a voltage is applied — copper's conductivity comes from roughly ten to the twenty-eight free electrons per cubic metre. Thermal conductivity follows because the same electrons carry kinetic energy, which is why a metal spoon feels cold: it is conducting heat out of your hand far faster than wood can. Lustre follows because the free electron sea reflects incident light across the visible range.

Malleability and ductility are the properties that most sharply separate metals from ionic solids, and the reason is structural. When a metal is struck, layers of ions slide past one another, but because the electron sea is not directional and simply flows with them, the bonding survives the rearrangement and the metal deforms. An ionic crystal struck the same way brings like charges into contact and shatters. Alloying works by disrupting that sliding: carbon atoms wedged into iron's lattice pin the layers in place, which is the whole basis of steel.

Bond strength varies enormously across metals — sodium melts at 98 degrees Celsius with one valence electron per atom, tungsten at 3,422 with six — which shows the sea model is describing a real, tunable attraction rather than a vague one.

Intermolecular forces are an entirely different and much weaker category: attractions between separate molecules, not within them. They set the melting and boiling points of molecular substances, and they come in three strengths. London dispersion forces exist in every molecule and arise from fleeting, random imbalances in the electron cloud that induce matching imbalances in a neighbour; they strengthen with molecular size and surface area, which is why methane is a gas, octane a liquid and candle wax a solid despite all three being hydrocarbons. Dipole-dipole forces act between permanently polar molecules, the positive end of one drawn to the negative end of another. Hydrogen bonds are a particularly strong dipole interaction available only when hydrogen is bonded directly to nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine, and at roughly 5 to 30 kilojoules per mole they are the strongest of the three — the reason water is liquid at room temperature, the reason DNA's two strands hold together yet can be unzipped by an enzyme, and the reason proteins fold into working shapes.

Boiling water breaks hydrogen bonds only. Every O-H covalent bond survives the kettle intact.

sections.heading: Practical applications, mistakes, and safety
sections.body:
Bonding theory earns its place because it predicts real behaviour. Soap works because each molecule carries a long nonpolar hydrocarbon tail that mixes happily with grease and a polar or ionic head that mixes happily with water; the molecules assemble into micelles with tails inward around a droplet of oil and heads outward facing the water, so the grease is carried away suspended rather than dissolved. Non-stick cookware uses polytetrafluoroethylene, whose C-F bonds are among the strongest in organic chemistry at about 485 kilojoules per mole and whose fluorine atoms hold their electrons so tightly that the surface has almost no attraction to offer anything else — the coating is not slippery so much as chemically uninterested.

Carbon makes the point about bonding arrangement most vividly. In diamond every carbon is covalently bonded to four others in a rigid three-dimensional network, giving the hardest natural material known. In graphite the same element bonds to three neighbours in flat sheets held to each other only by weak dispersion forces, so the sheets slide and the material works as a lubricant and as pencil lead. Same atoms, different bonding, opposite properties.

Three mistakes recur. The first is confusing bonds within a molecule with forces between molecules. Boiling water breaks intermolecular hydrogen bonds and leaves every covalent O-H bond untouched; if boiling really broke covalent bonds, steam would be a mixture of hydrogen and oxygen and kettles would be bombs. The second is assuming that polar bonds guarantee a polar molecule. Shape decides it: carbon dioxide has two strongly polar bonds pointing exactly opposite along a straight line, so they cancel and the molecule is nonpolar, which is why it does not dissolve in water nearly as well as its bond polarity suggests. The third is calling ionic compounds molecules. Sodium chloride is an extended lattice, and its formula states the simplest whole-number ratio of ions, not a two-atom particle — there is no individual NaCl unit to point at inside a salt crystal.

On safety, the same energetics that make bonding useful make it hazardous. Forming bonds releases energy, and a reaction that forms strong bonds from weak ones can release it faster than the surroundings absorb it, producing boiling, spattering or worse. Never mix household cleaning products: bleach with ammonia produces chloramine vapours, and bleach with an acidic descaler produces chlorine gas, both of which have killed people in ordinary bathrooms. Concentrated acid must always be added to water and never the reverse, because the heat of dilution released at the point of contact can flash the first drops to steam and eject acid from the vessel. The mnemonic is that you should do as you oughta and add the acid to the water, and it is worth memorising precisely because the intuitive order is the dangerous one.

sections.heading: Equipment for exploring bonds at home
sections.body:
Ionic, covalent and polar substances can be told apart physically with nothing more exotic than a battery, an LED and a few kitchen staples. These are simplified versions of genuine qualitative-analysis techniques, and knowing why each item is on the list matters more than owning any of it.

The model kit exists because molecular shape is a three-dimensional fact that flat diagrams misrepresent. Holding a tetrahedral carbon and trying to force its four bonds into a plane demonstrates in seconds what a paragraph struggles to convey, and the compression of water's angle by its lone pairs becomes obvious once you have built the thing.

Salt and sugar are chosen as a matched pair because they defeat appearances. Both are white crystalline solids that dissolve in water, and no amount of looking distinguishes them. Their behaviour in the conductivity test separates them absolutely, which is the point: a property test beats an appearance test every time.

The conductivity tester's resistor is not optional. An LED has almost no internal resistance once it conducts, so connecting it directly across nine volts passes far more current than its junction tolerates and destroys it, usually within a second. A resistor of 470 to 1,000 ohms limits the current to roughly 10 to 20 milliamps, which is bright and survivable. Stainless steel or graphite electrodes are specified because they resist corroding in salt solution; ordinary steel or copper will oxidise and drift during the test.

Distilled water alongside tap water is a control, not a redundancy. Tap water carries dissolved calcium, magnesium and bicarbonate ions in the tens to hundreds of milligrams per litre, and those ions conduct. Testing sugar in tap water produces a glow that has nothing to do with the sugar, and without the distilled comparison you would draw exactly the wrong conclusion.

The oil, water and food colouring demonstrate miscibility. Colouring is added because pure water and pale oil look similar in a jar, and the dye — being itself polar — stays in the water layer and marks the boundary unambiguously.

The balloon or comb works by triboelectric charging: rubbing transfers electrons and leaves a static charge strong enough to reorient polar water molecules in a falling stream and pull it visibly sideways.
ingredients: A ball-and-stick molecular model kit (an inexpensive plastic kit from a hobby, bookstore, or school-supply retailer) for building VSEPR shapes by hand.
Table salt (an ionic solid) and table sugar (a covalent molecular solid), for side-by-side comparison.

A 9-volt battery, two insulated wires with alligator clips, two stainless-steel nails or pencil-graphite electrodes, a small LED, and a 470–1,000 ohm resistor (inexpensive parts from an electronics/hobby store) to build a homemade conductivity tester — the resistor keeps the LED from burning out.
Distilled water AND tap water, to control for dissolved minerals confounding the conductivity test.
Vegetable oil and food coloring (to color a cup of water), for a polarity/miscibility demonstration.
A balloon or a plastic comb, for a quick static-charge polarity demo with a thin stream of tap water.
A kitchen scale accurate to about 1 gram, if you want to test conductivity at different concentrations.

sections.heading: Step-by-step: conductivity and solubility tests to distinguish bond types
sections.body:
This sequence builds a simple conductivity tester and, alongside two quick polarity demonstrations, uses it to tell ionic, covalent and polar substances apart. The results are only meaningful if you know what the lamp is reporting.

An electric current through a liquid requires mobile charge carriers. Metals supply free electrons; solutions must supply free ions. When an ionic solid dissolves, its lattice dissociates into separate charged particles that drift toward opposite electrodes and carry current. When a molecular solid such as sucrose dissolves, its molecules separate but remain intact and uncharged, so nothing carries current and the lamp stays dark. The test does not measure solubility at all — both substances dissolve perfectly well — it measures whether dissolving produced ions.

Pure water self-ionises only faintly, about one molecule in 550 million, giving a hydrogen-ion concentration near ten to the minus seven moles per litre — real, but far too small to light an LED. That is why distilled water is the correct baseline, and why a glow from it signals contamination.

Rinsing the electrodes between tests matters. A film of salt solution carried into the sugar cup will light the lamp and invert your result.
steps: Build the tester: connect one battery terminal directly to one electrode; connect the other terminal to the LED's long (positive) leg through the resistor and a wire; connect the LED's short leg to the second electrode. Keep the two electrodes about 2 cm apart, not touching.

Test distilled water alone by dipping both electrodes in a cup of it, not touching each other. The LED should stay dark or barely glow — pure water ionizes only slightly (about 1×10⁻⁷ M H⁺), far too little current to light it.
Dissolve a level teaspoon of table salt into the water, stir, and retest. The LED should light clearly: dissolved NaCl fully dissociates into mobile Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions that carry current.

Rinse the electrodes, refill with fresh distilled water, dissolve a level teaspoon of table sugar (sucrose), and retest. The LED should stay dark — sucrose dissolves as intact, uncharged covalent molecules with no free charge carriers.

For the polarity demo, turn on a thin, steady stream of water from a faucet, charge a balloon or comb by rubbing it on your hair for 10–15 seconds, then bring it close (not touching) to the stream. The stream bends toward the charged object — the water molecule's bent shape gives it an uneven, polar charge distribution that responds to an external field.

For the oil-and-water demo, pour water and vegetable oil into a clear jar, add a drop of food coloring, shake vigorously, and let it sit. The layers separate within seconds to a minute: polar water molecules hydrogen-bond to each other and exclude the nonpolar oil, the same principle behind soap's cleaning action and cell membranes.

Build a water molecule (or methane or ammonia) with the model kit, following the VSEPR electron-domain count for the central atom, and compare the bond angle you produce to the accepted value (104.5° for water) to see how lone-pair repulsion compresses the ideal tetrahedral angle.

sections.heading: Bond energy, bond length, and reaction energetics
sections.body:
Every bond has a characteristic bond energy, formally the bond dissociation energy: the energy needed to break one mole of that bond in the gas phase, quoted in kilojoules per mole. Bond energy rises with bond order and falls with bond length, and the two trends are the same fact seen twice — more shared electron density between two nuclei pulls them closer together and holds them more tightly.

Representative values make the pattern concrete. A carbon-hydrogen bond takes about 413 kilojoules per mole, an oxygen-hydrogen bond about 467. Within the carbon-carbon series the progression is unmistakable: a single bond is 347 kilojoules per mole at a length of 154 picometres, a double bond 614 at 134 picometres, a triple bond 839 at 120 picometres. Note that a double bond is not twice a single one, because the second bond is formed from sideways overlap that is less effective than the first — which is precisely why double bonds are reactive and single bonds are not. Nitrogen's triple bond stands at 941 kilojoules per mole, the strongest common bond in ordinary chemistry, and that single figure explains why atmospheric nitrogen is inert and why the Haber process needs 450 degrees Celsius, 200 atmospheres and an iron catalyst to break it into ammonia. At the other extreme, the chlorine-chlorine bond is only 242, which is why chlorine gas is so eager to react.

Breaking bonds always costs energy, because you are pulling apart particles that attract each other; forming bonds always releases it, because the atoms settle into a deeper energy well. Every reaction does both, and the net is the reaction's enthalpy change. The estimate is the sum of the bond energies broken minus the sum of those formed. A negative result means net energy released, an exothermic reaction; positive means energy absorbed, endothermic.

Work methane combustion through. For CH4 plus 2 O2 giving CO2 plus 2 H2O, the bonds broken are four C-H at 413 each, totalling 1,652, and two O=O at 498 each, totalling 996 — an input of 2,648 kilojoules per mole. The bonds formed are two C=O in carbon dioxide at 799 each, totalling 1,598, and four O-H across two water molecules at 467 each, totalling 1,868 — an output of 3,466. The difference is minus 818 kilojoules per mole, strongly exothermic, which is consistent with methane being an excellent fuel.

Two caveats are genuine. Tabulated bond energies are averages across many compounds, so this method typically lands within about 5 per cent of the measured value rather than matching it, and it applies strictly to gases, ignoring the energy of condensing the water. It is the same bookkeeping, less formally scaled, that underlies calorie counts on food labels.

sections.heading: Resonance and delocalization: when one structure isn't enough
sections.body:
Some molecules and ions cannot be drawn accurately with a single Lewis dot-and-line structure, because the real electron arrangement is a blend of more than one valid drawing. This is resonance, and the individual drawings are resonance structures. The single most important thing to get right is that the molecule does not flicker between them. A resonance hybrid is one fixed structure that is the average of the contributors, the way a mule is not an animal alternating between horse and donkey.

Ozone is the classic case. You can draw the central oxygen double-bonded to one outer oxygen and single-bonded to the other, or the mirror image, and there is no reason to prefer either. Experiment settles it: both O-O bonds are identical, measuring 128 picometres, intermediate between a normal single bond at 148 and a double bond at 121. The extra electron pair is delocalised, spread across both positions rather than confined to one.

The carbonate ion shows the same behaviour with three equivalent contributors, the double bond notionally occupying each of the three C-O positions in turn. The result is three identical bonds of intermediate length and a flat, symmetric triangular ion — which is exactly the shape that stacks so regularly in calcite, the mineral form of calcium carbonate that builds limestone, chalk and seashells.

The most consequential real case is benzene, six carbons in a ring, conventionally drawn with alternating single and double bonds. All six carbon-carbon bonds in fact measure 139 picometres, uniformly between a single bond at 154 and a double at 134, because six electrons are delocalised into a continuous ring-shaped cloud above and below the plane of the ring. Delocalisation lowers the molecule's energy substantially: benzene sits roughly 150 kilojoules per mole below a hypothetical molecule with three isolated double bonds, an amount called the aromatic stabilisation energy. The chemical consequence is dramatic. An ordinary alkene readily adds bromine across its double bond, decolourising the reagent in seconds; benzene does not, because addition would destroy the delocalised ring and forfeit that stabilisation. Instead benzene undergoes substitution, replacing a hydrogen and keeping the ring intact.

That resistance is why aromatic rings appear as the durable scaffold of an enormous fraction of useful molecules — aspirin, paracetamol, most dyes, polystyrene, Kevlar, and the bases of DNA. It also carries a warning: the same stability that makes aromatic compounds useful makes several of them persistent in the environment and in the body, and benzene itself is a recognised human carcinogen precisely because it is stable enough to circulate and be metabolised into reactive intermediates rather than being disposed of promptly. Stability and safety are different properties, and resonance delivers only the first of them.

guides.title: Chemical Reactions, Equations & Stoichiometry
guides.summary: How to read and balance chemical equations, the major reaction types, the mole concept, and how to calculate exactly how much reactant you need and product you get — the arithmetic of chemistry.

sections.heading: What a chemical reaction is
sections.body:
A chemical reaction is a process in which one set of substances, called the reactants, is turned into a different set of substances, called the products, by breaking existing chemical bonds and forming new ones. The atoms themselves survive unchanged; only their partnerships are rearranged. That constraint is the law of conservation of mass, stated by Antoine Lavoisier in 1789 after he weighed sealed vessels before and after burning things inside them: the total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products, to the limit of your balance. Combustion appears to destroy mass only because the carbon dioxide and water vapour drift away; capture them and the books balance to within a fraction of a percent. Burning 1.00 kg of methane, for instance, consumes 4.00 kg of oxygen and yields exactly 5.00 kg of carbon dioxide and water combined.

Distinguishing a chemical change from a merely physical one is the first practical skill. Melting ice, dissolving sugar, and boiling water are physical changes: the substance is still water or still sugar, and you can recover it unchanged by cooling or evaporating. A chemical change produces something genuinely new, and it usually announces itself. A colour appears or vanishes, as when grey iron becomes red-brown rust. A gas evolves, so the mixture fizzes, as vinegar does the instant it meets baking soda. A solid precipitate drops out of two liquids that were both clear. The temperature shifts noticeably without any heater involved. Light or sound is emitted, as in a struck match. None of these signs is individually conclusive — boiling also makes bubbles, and dissolving ammonium nitrate cools water sharply without any bond-breaking beyond the crystal lattice — so the honest test is whether the original substance can be recovered by a purely physical means such as filtering, evaporating, or freezing. If it can, the change was physical.

Every reaction also moves energy. An exothermic reaction releases energy to its surroundings, almost always as heat, because the bonds in the products are collectively stronger and therefore lower in stored chemical energy than the bonds in the reactants. Combustion, respiration, rusting, and the iron-oxidation hand-warmer in a winter glove are all exothermic. An endothermic reaction absorbs energy, because the products store more than the reactants did; photosynthesis, the thermal cracking of hydrocarbons, and the ammonium-nitrate instant cold pack that drops to near 2 degrees Celsius are the standard examples. Direction of energy flow is separate from ease of starting, though. Nearly every reaction, exothermic ones included, must first climb an activation-energy barrier: a minimum energy the colliding particles need before old bonds will break at all. That is why a petrol-air mixture, which will release roughly 44 kilojoules per gram once lit, sits inertly in a jar until a spark supplies the initial push.

sections.heading: Reading and balancing equations
sections.body:
A chemical equation is a sentence written in formulas. Reactants sit on the left, products on the right, and the arrow reads as yields or produces. Burning natural gas is written CH4 + 2 O2 -> CO2 + 2 H2O, and every symbol in that line carries a specific meaning. The large number in front of a formula is a coefficient, and it counts how many of that whole molecule take part: the 2 before O2 means two oxygen molecules. The small number tucked below and after an element symbol is a subscript, and it counts atoms inside a single molecule: the 4 in CH4 means one carbon bonded to four hydrogens. A coefficient multiplies everything in the formula that follows it, so 2 H2O contains four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms in total. Letters in brackets are state symbols, telling you what physical form each substance is in: (s) for solid, (l) for pure liquid, (g) for gas, and (aq) for aqueous, meaning dissolved in water. State symbols are not decoration. Whether silver chloride is written AgCl(s) or AgCl(aq) is the difference between a precipitate you can filter and a solution you cannot.

Because atoms are conserved, an equation is only correct when it is balanced, meaning each element appears in the same total number on both sides. Balancing is done by adjusting coefficients and by nothing else. Changing a subscript is not a mathematical fix but a substitution of one substance for another: H2O is water and H2O2 is hydrogen peroxide, a bleaching agent that decomposes on contact with blood. Beginners reach for subscripts because it makes the arithmetic collapse instantly, and it is the single most common way to produce a confidently wrong answer.

Work an example slowly. Start from H2 + O2 -> H2O. Counting gives two hydrogen and two oxygen on the left, but two hydrogen and only one oxygen on the right, so oxygen is short. Placing a 2 in front of water gives H2 + O2 -> 2 H2O, which now has four hydrogen and two oxygen on the right, so hydrogen has gone out of balance in the other direction. Placing a 2 in front of hydrogen gives 2 H2 + O2 -> 2 H2O, which has four hydrogen and two oxygen on each side. That is the balanced equation, and no smaller whole-number set works.

Three habits make this fast. Balance the most complicated molecule first and leave elements that appear alone, such as O2 or Na, until last, because a lone element can absorb any leftover imbalance without disturbing anything else. Treat a polyatomic ion such as sulfate or nitrate that survives intact on both sides as a single unit rather than balancing its atoms separately. And if a fraction such as one half is needed to make it work, accept it temporarily, then multiply every coefficient in the equation by two to clear it, since coefficients are conventionally whole numbers in their lowest ratio.

sections.heading: The major reaction types
sections.body:
Chemistry contains an unlimited number of specific reactions but only a handful of recurring shapes, and recognising the shape lets you predict products for a reaction you have never seen. Synthesis, also called combination, takes the form of two or more simple substances joining into one more complex one, as when sodium metal burns in chlorine gas to give table salt, 2 Na + Cl2 -> 2 NaCl. Decomposition is the exact reverse, one compound splitting into simpler pieces, usually driven by heat, light, or a catalyst. Hydrogen peroxide steadily decomposes to water and oxygen, 2 H2O2 -> 2 H2O + O2, which is why the drugstore bottle is opaque brown and why an old bottle no longer fizzes on a cut. Heating limestone above roughly 825 degrees Celsius decomposes calcium carbonate to quicklime and carbon dioxide, the reaction on which the entire cement industry rests.

Single replacement has one element displacing another out of a compound, following the general shape A plus BC yielding AC plus B. Dropping zinc into hydrochloric acid gives Zn + 2 HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2, with hydrogen bubbling off because zinc is the more reactive metal. Whether such a reaction happens at all is governed by the activity series, an experimentally determined ranking of metals: a metal displaces any metal below it and none above it, which is why copper wire in zinc sulfate solution does nothing while zinc in copper sulfate plates out visible copper within minutes. Double replacement has two dissolved compounds swapping partners, AB plus CD yielding AD plus CB, and it proceeds only when one of the new pairings leaves the solution as an insoluble precipitate, an escaping gas, or water. Mixing silver nitrate with sodium chloride gives AgNO3 + NaCl -> AgCl + NaNO3, and the silver chloride drops out immediately as a curdy white solid.

Combustion is the rapid reaction of a fuel with oxygen. Complete combustion of any hydrocarbon gives carbon dioxide and water plus a large release of heat, as in propane in a camp stove, C3H8 + 5 O2 -> 3 CO2 + 4 H2O. Incomplete combustion, when oxygen is short, gives carbon monoxide and soot instead, which is the mechanism behind every fatal poisoning from an unvented heater or a generator run indoors. Neutralisation is an acid meeting a base to give a salt and water, such as HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O.

Cutting across several of these is the redox category, defined not by what visibly happens but by where the electrons go. Oxidation is loss of electrons, reduction is gain, and the two always occur together because electrons cannot simply vanish. The mnemonic OIL RIG, for oxidation is loss and reduction is gain, is worth memorising once. Rusting, every battery, cellular respiration, photosynthesis, and all combustion are redox processes, which is why redox is often treated as the most consequential reaction class of all.

sections.heading: The mole: chemistry's counting unit
sections.body:
Atoms are far too small and far too numerous to count one at a time, so chemistry uses a counting unit called the mole, which functions exactly the way a dozen or a ream does. One mole is Avogadro's number of particles, 6.022 times ten to the twenty-third, written out as roughly six hundred and two thousand billion billion. You can have a mole of atoms, a mole of molecules, a mole of ions, or a mole of electrons, but you must say which, because a mole of water molecules contains three moles of atoms. Since 2019 the mole is defined by fixing that number exactly at 6.02214076 times ten to the twenty-third, rather than by reference to a sample of carbon, so the constant is now a definition rather than a measurement.

The reason chemists tolerate such an unwieldy number is that it was deliberately chosen to make the atomic mass scale line up with the gram. One mole of any element has a mass in grams numerically equal to its atomic mass in the periodic table. Carbon's atomic mass is 12.01, so 12.01 grams of carbon is one mole and contains 6.022 times ten to the twenty-third atoms. This quantity is the molar mass, symbol M, in units of grams per mole. For a compound you simply add up the molar masses of every atom in the formula. Water is two hydrogens at 1.008 plus one oxygen at 16.00, giving 18.02 grams per mole, which means a single mole of water is a little over a tablespoon and weighs about the same as a large paperclip and a half. Sodium chloride is 22.99 plus 35.45, giving 58.44 grams per mole, so roughly a level tablespoon of table salt is close to one mole.

The single equation that connects the weighable world to the countable one is that the number of moles equals the mass in grams divided by the molar mass in grams per mole, usually written n equals m over M. Rearranged, mass equals moles times molar mass, and number of particles equals moles times Avogadro's number. These three relationships handle almost every quantitative problem in introductory chemistry.

A worked example fixes the method. Asked how many moles are in 50.0 grams of table salt, first compute the molar mass of sodium chloride as 58.44 grams per mole, then divide: 50.0 divided by 58.44 is 0.856 moles. Multiplying by Avogadro's number gives about 5.15 times ten to the twenty-third formula units, and because each unit contributes one sodium ion and one chloride ion, that is 0.856 moles of each ion. Two cautions save trouble. Molar mass depends on the exact formula, so the hydrated crystal copper sulfate pentahydrate weighs 249.7 grams per mole against 159.6 for the anhydrous form, an error of over fifty percent if you use the wrong one. And for gases at standard conditions, one mole occupies about 22.4 litres, which lets you convert volume directly to moles without weighing anything.

sections.heading: Stoichiometry: calculating amounts
sections.body:
Stoichiometry, pronounced stoy-kee-OM-etry, is the arithmetic that turns a balanced equation into a prediction of how much. Its entire foundation is that the coefficients in a balanced equation are ratios of moles, not of grams and not of volumes. In 2 H2 + O2 -> 2 H2O, the numbers say that two moles of hydrogen react with one mole of oxygen to give two moles of water. They emphatically do not say that two grams of hydrogen react with one gram of oxygen, because a mole of oxygen weighs sixteen times what a mole of hydrogen does. Every mass-to-mass calculation therefore has the same three-stage shape: convert out of grams into moles, apply the mole ratio, then convert back from moles into grams. Some people picture it as a bridge, with grams on each bank and the mole ratio as the only span across.

The full procedure runs as follows. Write the equation and balance it, because an unbalanced equation gives a wrong ratio and therefore a wrong answer no matter how careful the rest of the arithmetic is. Convert the known mass to moles by dividing by that substance's molar mass. Multiply by the ratio of the target substance's coefficient to the known substance's coefficient. Finally multiply by the target's molar mass to return to grams.

Consider burning 8.0 grams of hydrogen in ample oxygen. The balanced equation is 2 H2 + O2 -> 2 H2O. Hydrogen gas has a molar mass of 2.016 grams per mole, so 8.0 divided by 2.016 gives 3.97 moles of H2. The coefficients for hydrogen and water are both 2, a one-to-one ratio, so 3.97 moles of hydrogen produce 3.97 moles of water. Water's molar mass is 18.02 grams per mole, so the product mass is 3.97 times 18.02, or about 71.5 grams. Eight grams of fuel has become seventy-one grams of water, and the extra sixty-three grams is precisely the oxygen that combined in, which the same calculation confirms: 1.98 moles of O2 at 32.00 grams per mole is 63.5 grams.

Reality intrudes through the limiting reagent. Reactants are rarely supplied in the exact ratio the equation demands, and the moment one of them is exhausted the reaction stops regardless of how much of the others remains. That exhausted substance is the limiting reagent, and it alone sets the maximum possible product; the others are said to be in excess. The reliable way to identify it is not to compare masses or even moles directly, since the coefficients differ, but to calculate how much product each reactant could make on its own and take the smaller answer.
