The molar mass is the master conversion factor of quantitative chemistry: dividing a measured mass in grams by the molar mass gives the number of moles, and multiplying moles by molar mass returns the mass. This relationship, moles equal mass divided by molar mass, is used constantly in formula determination, because the whole procedure hinges on converting the measured mass of each element in a sample into moles, since only in moles do the elements stand in the same ratio as their subscripts in the formula. A key subtlety concerns atomic masses being averages over natural isotopic abundance. The periodic table value for chlorine, about 35.45, is not the mass of any single chlorine atom but the average of chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 weighted by their abundances, and it is these averaged values that must be used when computing molar masses for ordinary samples. The mole also connects to volume for gases, since one mole of any ideal gas occupies the same volume under the same conditions of temperature and pressure, about 22.4 liters at standard temperature and pressure, a fact exploited in determining molar masses of gases. Mastery of the mole and molar mass is therefore a prerequisite for everything that follows, because determining a formula is fundamentally the act of translating measured masses into counted atoms, and the mole is the unit in which that translation is done.

sections.heading: Percent Composition by Mass
sections.body: The percent composition of a compound states what fraction of its total mass is contributed by each element, expressed as a percentage. It is the natural output of elemental analysis, which measures how much of each element a sample contains, and it is the usual starting point for finding an empirical formula. Percent composition can be calculated in two directions, and understanding both illuminates the relationship between mass and formula. If the formula is already known, the percent composition follows directly. One computes the molar mass of the compound, then for each element multiplies the number of its atoms by its atomic mass, divides by the total molar mass, and multiplies by one hundred. For water, the molar mass is 18.02 grams per mole; hydrogen contributes two times 1.008, or 2.016 grams, which is 2.016 divided by 18.02 times one hundred, about 11.19 percent, and oxygen contributes 16.00 divided by 18.02 times one hundred, about 88.81 percent. The two percentages sum to one hundred, as they must, providing a built-in check. For glucose, C6H12O6 with molar mass 180.16, carbon is six times 12.01 divided by 180.16, about 40.0 percent; hydrogen is twelve times 1.008 divided by 180.16, about 6.71 percent; and oxygen is six times 16.00 divided by 180.16, about 53.3 percent. Running the calculation forward from a known formula is valuable for predicting what an analysis should yield and for checking a proposed formula against experimental percentages. The reverse direction, from measured percent composition to an unknown formula, is the heart of empirical formula determination, treated in the next section. Percent composition is useful in its own right beyond formula finding. It allows the calculation of how much of a desired element can be obtained from a given mass of a compound, important in metallurgy, agriculture, and industrial chemistry; a farmer choosing a fertilizer compares the percent nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium of different products, and a metallurgist calculates the iron yield of an ore from its percent iron. It also permits comparison of the richness of different sources of an element. A subtle but important point is that percent composition, like the empirical formula it leads to, cannot distinguish compounds with the same elemental proportions; formaldehyde, acetic acid, and glucose all share the composition 40.0 percent carbon, 6.7 percent hydrogen, and 53.3 percent oxygen, because they share the empirical formula CH2O. This again underscores that composition data alone give only ratios. When performing these calculations, one must use consistent atomic masses, carry enough significant figures through intermediate steps to avoid rounding error, and verify that the percentages of all elements sum to approximately one hundred; a sum noticeably different from one hundred signals either an analytical error or the presence of an unmeasured element, such as oxygen determined only by difference. Percent composition is thus both a practical quantity and the crucial link between the mass measurements a chemist can make and the atomic ratios a formula expresses.

sections.heading: From Composition to the Empirical Formula
sections.body: Determining an empirical formula from composition data is a systematic procedure that converts masses or percentages into a whole-number ratio of atoms. The logic is straightforward: because subscripts in a formula are ratios of numbers of atoms, and numbers of atoms are proportional to numbers of moles, one must convert the measured mass of each element into moles and then reduce those mole quantities to the simplest whole-number ratio. A convenient trick makes percent data easy to handle: assume a sample of exactly one hundred grams, so that each element's percentage becomes its mass in grams directly. Take a compound analyzed as 40.0 percent carbon, 6.71 percent hydrogen, and 53.3 percent oxygen. Assuming one hundred grams gives 40.0 grams of carbon, 6.71 grams of hydrogen, and 53.3 grams of oxygen. Dividing each by its atomic mass converts to moles: carbon, 40.0 divided by 12.01, is 3.33 moles; hydrogen, 6.71 divided by 1.008, is 6.66 moles; oxygen, 53.3 divided by 16.00, is 3.33 moles. These mole values are the raw atom ratio, but they are not yet whole numbers. To simplify, divide every mole value by the smallest of them, here 3.33. Carbon becomes 1.00, hydrogen becomes 2.00, and oxygen becomes 1.00, giving the ratio one to two to one and the empirical formula CH2O. The procedure works identically when the data are given as masses of elements rather than percentages; one simply skips the hundred-gram assumption and converts the given masses to moles directly. Sometimes dividing by the smallest value does not yield whole numbers but instead produces ratios ending in a clear fraction such as .5, .33, or .25. In that case one multiplies every value by the small integer that clears the fraction, two for .5, three for .33, four for .25, to reach whole numbers. For example, if the reduced ratios were one to 1.5, multiplying both by two gives two to three. The empirical formula for a compound found to be 43.6 percent phosphorus and 56.4 percent oxygen illustrates this: phosphorus, 43.6 divided by 30.97, is 1.408 moles; oxygen, 56.4 divided by 16.00, is 3.525 moles; dividing by the smaller gives one to 2.50; multiplying by two gives two to five, so the empirical formula is P2O5. Care with significant figures is essential, because small rounding errors in the mole values can obscure whether a ratio is truly a simple fraction; carrying three or four significant figures usually resolves the ambiguity. The result of this procedure is always and only the empirical formula, the simplest ratio, never the molecular formula, a limitation that flows inevitably from the fact that composition data contain no information about absolute molecular size. With the empirical formula in hand, the determination is half complete, and the next step requires the compound's molar mass to establish how many empirical units make up an actual molecule.
steps: If given percentages, assume a 100 gram sample so each percent becomes grams; if given masses, use them directly.
Convert the mass of each element to moles by dividing by that element's atomic mass.
Divide every mole value by the smallest mole value among them.
If the results are all whole numbers within rounding, they are the subscripts of the empirical formula.
If a result ends in a clear fraction (.5, .33, .25), multiply all values by the small integer that clears it (2, 3, 4).
Write the empirical formula using the resulting whole numbers as subscripts.

sections.heading: From Empirical Formula to Molecular Formula
sections.body: The empirical formula gives only the simplest ratio of atoms; to find the molecular formula, the actual count of atoms in one molecule, one additional experimental quantity is required, the molar mass of the compound. The molecular formula is always a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula, and that multiple is found by comparing the compound's measured molar mass with the mass of one empirical-formula unit. The procedure is compact. First, compute the empirical formula mass, the sum of the atomic masses of the atoms in the empirical formula. Second, divide the measured molar mass of the compound by this empirical formula mass. The quotient, which should be very close to a whole number, is the multiplier, usually denoted n. Third, multiply every subscript in the empirical formula by n to obtain the molecular formula. Return to the compound with empirical formula CH2O. The empirical formula mass is 12.01 plus two times 1.008 plus 16.00, which is 30.03 grams per mole. Suppose a separate experiment gives the molar mass of the compound as 180 grams per mole. Dividing 180 by 30.03 gives 5.99, which rounds to six, so n is six. Multiplying the empirical subscripts by six gives C6H12O6, the molecular formula of glucose. Had the measured molar mass instead been about 60 grams per mole, n would be two and the molecular formula C2H4O2, which is acetic acid; had it been about 30, n would be one and the compound formaldehyde, CH2O itself. This single worked family shows vividly how the molar mass, and only the molar mass, distinguishes compounds that share an empirical formula. Because the multiplier n must be a whole number, a computed value close to but not exactly an integer, such as 5.99 or 4.03, is simply rounded to the nearest integer, the small discrepancy arising from experimental uncertainty in the measured molar mass and from rounding in atomic masses. A value that is genuinely far from a whole number, however, is a warning sign, indicating an error in the empirical formula, in the molar mass measurement, or in the arithmetic, and it should prompt rechecking rather than forced rounding. It is worth emphasizing that if the measured molar mass equals the empirical formula mass, then n is one and the molecular and empirical formulas are identical, which is the case for many simple compounds such as water and carbon dioxide. The dependence of this step on a measured molar mass is why the determination of molecular formulas historically advanced only as methods for measuring molar mass improved, a theme taken up in a later section. In summary, the molecular formula equals the empirical formula multiplied by n, where n is the measured molar mass divided by the empirical formula mass, rounded to the nearest whole number. This clean relationship completes the determination and turns a ratio of atoms into a full molecular description.

sections.heading: Combustion Analysis of Organic Compounds
sections.body: For organic compounds, those built mainly of carbon and hydrogen and often oxygen, the standard laboratory method of determining composition is combustion analysis, a technique that measures carbon and hydrogen content by completely burning a weighed sample and capturing the products. The principle is that when a compound containing carbon and hydrogen is burned in an excess of oxygen, all its carbon is converted to carbon dioxide and all its hydrogen to water. If the masses of carbon dioxide and water produced are measured, the amounts of carbon and hydrogen in the original sample can be calculated, and from them the empirical formula. In practice a precisely weighed sample is placed in a stream of oxygen and heated, and the combustion products pass through absorbers: water is captured by a hygroscopic drying agent and carbon dioxide by a base such as sodium hydroxide on a support. The increase in mass of each absorber gives the mass of water and of carbon dioxide produced. The calculation proceeds by working backward from the products. Each mole of carbon dioxide contains one mole of carbon, so the mass of carbon equals the moles of carbon dioxide times the atomic mass of carbon; equivalently, mass of carbon equals mass of carbon dioxide times 12.01 divided by 44.01, the molar mass of carbon dioxide. Each mole of water contains two moles of hydrogen, so the mass of hydrogen equals the moles of water times two times the atomic mass of hydrogen; equivalently, mass of hydrogen equals mass of water times 2.016 divided by 18.02. Consider a 0.250 gram sample of a compound containing only carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen that on combustion yields 0.366 grams of carbon dioxide and 0.150 grams of water. The carbon mass is 0.366 times 12.01 over 44.01, about 0.0999 grams; the hydrogen mass is 0.150 times 2.016 over 18.02, about 0.0168 grams. Crucially, oxygen cannot be measured directly this way because the burning is done in oxygen, so the oxygen in the original sample is found by difference: the mass of oxygen equals the sample mass minus the masses of carbon and hydrogen, here 0.250 minus 0.0999 minus 0.0168, about 0.133 grams. Converting each to moles and reducing, as in the standard empirical-formula procedure, yields the ratio of atoms and the empirical formula. This oxygen-by-difference step is a defining and error-prone feature of combustion analysis; it assumes the sample contains only the elements accounted for, so if nitrogen, sulfur, or halogens are present they must be determined separately or the difference calculation fails. Modern automated elemental analyzers perform this measurement rapidly on milligram samples and can determine carbon, hydrogen, and nitrogen simultaneously. Combustion analysis was historically the workhorse of organic chemistry, developed to high precision by Justus von Liebig in the 1830s, and it remains a standard confirmation that a synthesized compound has the expected composition. It yields the empirical formula only, so as always a separate molar mass measurement is needed to reach the molecular formula.
steps: Weigh the sample precisely and combust it completely in a stream of excess oxygen.
Capture and weigh the water produced in a drying absorber and the carbon dioxide in a base absorber.
Compute mass of carbon as mass of carbon dioxide times 12.01 divided by 44.01.
Compute mass of hydrogen as mass of water times 2.016 divided by 18.02.
Find mass of oxygen (if present) by subtracting the carbon and hydrogen masses from the sample mass.
Convert each element's mass to moles and reduce to the simplest whole-number ratio for the empirical formula.

sections.heading: Measuring Molar Mass Experimentally
sections.body: Because the molecular formula cannot be reached without the molar mass, methods for measuring molar mass are an essential companion to composition analysis. Several independent techniques exist, each suited to different substances and eras of chemistry. The most powerful modern method is mass spectrometry. In a mass spectrometer a sample is ionized, and the resulting ions are separated according to their mass-to-charge ratio and detected. The mass of the intact molecular ion, the peak corresponding to the whole molecule stripped of an electron, gives the molecular mass directly and with high precision, and the pattern of fragment ions provides structural clues as well. Mass spectrometry has made molar mass determination fast and accurate even for tiny samples and is standard in identifying unknown organic compounds. For volatile substances or gases, molar mass can be found from gas density using the ideal gas law. The ideal gas law, PV equals nRT, relates pressure, volume, amount, and temperature, and since the number of moles n equals mass divided by molar mass, substitution gives molar mass equals mass times R times T divided by P times V, or equivalently molar mass equals density times R times T divided by P. Measuring the mass of a known volume of a gas at a known temperature and pressure therefore yields its molar mass. A related historical approach, associated with Victor Meyer and with Avogadro's principle, uses the fact that equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules, so relative molar masses follow from relative densities. For substances that are neither gaseous nor easily ionized, colligative properties provide a route. Colligative properties, those depending on the number of dissolved particles rather than their identity, include freezing-point depression and boiling-point elevation. Dissolving a known mass of a solute in a known mass of solvent lowers the freezing point by an amount proportional to the molal concentration of solute; measuring that depression gives the number of moles of solute, and dividing the known mass by the moles gives the molar mass. Osmotic pressure, especially sensitive, is used for large molecules such as polymers and proteins. Each method has domains of applicability and characteristic errors. Gas-density methods require the substance to be a well-behaved vapor and can be thrown off by non-ideal behavior or dissociation. Colligative methods require the solute to dissolve without dissociating or associating, since ionic compounds that split into several ions, or molecules that pair up, give apparent molar masses that must be corrected by a factor accounting for the number of particles. Mass spectrometry, though powerful, requires the molecule to survive ionization intact enough to show a molecular ion. The historical importance of these methods is large: reliable molar masses, particularly for gases via Avogadro's principle, were what allowed nineteenth-century chemists to move from empirical to molecular formulas and to establish a consistent table of atomic masses. Choosing an appropriate molar-mass method for the substance at hand is therefore the practical key to completing a formula determination.

sections.heading: Hydrates and Formulas from Mass Loss on Heating
sections.body: A particularly instructive class of formula problems concerns hydrates, crystalline compounds that incorporate a definite number of water molecules within their structure. Many salts crystallize with water bound in their lattice in fixed proportion, written with a raised dot before the water, as in copper sulfate pentahydrate, CuSO4 and five H2O. The number of water molecules per formula unit of the anhydrous salt, called the degree of hydration, is itself a formula quantity to be determined, and it is found by a simple and elegant experiment: heating the hydrate to drive off the water and measuring the mass lost. The procedure is gravimetric. A sample of the hydrate is weighed, then heated in a crucible until all the water of crystallization is expelled, leaving the anhydrous salt; the sample is cooled in a desiccator and reweighed, and heating is repeated until the mass no longer changes, a state called constant mass that signals complete dehydration. The mass lost is the mass of water that was bound in the crystal, and the remaining mass is that of the anhydrous salt. From these two masses the formula is deduced by converting each to moles and finding their ratio, exactly the empirical-formula logic applied to water and anhydrous salt as the two components. Suppose 2.500 grams of hydrated copper sulfate is heated and, after reaching constant mass, leaves 1.599 grams of white anhydrous copper sulfate; the water lost is 2.500 minus 1.599, or 0.901 grams. Converting to moles: anhydrous copper sulfate, molar mass about 159.6, gives 1.599 divided by 159.6, or 0.01002 moles; water, molar mass 18.02, gives 0.901 divided by 18.02, or 0.0500 moles. The ratio of water to salt is 0.0500 divided by 0.01002, which is 4.99, essentially five, so the formula is CuSO4 and five H2O, the familiar pentahydrate, and the color change from blue to white confirms the dehydration. This experiment is a staple of teaching laboratories precisely because it makes formula determination tangible and requires only a balance and a heat source. Several practical cautions apply. The sample must be heated strongly enough and long enough to remove all water but not so strongly that the anhydrous salt itself decomposes, which would remove more mass and give a falsely high water content. Reaching constant mass by repeated heating and weighing guards against incomplete dehydration. Some substances lose water in stages, forming intermediate hydrates, and some are hygroscopic and reabsorb moisture from the air during weighing, which is why cooling in a desiccator matters. The same mass-loss logic extends beyond hydrates to any decomposition in which a weighed solid loses a volatile component of known identity, such as a carbonate losing carbon dioxide on heating, allowing the original composition to be reconstructed. Hydrate analysis thus embodies, in a single accessible experiment, the whole principle that a formula can be read out of carefully measured masses.
steps: Weigh an empty crucible, then add the hydrate sample and weigh again to find the hydrate mass.
Heat the crucible strongly to drive off the water of crystallization.
Cool the crucible in a desiccator and reweigh; repeat heating and weighing until the mass is constant.
Calculate the mass of water lost as the hydrate mass minus the final anhydrous mass.
Convert the anhydrous salt mass and the water mass to moles using their molar masses.
Divide the moles of water by the moles of anhydrous salt to get the whole-number degree of hydration.

sections.heading: Worked Problems and Numerical Techniques
sections.body: The reliability of a formula determination depends as much on careful arithmetic as on good data, and several numerical techniques recur across all the methods discussed. This section consolidates them through representative problems. The core skill is recognizing when a set of mole values represents a simple whole-number ratio despite not being exactly integers. Because atomic masses are known only to a few significant figures and experimental measurements carry error, computed ratios such as 1.98, 3.01, or 0.99 should be read as 2, 3, and 1. A working rule is that values within about one or two percent of a whole number may be rounded, while values clearly between whole numbers, near .5, .33, .25, or .67, are genuine fractions to be cleared by multiplication rather than rounded away. Consider a compound that is 32.4 percent sodium, 22.6 percent sulfur, and 45.0 percent oxygen. Assuming one hundred grams and converting to moles gives sodium 32.4 over 22.99, or 1.409; sulfur 22.6 over 32.07, or 0.705; oxygen 45.0 over 16.00, or 2.813. Dividing by the smallest, 0.705, gives sodium 2.00, sulfur 1.00, oxygen 3.99, which rounds to the ratio two to one to four, the empirical formula Na2SO4. Now suppose a second experiment shows this compound's molar mass is about 142 grams per mole; the empirical formula mass of Na2SO4 is about 142, so n is one and the molecular formula equals the empirical formula. A second illustrative pattern is the fractional ratio requiring multiplication. A compound that is 27.3 percent carbon and 72.7 percent oxygen gives carbon 27.3 over 12.01, or 2.273, and oxygen 72.7 over 16.00, or 4.544; dividing by the smaller gives one to 2.00, so the formula is CO2, showing that not all fractional-looking intermediate values persist to the final ratio. A third technique concerns oxygen by difference in combustion analysis, where oxygen mass is the sample mass minus measured carbon and hydrogen, and any error in the carbon or hydrogen measurements propagates entirely into the oxygen value, making it the least certain figure. A fourth is significant-figure discipline: intermediate mole values should retain at least three or four significant figures, because premature rounding can turn a true 2.00 into an ambiguous 1.9 or 2.1 and obscure the correct ratio. A fifth is the sanity check that element percentages sum to one hundred, or that a computed n lands near a whole number; failures of these checks flag errors before they propagate. Finally, unit consistency must be maintained throughout, always converting mass to moles before comparing quantities of different elements, because masses cannot be compared directly, only moles reflect atom counts. Working many problems builds the pattern recognition that lets a chemist glance at a set of mole values and see the underlying integer ratio. The arithmetic is elementary, but the discipline of carrying enough figures, distinguishing rounding from genuine fractions, and checking results is what separates a correct determination from a plausible-looking mistake, and it is the practical craft that supports the theory.

sections.heading: Ionic Compounds, Formula Units, and Nonstoichiometry
sections.body: The concepts of empirical and molecular formula apply most cleanly to molecular substances, discrete molecules such as glucose or carbon dioxide, but a large part of chemistry concerns ionic compounds, which behave differently and require a careful adjustment of ideas. Ionic compounds, such as sodium chloride or calcium fluoride, do not consist of individual molecules. Instead they are extended three-dimensional lattices of alternating positive and negative ions held together by electrostatic attraction, in which no single ion belongs to any particular partner. For such substances there is no molecule and therefore no molecular formula in the strict sense; the formula written, NaCl or CaF2, is by nature an empirical formula, giving the simplest ratio of ions that makes the compound electrically neutral. This ratio, one sodium to one chloride, or one calcium to two fluoride, is called a formula unit, and it represents the smallest electrically neutral collection of ions, not a physically separate particle. The formula of an ionic compound is thus determined by the requirement of charge balance: the total positive charge of the cations must equal the total negative charge of the anions. Knowing the charges of the ions, one writes the smallest whole-number ratio that achieves neutrality; aluminum, charge plus three, and oxygen, charge minus two, combine as two aluminum to three oxygen, Al2O3, so that six positive charges balance six negative. This crossing-over of charges to become subscripts is the standard method for predicting ionic formulas and is really an application of the same simplest-ratio principle that underlies empirical formulas generally. Because ionic formulas are inherently empirical, the question of finding a molecular formula does not arise for them, and molar mass measurements on ionic compounds in solution must account for the fact that the compound dissociates into multiple ions, which affects colligative-property measurements through the number of particles produced. A further and genuinely subtle point is nonstoichiometry. The law of definite proportions, which underlies the whole idea that a compound has a fixed formula, holds strictly for most substances but is violated by certain solid compounds, called nonstoichiometric compounds or berthollides, in which the ratio of elements is not a ratio of small whole numbers and can vary continuously over a range. These arise in some metal oxides, sulfides, and other solids where the crystal can tolerate a variable number of vacancies or extra atoms in its lattice while remaining a single phase; iron oxide often written FeO is in reality slightly iron-deficient, with a composition closer to Fe0.95O that varies with preparation. Such compounds remind us that the tidy whole-number formulas of introductory chemistry, though nearly universal, are an idealization to which real matter mostly but not perfectly conforms. For the overwhelming majority of compounds, however, the law of definite proportions holds and formulas are simple whole-number ratios, so the methods of this guide apply directly. Recognizing the distinction between molecular and ionic substances, and knowing that ionic formulas are formula units fixed by charge balance, prevents the error of seeking a molecular formula where none exists and clarifies why molar mass plays a different role for the two classes of compound.

sections.heading: Historical Foundations: The Laws of Chemical Combination
sections.body: The confident modern practice of writing formulas for compounds rests on a set of empirical laws discovered around the turn of the nineteenth century, and understanding them reveals why formulas have the form they do and how the very idea of a fixed formula was established. The first pillar is the law of conservation of mass, articulated by Antoine Lavoisier in the 1780s, which states that matter is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction, so the total mass of products equals the total mass of reactants. This law makes quantitative analysis meaningful, since it guarantees that the elements in a sample are all accounted for in its combustion or decomposition products. The second pillar is the law of definite proportions, established by Joseph Proust around 1799 after a famous dispute with Claude Berthollet, which states that a given compound always contains the same elements in the same fixed proportion by mass, regardless of how it was made. This law is the direct justification for the concept of a formula: because water is always about eleven percent hydrogen and eighty-nine percent oxygen by mass, it makes sense to assign it a definite composition and hence a formula. The third pillar is the law of multiple proportions, formulated by John Dalton around 1803, which states that when two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other stand in ratios of small whole numbers. Carbon and oxygen, for instance, form carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide, and the oxygen combining with a fixed mass of carbon in the two is in the ratio one to two. Dalton recognized that these whole-number ratios pointed to the existence of atoms combining in whole-number counts, and his atomic theory gave the laws a physical explanation, transforming formula writing from bookkeeping into a statement about atoms. A crucial complication delayed progress: early chemists could measure combining masses and hence empirical formulas, but they could not easily determine molecular formulas because they lacked reliable atomic masses and could not tell how many atoms were in a molecule. The resolution came from the study of gases. Joseph Gay-Lussac observed around 1808 that gases combine in simple whole-number volume ratios, and Amedeo Avogadro in 1811 proposed that equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules, and that elemental gases such as hydrogen and oxygen are diatomic. Avogadro's hypothesis, largely ignored for half a century, was revived and championed by Stanislao Cannizzaro at the Karlsruhe Congress of 1860, whose consistent use of it finally allowed chemists to determine relative molecular masses and hence a self-consistent set of atomic masses, resolving decades of confusion over formulas. This history matters because it shows that the arithmetic of formula determination is not arbitrary convention but the expression of hard-won empirical laws, and that the distinction between empirical and molecular formulas is precisely the distinction that took chemistry half a century of effort to draw clearly.

sections.heading: Pitfalls, Rounding Traps, and Misconceptions
sections.body: Formula determination is arithmetically simple but riddled with traps that catch the unwary, and awareness of them is as important as knowing the procedure. The most frequent error is mishandling near-integer mole ratios. After dividing by the smallest mole value, students often round aggressively, turning a genuine 2.50 into 3 or a genuine 1.33 into 1, and thereby destroying the correct fractional ratio that should have been cleared by multiplication. The discipline is to distinguish small deviations caused by experimental error, which are rounded, from real fractions such as .5, .33, .25, and .67, which signal that the whole ratio must be scaled up by two, three, four, or three respectively. A related trap is premature rounding of intermediate values; carrying too few significant figures through the mole calculations can blur a true ratio, so intermediate results should retain three or four significant figures until the final step. A second major misconception is expecting composition data to yield a molecular formula. Percent composition and combustion analysis give only the empirical formula, the simplest ratio, and no amount of arithmetic on them can produce the molecular formula without an independently measured molar mass; forgetting this leads to reporting CH2O when the compound is glucose. Conversely, some assume the empirical and molecular formulas always differ, whereas for many compounds, such as water, carbon dioxide, and ammonia, they are identical because the multiplier n is one. A third pitfall specific to combustion analysis is the oxygen-by-difference calculation. Because oxygen is found by subtracting measured carbon and hydrogen from the sample mass, it silently absorbs all measurement error and, more dangerously, assumes no other elements are present; if the compound contains nitrogen, sulfur, or a halogen, the difference no longer represents oxygen and the result is wrong. One must know or determine which elements are present before trusting oxygen by difference. A fourth error is using the wrong atomic masses, for instance treating chlorine as 35 rather than the isotopically averaged 35.45, which can shift a marginal ratio across a rounding boundary. A fifth is unit confusion, comparing masses of different elements directly instead of converting to moles first; only moles reflect atom counts, and a formula is a ratio of atoms, not of masses. A sixth is forgetting the fundamental limitation that a formula, empirical or even molecular, does not specify structure, so isomers such as ethanol and dimethyl ether, both C2H6O, share a molecular formula while being different substances; determining that two samples have the same formula does not prove they are the same compound. A seventh, subtler misconception is treating all matter as strictly stoichiometric, whereas nonstoichiometric solids genuinely violate simple whole-number ratios. Finally, a practical laboratory pitfall in hydrate and gravimetric work is failing to heat to constant mass or allowing a hygroscopic residue to reabsorb water before weighing, both of which corrupt the mass data on which the whole calculation depends. Avoiding these traps requires understanding not just the steps but the reasoning behind them, so that anomalous results are recognized as errors to investigate rather than numbers to force into shape.

sections.heading: Where Formula Determination Connects Onward
sections.body: Determining empirical and molecular formulas is a foundational skill that opens onto much of the rest of chemistry, and seeing those connections gives the topic its full significance. The most immediate link is to stoichiometry, the quantitative accounting of reactants and products in chemical reactions. A balanced chemical equation is written in terms of formulas, and every calculation of how much product a reaction yields, or how much reactant is needed, depends on knowing the correct formulas of the substances involved. Formula determination is therefore the entry point to reaction stoichiometry, limiting-reagent calculations, and the computation of theoretical and percent yields that pervade both laboratory and industrial chemistry. A second connection is to the identification of unknown substances. When a chemist synthesizes a new compound or isolates a natural product, establishing its formula is among the first steps in characterizing it, providing a check that the material is what was intended and narrowing the possibilities for its identity. Combustion analysis and mass spectrometry, discussed earlier, are routine parts of this characterization, and a formula inconsistent with expectation immediately signals impurity or an unexpected product. A third connection is to structure determination, which begins where formula determination ends. The molecular formula fixes the atoms present but not their arrangement, and elucidating structure requires further techniques such as nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, infrared spectroscopy, and X-ray crystallography. The molecular formula constrains these efforts powerfully, for instance by fixing the degree of unsaturation, the number of rings and multiple bonds, which can be calculated directly from the formula and guides the interpretation of spectra. The recognition that isomers share a molecular formula but differ in structure, mentioned earlier, makes structure determination a necessary sequel to formula determination for any but the simplest compounds. A fourth connection reaches into analytical chemistry and quality control, where percent composition and formula verification are used to assess purity, to confirm the identity of pharmaceuticals and materials, and to monitor industrial processes. A fifth reaches back into the conceptual foundations of chemistry, since the laws of definite and multiple proportions that make formulas possible are also the empirical footing of atomic theory itself, tying this practical skill to the deepest ideas about the particulate nature of matter. Formula determination also connects to fields beyond chemistry proper: to geology and mineralogy, where mineral formulas are determined from elemental analysis; to biochemistry, where the formulas and molar masses of biomolecules underpin their study; and to materials science, where nonstoichiometric compounds and their variable formulas govern important electronic and catalytic properties. In every direction, the humble act of converting measured masses into a ratio of atoms proves to be a gateway. Mastering it means acquiring not only a self-contained technique but a way of thinking, quantitative, atom-counting, and empirically grounded, that is the habit of mind chemistry demands and that supports the far more elaborate analyses built upon it.

guides.title: Percent Composition and Chemical Formulas
guides.summary: How the mass of a substance reveals the atoms inside it: molar mass, percent composition by mass, the laws of definite and multiple proportions, and the full procedure for turning analytical data into empirical and molecular formulas, with worked examples, combustion analysis, hydrates, and the genuine limits of the method.

sections.heading: The Bridge Between What You Can Weigh and What You Cannot See
sections.body:
Chemistry has a permanent practical problem. The things it is about, atoms and molecules, are far too small to count, while the things a laboratory can actually measure are masses, volumes and temperatures. A chemist can put a white powder on a balance and read 4.372 grams, but cannot look at it and see how many molecules are present or what atoms they contain. Percent composition and chemical formulas are the machinery that connects those two worlds. They let you take a measurable mass and work backwards to the invisible arrangement of atoms that produced it.

The logic runs in both directions, and both are useful. If you know the formula of a substance, you can predict exactly what fraction of its mass is any given element. Pure water is always 11.19 percent hydrogen and 88.81 percent oxygen by mass, everywhere, whether it came from a glacier or a laboratory synthesis. Run the other way, and a measured composition tells you the ratio of atoms in the substance, which for an unknown compound is often the first real information anybody has about it.

This second direction is how the molecular structure of the natural world was originally mapped. Through the nineteenth century, before spectroscopy or any method of seeing molecules existed, chemists determined the formulas of thousands of compounds by burning carefully weighed samples and weighing the products. The formulas of urea, glucose, morphine, quinine and countless other substances were established by nothing more sophisticated than combustion and a good balance. That entire body of knowledge rests on the arithmetic described here.

The practical reach is wide and still current. A metallurgist assays an ore to decide whether it is worth mining, and the decision turns on percent composition: copper ores at 0.5 percent copper are economically marginal, while 2 percent is a rich deposit. A fertilizer bag is labelled with numbers that are percent composition figures. A pharmaceutical manufacturer confirms the identity and purity of a batch partly by elemental analysis, and a result deviating by more than about 0.4 percentage points from the calculated value is conventionally treated as evidence that the sample is not what it claims to be. Nutrition labels, alloy specifications, cement chemistry, environmental limits on lead in soil, and the certification of reference materials all speak this language.

Two ideas carry the whole subject, and they are worth stating plainly before anything else. First, the mole is a counting unit that lets a mass measurement be converted into a number of particles. Second, a chemical formula is a ratio, and a percent composition is that same ratio expressed in the units a balance can read. Everything that follows is the careful working out of those two statements, including where they hold exactly, where they hold approximately, and the small number of genuine cases where they break down.

sections.heading: The Mole: Counting Particles by Weighing Them
sections.body:
The central trick of quantitative chemistry is the mole, a unit that solves the counting problem by exploiting a proportionality. Atoms of a given element all have nearly the same mass, so if you know the mass of one atom, a total mass tells you how many atoms are present. The mole packages this conversion into a single number.

One mole is defined as exactly 6.02214076 times ten to the twenty-third elementary entities. That figure is the Avogadro constant, and since the redefinition of the International System of Units that took effect on the twentieth of May 2019 it is a fixed, exact number rather than something measured. Before that date the mole was defined as the number of atoms in exactly twelve grams of carbon-12, and Avogadro's constant was an experimental quantity with an uncertainty attached. The change was made to base all SI units on fixed constants of nature rather than on physical artefacts or particular substances.

A subtle consequence of the redefinition is worth knowing because textbooks vary in how they handle it. Under the old definition, the molar mass of carbon-12 was exactly 12 grams per mole by construction. Under the new definition that equality is no longer exact but is experimentally determined, and it holds to within about one part in a billion. For every purpose short of the most precise metrology, the practical rule is unchanged: the molar mass of a substance in grams per mole is numerically equal to its atomic or molecular mass in unified atomic mass units.

That numerical equality is what makes the whole system workable, and it is worth appreciating how convenient it is. The mass of a single carbon-12 atom is about 1.99 times ten to the minus twenty-six kilograms, a number nobody wants to handle routinely. Because a mole of them weighs twelve grams, a chemist can work with grams and get answers in moles by simple division, never touching the tiny numbers at all.

The unified atomic mass unit itself, symbol u and also called the dalton, is defined as one twelfth of the mass of a single unbound carbon-12 atom in its ground state, approximately 1.66054 times ten to the minus twenty-seven kilograms. Carbon-12 was chosen as the reference in 1961, replacing two competing oxygen-based scales that physicists and chemists had used separately and which differed by a few parts in ten thousand, a genuine nuisance that caused real confusion in the literature.

The practical relationships that flow from all this are three. The number of moles equals the mass in grams divided by the molar mass in grams per mole. The number of particles equals the number of moles times Avogadro's constant. And the mass equals moles times molar mass. Nearly every calculation in this area is one of these three applied repeatedly.

sections.heading: Where Atomic Masses Come From, and Why They Are Not Whole Numbers
sections.body:
Open any periodic table and the atomic masses look untidy. Chlorine is listed as 35.45, copper as 63.546, magnesium as 24.305. Only carbon-12, by definition, and a handful of monoisotopic elements come out clean. The reason is isotopes, and understanding it prevents a persistent confusion about what these numbers actually mean.

An element is defined by its number of protons, but atoms of the same element can carry different numbers of neutrons. These variants are isotopes. Chlorine occurs naturally as two stable isotopes: chlorine-35, with a mass of 34.96885 u, making up about 75.8 percent of natural chlorine, and chlorine-37, at 36.96590 u, making up about 24.2 percent. Neither individual atom weighs 35.45 u. The tabulated value is a weighted average across the natural mixture, calculated as 0.758 times 34.96885 plus 0.242 times 36.96590, which gives approximately 35.45. This is exactly what you want for laboratory work, because any real sample of chlorine contains billions of atoms in roughly the natural proportions, so the average is the practically relevant quantity.

There is a second, smaller reason the numbers are not whole. Even a single isotope does not have a mass that is an exact multiple of the proton or neutron mass, because binding energy in the nucleus converts a small amount of mass into energy, following the relation between mass and energy that Einstein published in 1905. The mass defect is around 0.8 percent for medium-weight nuclei. Chlorine-35 weighs 34.96885 u, slightly less than 35, and that deficit is the energy holding the nucleus together.

IUPAC, the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry, publishes standard atomic weights and revises them periodically. For a number of elements the modern tables give an interval rather than a single value, because the isotopic composition genuinely varies between natural sources by more than the measurement uncertainty. Hydrogen is given as the interval from 1.00784 to 1.00811, and carbon from 12.0096 to 12.0116, reflecting real variation in deuterium and carbon-13 content between, for example, marine and terrestrial samples. This variation is not a nuisance; it is the basis of isotope-ratio forensics, used to trace the geographic origin of food, drugs and archaeological remains.

For ordinary calculation these fine points rarely matter, and using conventional values such as hydrogen 1.008, carbon 12.011, nitrogen 14.007, oxygen 15.999 and sulfur 32.06 is entirely appropriate. The important habit is knowing which precision you are using and carrying it consistently. A common source of small discrepancies between a student's answer and a textbook's is simply that one used hydrogen as 1.0 and the other as 1.008.

sections.heading: Calculating Formula Mass and Molar Mass
sections.body:
Formula mass is the sum of the atomic masses of every atom in the formula. The calculation is mechanical, but it is worth doing carefully and in a consistent layout, because the overwhelming majority of errors in this entire subject are bookkeeping errors rather than conceptual ones.

Take sulfuric acid, formula H2SO4. There are two hydrogens at 1.008 u each, contributing 2.016; one sulfur at 32.06; and four oxygens at 15.999 each, contributing 63.996. The total is 98.07 u, so the molar mass is 98.07 grams per mole. Take calcium carbonate, CaCO3, the principal component of limestone and chalk. Calcium contributes 40.078, carbon 12.011, and three oxygens contribute 47.997, giving 100.09 grams per mole. That convenient near-hundred value is why limestone appears so often in worked examples.

Parentheses in a formula multiply everything inside them, and this is where errors cluster. Calcium nitrate is written Ca(NO3)2, which means one calcium, two nitrogens and six oxygens, not two nitrogens and three oxygens. The mass is 40.078 plus 2 times 14.007 plus 6 times 15.999, giving 164.09 grams per mole. Aluminium sulfate, Al2(SO4)3, contains two aluminium, three sulfur and twelve oxygen atoms, totalling 342.15 grams per mole. Writing out the atom inventory explicitly before multiplying anything is a habit worth forming, and it costs ten seconds.

Hydrates use a centred dot, as in copper sulfate pentahydrate, CuSO4·5H2O. The dot does not indicate multiplication of the whole formula and it does not indicate a covalent bond; it means the crystal structure incorporates five water molecules per formula unit. The mass is the anhydrous salt at 159.61 plus five waters at 18.015 each, giving 249.69 grams per mole.

Terminology deserves a brief note because examiners are fussy about it and the distinction is real. Molecular mass properly applies to substances that exist as discrete molecules, such as water, glucose or carbon dioxide. Formula mass is the more general term and is the correct one for ionic compounds, which have no molecules at all. There is no such thing as a sodium chloride molecule; a crystal is an extended lattice of sodium and chloride ions in a one-to-one ratio, and NaCl is simply the simplest formula unit expressing that ratio. Its formula mass is 58.44. The term molar mass applies to both cases and is the mass of one mole in grams. In practice most working chemists use the terms loosely, but knowing why the distinction exists tells you something important about how ionic solids are put together.

sections.heading: Percent Composition by Mass
sections.body:
Percent composition states what fraction of a compound's mass is contributed by each element. The definition is a single expression: for any element, take the number of atoms of that element in the formula, multiply by its atomic mass, divide by the total formula mass, and multiply by one hundred. Because every element in the compound is accounted for, the percentages must sum to one hundred, and checking that sum is a free and reliable error detector.

Water makes the cleanest first example. Its molar mass is 18.015 grams per mole. Hydrogen contributes 2 times 1.008, which is 2.016, so the hydrogen percentage is 2.016 divided by 18.015 times 100, giving 11.19 percent. Oxygen contributes 15.999, so its percentage is 88.81 percent. The two sum to 100.00, as they must. Notice the striking result: hydrogen makes up two thirds of the atoms in water but only about a ninth of its mass, because a hydrogen atom is roughly sixteen times lighter than an oxygen atom. Confusing atom fraction with mass fraction is one of the most common misunderstandings in introductory chemistry, and this example is the standard cure.

Glucose, C6H12O6, has a molar mass of 180.16 grams per mole. Carbon contributes 6 times 12.011, which is 72.066, giving 40.00 percent. Hydrogen contributes 12 times 1.008, which is 12.096, giving 6.71 percent. Oxygen contributes 6 times 15.999, which is 95.994, giving 53.28 percent. These sum to 99.99, the small shortfall being rounding, which is normal and acceptable.

A practically important use is calculating how much of a desired element a given mass of compound will supply. If a fertilizer contains ammonium nitrate, NH4NO3, with molar mass 80.04, the nitrogen content is 2 times 14.007 divided by 80.04 times 100, which is 35.00 percent. A fifty kilogram bag therefore delivers 17.5 kilograms of nitrogen. Compare urea, CO(NH2)2, molar mass 60.06, whose nitrogen content is 28.014 divided by 60.06 times 100, or 46.64 percent. Urea delivers considerably more nitrogen per kilogram, which is precisely why it dominates world fertilizer production, though it behaves differently in soil and is more prone to loss as ammonia gas.

The same reasoning governs ore assessment. Hematite, Fe2O3, is 69.94 percent iron by mass; magnetite, Fe3O4, is 72.36 percent. Both are worked commercially, and the difference in grade is one input into which deposit is profitable.

One caution frames everything else. Percent composition is a property of a pure substance. Applied to a mixture the number is still meaningful as a description of that particular mixture, but it no longer identifies a compound, since any composition whatever can be produced by mixing in suitable proportions. Establishing purity is therefore a prerequisite, not an afterthought.

sections.heading: The Laws of Definite and Multiple Proportions
sections.body:
The reason percent composition identifies a compound at all rests on a law that took decades of argument to settle. The law of definite proportions, also called the law of constant composition, states that a given chemical compound always contains its constituent elements in the same fixed proportion by mass, regardless of its source or how it was prepared. Copper carbonate scraped from a Cornish mine and copper carbonate synthesized in a laboratory have identical composition.

This now seems obvious and was not. The French chemist Joseph Proust argued for it from around 1794, based on painstaking analyses of metal oxides and sulfides. He was opposed, seriously and in good faith, by his eminent countryman Claude Louis Berthollet, who held that composition could vary continuously depending on the conditions of formation and the relative amounts of reactants present. Berthollet had evidence: he had studied alloys, glasses and solutions, all of which do vary continuously. The dispute ran for roughly eight years and was substantially resolved in Proust's favour by 1804, largely because he could show that Berthollet's variable cases were mixtures or solutions rather than compounds. The irony, taken up later, is that Berthollet was not entirely wrong about certain solid materials, and the exceptions now bear his name.

John Dalton then supplied the interpretation. In work published between 1803 and 1808 he proposed that matter consists of indivisible atoms, that all atoms of an element are identical in mass, and that compounds form when atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios. Constant composition follows immediately: if every molecule of a compound contains the same atoms, every sample must have the same mass proportions.

Dalton also formulated a second and sharper law that provided strong evidence for the atomic hypothesis. The law of multiple proportions states that when two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other stand in a ratio of small whole numbers. Carbon and oxygen illustrate it well. In carbon monoxide, 12.011 grams of carbon combine with 15.999 grams of oxygen. In carbon dioxide, the same 12.011 grams of carbon combine with 31.998 grams. The ratio of oxygen masses is exactly 2 to 1. Nitrogen and oxygen form an even better series: N2O, NO, N2O3, NO2 and N2O5 give oxygen ratios of 1 to 2 to 3 to 4 to 5 for a fixed mass of nitrogen.

That such clean small-integer ratios appear repeatedly is very difficult to explain unless matter comes in discrete units. This was the strongest argument for atoms available in the early nineteenth century, and it was made entirely with balances, long before any direct evidence for atoms existed.

sections.heading: From Percent Composition to an Empirical Formula
sections.body:
The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound. Determining it from percent composition data is the central procedure of this subject, and it is worth learning as a fixed routine because the same sequence works every time.

The conceptual step that makes it work is deceptively simple. Percentages are mass ratios, and mass ratios cannot be compared directly because atoms have different masses. Dividing each element's mass by its atomic mass converts masses into mole counts, and mole counts are directly proportional to atom counts. Once you have atom counts, reducing them to their simplest whole-number ratio gives the formula.

Assuming a 100 gram sample is a convenience that removes a step: in a 100 gram sample, a percentage becomes a mass in grams directly, with no arithmetic. The final formula is a ratio and is unaffected by the assumed sample size, so nothing is lost.

Dividing by the smallest mole value deserves a word of justification, because it looks like an arbitrary trick and is not. Any set of atom counts can be scaled by a common factor without changing the ratio they express, and dividing by the smallest is simply the scaling that forces the least abundant element to 1. That choice guarantees every other value is at least 1, which makes fractional ratios easy to recognise by eye. Dividing by any other value would work equally well arithmetically but would scatter the results around awkward numbers and hide the fractions.

One caveat about oxygen determined by difference is worth stating plainly, because it silently degrades a great deal of published data. When oxygen is assigned the remainder rather than measured, every experimental error in every other element accumulates in the oxygen figure. If carbon and hydrogen each carry an uncertainty of 0.3 percentage points, the oxygen value inherits both, and a formula that hinges on the oxygen subscript is correspondingly less trustworthy than one that hinges on carbon. This is not a reason to distrust the method, which remains the workhorse of the field, but it is a reason to treat a marginal oxygen ratio with more suspicion than a marginal carbon one.
steps: Assume exactly 100 grams of the compound, which turns each percentage directly into a mass in grams. If you were given masses rather than percentages, use those masses as they are.
If the percentages do not sum to 100 and one element is unstated, assign the remainder to that element. This is standard practice when oxygen is determined by difference rather than measured.
Divide each element's mass by that element's atomic mass to obtain moles. Keep at least four significant figures at this stage; premature rounding is the single most common cause of a wrong answer.
Identify the smallest of the mole values and divide every mole value by it. This produces a set of ratios in which the smallest element is exactly 1.
Inspect the resulting ratios. If all are within about 0.02 of a whole number, round them and you have the subscripts.

If any ratio sits near a simple fraction, multiply every ratio by the smallest integer that clears it: multiply by 2 for values near .5, by 3 for .33 or .67, by 4 for .25 or .75, and by 5 for .2, .4, .6 or .8.
Write the empirical formula using the rounded whole numbers as subscripts, conventionally listing carbon first, then hydrogen, then remaining elements alphabetically for organic compounds.

Verify by working backwards: calculate the percent composition of your proposed formula and confirm it reproduces the original data to within experimental error, typically a few tenths of a percentage point.

sections.heading: Worked Examples, Including the Fractional Cases
sections.body:
The routine is best absorbed through examples of increasing awkwardness, because the difficulty is never the concept but the judgment about rounding.

A straightforward case first. A compound is found to be 40.00 percent carbon, 6.71 percent hydrogen and 53.29 percent oxygen. Assume 100 grams. Carbon: 40.00 divided by 12.011 gives 3.330 moles. Hydrogen: 6.71 divided by 1.008 gives 6.657 moles. Oxygen: 53.29 divided by 15.999 gives 3.331 moles. The smallest is 3.330. Dividing through gives carbon 1.000, hydrogen 1.999, oxygen 1.000. The empirical formula is CH2O. This is the composition of glucose, but also of formaldehyde, acetic acid and ribose, a point of real importance.

Now a case with a fractional ratio. A compound is 43.64 percent phosphorus and 56.36 percent oxygen. Phosphorus: 43.64 divided by 30.974 gives 1.409 moles. Oxygen: 56.36 divided by 15.999 gives 3.523 moles. Dividing by the smaller, phosphorus is 1.000 and oxygen is 2.500. Rounding 2.5 to either 2 or 3 would be wrong; the correct response is to multiply both by 2, giving P2O5. The compound is phosphorus pentoxide, whose actual molecular formula is P4O10.

A third case, deliberately messier. A compound is 26.58 percent potassium, 35.35 percent chromium and 38.07 percent oxygen. Potassium: 26.58 divided by 39.098 gives 0.6798. Chromium: 35.35 divided by 51.996 gives 0.6799. Oxygen: 38.07 divided by 15.999 gives 2.3795. Dividing by 0.6798 gives potassium 1.000, chromium 1.000 and oxygen 3.500. Multiplying by 2 gives K2Cr2O7, potassium dichromate.

The judgment required at the rounding step deserves emphasis because it is where students most often go astray in both directions. A value of 1.98 is a rounding artefact and should become 2. A value of 1.5 is a genuine fraction and must be cleared by multiplication. A value of 2.15 is ambiguous and usually signals experimental error, an impure sample, or an arithmetic slip earlier in the working, and the honest response is to check the arithmetic and then question the data rather than to force a formula. Good analytical data will give ratios within roughly one percent of whole numbers or clean fractions. Ratios that stubbornly refuse to resolve, such as 1 to 2.37, are telling you something is wrong with the sample or the measurement, and no amount of rounding will fix it.

A final practical note concerns significant figures in the atomic masses themselves. Using 12 for carbon instead of 12.011, or 1 for hydrogen instead of 1.008, introduces errors of roughly 0.1 and 0.8 percent respectively. For a small molecule those errors are usually swamped by the rounding step and cause no harm, but in a compound containing many hydrogens they compound: a formula with twelve hydrogen atoms accumulates almost a full percentage point of error from that approximation alone, which is comparable to the experimental uncertainty the method is trying to resolve. Carrying the full tabulated masses costs nothing and removes an entire category of avoidable failure.

sections.heading: Empirical Versus Molecular Formulas
sections.body:
An empirical formula gives the ratio of atoms; a molecular formula gives the actual number of atoms in one molecule. The two are frequently different, and the difference is always a whole-number multiplier.

The relationship is direct. The molecular mass divided by the empirical formula mass gives an integer, and multiplying every subscript in the empirical formula by that integer gives the molecular formula. Take the empirical formula CH2O, whose formula mass is 30.03. If an independent measurement shows the molecular mass to be 180.16, then 180.16 divided by 30.03 is 5.999, which rounds to 6, and the molecular formula is C6H12O6, glucose. If the molecular mass had been 60.05, the multiplier would be 2 and the formula C2H4O2, acetic acid. If it had been 30.03, the multiplier is 1 and the compound is formaldehyde, CH2O, whose empirical and molecular formulas coincide.

This is the crucial limitation of composition analysis taken alone: percent composition can never determine a molecular formula by itself. Formaldehyde, acetic acid, lactic acid, glyceraldehyde, ribose and glucose all have exactly the same percent composition, because they all reduce to CH2O. They are wildly different substances, one a preservative and carcinogen, one the acid in vinegar, one a sugar. Distinguishing them requires a molecular mass, obtained by mass spectrometry, or historically by freezing-point depression, boiling-point elevation, osmotic pressure or vapour density measurements.

Many familiar compounds have empirical formulas that differ from their molecular ones. Benzene is C6H6 with empirical formula CH; acetylene is C2H2 with the same empirical formula CH, which is why the two cannot be told apart by combustion analysis alone. Hydrogen peroxide is H2O2 with empirical formula HO. Glucose and fructose are both C6H12O6 and differ only in how the atoms are connected, so neither composition nor molecular mass separates them; that requires structural methods.

Ionic compounds are a special case worth stating clearly. For sodium chloride, calcium carbonate or magnesium oxide the empirical formula is the only formula there is, because no molecules exist. The formula NaCl describes a one-to-one ratio of ions in an extended crystal lattice, and writing Na2Cl2 would be meaningless rather than merely unusual. The same applies to most metals, network solids such as silicon dioxide and diamond, and most salts. Asking for the molecular formula of table salt is a category error.

The practical consequence is that a complete determination requires two independent pieces of information: a composition, which gives the ratio, and a molecular mass, which gives the scale. Historically these came from two entirely different experiments performed days apart. Modern high-resolution mass spectrometry can supply both at once from a fraction of a milligram, which is why classical combustion analysis has retreated to a confirmatory role.

sections.heading: Combustion Analysis: How the Numbers Are Actually Measured
sections.body:
For organic compounds, percent composition is traditionally determined by combustion analysis, a technique whose modern form was developed by the German chemist Justus von Liebig around 1830. Liebig's apparatus, the Kaliapparat, a distinctive five-bulb glass device for absorbing carbon dioxide, was so central to organic chemistry that it became the emblem of the American Chemical Society.

The principle is straightforward. A precisely weighed sample, typically one to three milligrams in modern instruments, is burned in a stream of pure oxygen at around 900 to 1000 degrees Celsius, often over a catalyst to ensure complete combustion. All carbon is converted to carbon dioxide and all hydrogen to water. These products are swept along by a carrier gas and quantified, historically by absorbing them in weighed tubes and measuring the mass increase, and in modern instruments by gas chromatography with thermal conductivity detection or by infrared absorption.

The arithmetic then runs backwards. Every mole of carbon dioxide collected came from one mole of carbon in the sample, so the mass of carbon equals the mass of carbon dioxide times 12.011 divided by 44.009, a factor of 0.2729. Every mole of water came from two moles of hydrogen, so the mass of hydrogen equals the mass of water times 2.016 divided by 18.015, a factor of 0.1119. Dividing each by the original sample mass gives the percentages. Nitrogen is measured on the same instrument by reducing nitrogen oxides to nitrogen gas over hot copper. Oxygen is almost never measured directly, because the combustion is carried out in oxygen; instead it is determined by difference, as one hundred minus the sum of the other elements.

A worked example fixes the method. Suppose 5.000 milligrams of a compound containing only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen yields 11.44 milligrams of carbon dioxide and 4.684 milligrams of water. Carbon is 11.44 times 0.2729, or 3.122 milligrams, which is 62.44 percent. Hydrogen is 4.684 times 0.1119, or 0.5241 milligrams, which is 10.48 percent. Oxygen by difference is 27.08 percent. Converting to moles per 100 grams gives carbon 5.199, hydrogen 10.40 and oxygen 1.693. Dividing by 1.693 gives 3.07, 6.14 and 1.00, which rounds to C3H6O, the empirical formula of acetone or of propanal.

Determining oxygen by difference has an important weakness that is easy to overlook. Every error in the other measurements, plus any unaccounted element such as sulfur, halogen or metal, and any residual moisture or solvent in the sample, is pushed entirely into the oxygen figure. A sample that appears to contain more oxygen than expected is far more often damp or impure than genuinely oxygen-rich.
ingredients: An analytical microbalance readable to one microgram, since sample masses are typically one to three milligrams and the mass is the largest single source of error
A combustion tube furnace capable of a stable 900 to 1000 degrees Celsius, with an oxidation catalyst such as copper oxide, cobalt oxide or tungsten trioxide
A supply of high-purity oxygen for combustion and an inert carrier gas, usually helium, both dried and free of carbon dioxide
Absorbents for the classical gravimetric method: magnesium perchlorate or calcium chloride for water, and soda lime or sodium hydroxide on a solid support for carbon dioxide
A reduction section containing hot copper at around 600 degrees Celsius to convert nitrogen oxides to nitrogen and remove excess oxygen
Tin or silver sample capsules, which combust exothermically and help drive complete oxidation of the sample
Certified reference standards such as acetanilide or benzoic acid, run before and between samples to calibrate the instrument and confirm it is performing correctly
A vacuum oven or desiccator for drying samples to constant mass, since adsorbed water inflates the apparent hydrogen and oxygen content

sections.heading: Hydrates and Water of Crystallization
sections.body:
Many salts crystallize with water molecules built into the crystal lattice in a fixed ratio. These are hydrates, and they provide one of the neatest laboratory demonstrations of definite proportions because the water can be driven off and weighed.

Copper sulfate pentahydrate, CuSO4·5H2O, is the standard example and is visually memorable. The hydrated form is a deep blue crystal; heating it above roughly 250 degrees Celsius drives off all five water molecules and leaves anhydrous copper sulfate as a pale grey-white powder. Adding water reverses the change and restores the blue instantly, which is why anhydrous copper sulfate is used as a test for the presence of water. The water content is calculable: five waters at 18.015 is 90.08 out of a total of 249.69, or 36.08 percent of the mass.

Determining the formula of a hydrate experimentally is a classic teaching exercise and a genuinely useful analytical method. Weigh a clean dry crucible, add the hydrate and weigh again, heat gently to avoid decomposing the salt itself, cool in a desiccator, and reweigh. Repeat the heating and weighing until two successive masses agree, which is what heating to constant mass means and is the only reliable way to know the dehydration is complete. The mass lost is water; the mass remaining is the anhydrous salt. Converting each to moles and taking the ratio gives the number of waters per formula unit.

Suppose 4.000 grams of a magnesium sulfate hydrate is heated and 1.953 grams remain. The water lost is 2.047 grams, which is 0.1136 moles. The anhydrous magnesium sulfate, molar mass 120.37, amounts to 0.01622 moles. The ratio of water to salt is 7.00, so the formula is MgSO4·7H2O, Epsom salt.

Other common hydrates include sodium carbonate decahydrate, Na2CO3·10H2O, known as washing soda, which loses water simply on standing in dry air, a behaviour called efflorescence; calcium sulfate dihydrate, CaSO4·2H2O, which is gypsum, and its hemihydrate CaSO4·½H2O, plaster of Paris, whose setting reaction is nothing more than rehydration back to gypsum; and cobalt chloride hexahydrate, which shifts from pink to blue on dehydration and was long used in humidity indicator papers.

Two practical cautions apply. Some substances are hygroscopic or deliquescent, absorbing water from the air, so a sample left out will gain mass and give a falsely high water content; weighing bottles and desiccators exist for this reason. And some salts decompose rather than merely dehydrate if overheated. Hydrated iron sulfate, for instance, will eventually give off sulfur trioxide and leave an oxide, which would produce a nonsensical result. Gentle, controlled heating is the whole skill.

sections.heading: What Different Kinds of Formula Actually Tell You
sections.body:
Chemistry uses several kinds of formula, each carrying a different amount of information, and confusing them causes real misunderstanding. Arranged from least to most informative, they form a ladder worth knowing.

An empirical formula gives only the simplest atom ratio. CH tells you there is one hydrogen per carbon and nothing else. A molecular formula gives the actual atom counts in one molecule: C6H6 for benzene, C2H2 for acetylene. Both have the empirical formula CH, and they are entirely different substances, one a liquid aromatic solvent and one a gas that burns at over three thousand degrees in an oxy-acetylene torch.

A structural formula shows which atoms are bonded to which. This is the level at which isomers separate. Ethanol and dimethyl ether share the molecular formula C2H6O and the same percent composition, 52.14 percent carbon, 13.13 percent hydrogen and 34.73 percent oxygen. Ethanol, written CH3CH2OH, is a liquid boiling at 78 degrees Celsius, drinkable in moderation and miscible with water. Dimethyl ether, CH3OCH3, is a gas boiling at minus 24 degrees. No mass measurement whatever can distinguish them, because they are identical in composition; only their connectivity differs. Condensed formulas such as CH3COOH are a compact way of writing structure in a single line, and skeletal or line-angle formulas are the shorthand used throughout organic chemistry, where carbons sit at line vertices and hydrogens on carbon are left implicit.

Beyond structure lies stereochemistry, where atoms are connected identically but arranged differently in space. Glucose and galactose differ in the orientation of a single hydroxyl group at one carbon; the human body metabolizes one readily and the other only via a specific enzyme pathway, and people lacking that enzyme develop galactosemia. The two enantiomers of thalidomide have identical composition, identical connectivity and mirror-image geometry, and the tragedy that unfolded between 1957 and 1961, in which the drug caused severe birth defects in an estimated ten thousand children, is the most consequential demonstration in history that composition is not the whole story.

The general principle is that each step up the ladder adds information that the level below cannot supply, and that percent composition sits at the very bottom. It is genuinely powerful for what it does: it identifies the elements present and their proportions, it can confirm purity, and it was sufficient to build the entire nineteenth-century edifice of organic chemistry. But it cannot see connectivity and it cannot see geometry.

This is why a modern identification never relies on elemental analysis alone. A compound is characterized by combining composition with a molecular mass from mass spectrometry, connectivity from nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, functional groups from infrared spectroscopy, and where a crystal can be grown, full three-dimensional structure from X-ray diffraction. Elemental analysis survives in that suite chiefly as a purity check, because it is uniquely sensitive to the presence of things that should not be there.

sections.heading: When Definite Proportions Fails: Non-Stoichiometric Compounds
sections.body:
The law of definite proportions is treated as absolute in introductory teaching, and for molecular compounds and most salts it effectively is. But Berthollet, who lost the argument to Proust two centuries ago, turns out to have been partly right about a class of solids, and these exceptions are important in materials science rather than being curiosities.

Non-stoichiometric compounds, also called berthollides in his honour as against daltonides for well-behaved ones, are crystalline solids whose elemental ratios are not exact small integers and which vary continuously over a range. The classic case is iron monoxide, conventionally written FeO but in reality almost never exactly one to one. The mineral wüstite has the composition Fe(1−x)O with x typically between about 0.05 and 0.17, meaning the crystal contains vacancies where iron ions ought to be. Charge balance is preserved by some of the remaining iron being present as iron(III) rather than iron(II). Stoichiometric FeO is in fact thermodynamically unstable at ordinary pressures; the deficient form is the stable one.

The mechanism is defect chemistry. A real crystal is not a perfect lattice. It contains vacant sites, extra atoms squeezed into interstitial positions, and substituted ions, and at any temperature above absolute zero a certain concentration of such defects is thermodynamically favoured because they increase entropy. In most compounds these defects are too few to shift the measured composition. In compounds where an element has accessible multiple oxidation states, charge compensation is easy and defect concentrations can become large enough to change the formula measurably.

Examples matter industrially. Titanium monoxide ranges roughly from TiO0.7 to TiO1.3. Palladium absorbs hydrogen to form PdHx with x varying continuously up to about 0.7, the basis of hydrogen storage and purification. Zirconium dioxide and cerium dioxide tolerate oxygen deficiency, which is precisely what makes them useful in oxygen sensors and catalytic converters, since the ability to give up and reabsorb oxygen is the working mechanism. The high-temperature superconductor YBa2Cu3O(7−δ) has a superconducting transition temperature that depends sensitively on δ, the oxygen deficiency, and controlling that number to within a few hundredths is the central difficulty in making the material. Lithium-ion battery cathodes such as LiCoO2 function by lithium content varying continuously during charge and discharge, which is non-stoichiometry deliberately exploited.

There is a second, quite different sense in which composition can vary: isotopic variation. Heavy water, D2O, has the same chemical formula as ordinary water but a molar mass of 20.03 rather than 18.015, and its percent composition differs substantially. This is not a violation of definite proportions, since the law concerns elements rather than isotopes, but it does mean that a precise mass measurement can depend on isotopic source. For most work the effect is negligible; for isotope-ratio mass spectrometry it is the entire signal.

sections.heading: Errors, Rounding Traps, and Significant Figures
sections.body:
Almost every wrong answer in this subject comes from a small number of recurring mistakes rather than from misunderstanding the chemistry. Knowing the list is worth more than any amount of additional theory.

Rounding too early is by a wide margin the most common. Because the procedure divides mole values by the smallest of them, any error introduced earlier is amplified by that division. Carrying only two significant figures through the mole calculation can turn a true ratio of 2.00 into something reading 1.9 or 2.1, and worse, can turn a genuine 2.50 into an ambiguous 2.4 that invites incorrect rounding. Carry four or five significant figures throughout and round only at the final step.

Mishandling parentheses is second. Ca(NO3)2 contains six oxygens, not three. Al2(SO4)3 contains twelve oxygens and three sulfurs. Writing out the atom inventory explicitly before touching a calculator eliminates this error entirely and costs almost nothing.
