Forcing a fractional ratio to a whole number is third, and it is a conceptual error rather than an arithmetic one. A ratio of 1.50 is not 2. A ratio of 1.33 is not 1. These must be cleared by multiplying every ratio by 2 or 3 respectively. Conversely, treating 1.98 as a genuine fraction and multiplying everything by 50 to clear it produces an absurd formula and is a sign that the rounding judgment has been misapplied in the other direction. The working rule is that values within roughly 0.02 of an integer are rounding artefacts, values within 0.02 of a clean fraction such as one half, one third or one quarter are real, and anything else indicates a problem with the data.

Confusing mass percent with mole percent is a fourth and conceptually deeper error. Water is two-thirds hydrogen by atom count and one-ninth hydrogen by mass. These are different quantities answering different questions, and the units must be stated.

Significant figures deserve a plain rule. Multiplication and division carry the number of significant figures of the least precise input. If a sample mass is given as 5.00 grams, three figures, no downstream result can honestly carry five. Percent compositions are conventionally reported to two decimal places in analytical work because that is roughly the precision good instrumentation achieves.

Finally, the sum check. Percentages must total 100 within rounding, typically 99.9 to 100.1. A total of 97 or 103 means an arithmetic error, an unaccounted element, or an impure sample, and it should stop you rather than be waved through. In professional analytical practice, agreement between found and calculated composition to within 0.4 percentage points on carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen is the conventional threshold for accepting that a compound is what it is claimed to be and is adequately pure.

sections.heading: Modern Methods and the Limits of Composition
sections.body:
Classical combustion analysis has not disappeared, but it now occupies a narrower role, and understanding what displaced it clarifies what percent composition can and cannot do.

High-resolution mass spectrometry is the principal successor. Rather than measuring bulk elemental proportions, it measures the mass of individual molecular ions with enough precision to determine composition directly. The insight that makes this possible is that atomic masses are not whole numbers, so different elemental combinations with the same nominal mass have measurably different exact masses. Carbon monoxide, nitrogen gas and ethylene all have nominal mass 28, but their exact masses are 27.9949, 28.0062 and 28.0313 respectively. An instrument resolving to a few parts per million can distinguish them unambiguously and can often assign a unique molecular formula from a single measurement on a few nanograms of material.

Other techniques address elements that combustion handles poorly. Inductively coupled plasma methods, either optical emission or mass spectrometry, determine metals and many non-metals at parts-per-billion levels and are the standard for ores, alloys, soils, water and biological samples. X-ray fluorescence gives rapid non-destructive elemental analysis and is used on production lines, in museums for pigment analysis, and in handheld form for scrap-metal sorting. Ion chromatography quantifies halides and other anions. Atomic absorption spectroscopy, older but still widespread, remains a workhorse for specific metals.

For all the sophistication, the underlying arithmetic is unchanged. Every one of these methods returns proportions, and converting proportions to a formula is still the mole-ratio calculation. The instrumentation improved; the logic did not.

The honest limits are worth restating together. Percent composition cannot distinguish isomers, since ethanol and dimethyl ether are compositionally identical. It cannot distinguish a compound from a mixture that happens to have the same overall composition, which is why purity must be independently established. It cannot give a molecular formula without an independent mass. It says nothing about structure, bonding, geometry or reactivity. And in the specific case of non-stoichiometric solids the very idea of a fixed composition partially breaks down.

What it does, it does uniquely well. It tells you which elements are present and in what proportion, using nothing but a balance and a furnace. It is the most direct available check that a synthesized compound contains what it should and not what it should not. It converts a quantity you can weigh into a statement about atoms you will never see. For anyone working through a problem with no instrument beyond a balance, the sequence remains exactly what it was in Liebig's laboratory in 1830: measure masses, divide by atomic masses to get moles, reduce to the simplest whole-number ratio, and check the answer by working backwards to the percentages you started from.

guides.title: Solution Stoichiometry and Titration Calculations
guides.summary: How to count molecules by measuring volumes: the mole, concentration units, dilution, reacting ratios in solution, and the full arithmetic and practice of titration, including acid-base, redox, complexometric and precipitation methods, with worked numbers and error analysis.

sections.heading: Why Chemists Count by Volume
sections.body: Chemical reactions happen between individual particles in fixed whole-number ratios. One molecule of methane needs exactly two molecules of oxygen; one hydroxide ion neutralises exactly one hydrogen ion. But nobody can count particles directly, and the numbers involved are absurd: a teaspoon of water contains about 1.7 times ten to the twenty-third molecules. The entire practical apparatus of stoichiometry exists to bridge that gap, converting quantities we can measure — mass on a balance, volume in a burette — into the particle counts that the chemistry actually obeys. For solids the bridge is mass, and the tool is molar mass. For solutions it is volume, and the tool is concentration. This second route is enormously more convenient in practice, which is why so much of analytical chemistry happens in water. Delivering 24.85 millilitres of a solution from a burette takes seconds and is reproducible to better than a part in a thousand; weighing out the corresponding fifty milligrams of a hygroscopic solid to the same relative precision is far harder, and the solid may absorb water from the air while you do it. Solution methods also let reactions proceed at useful rates, because dissolved ions meet one another billions of times a second, whereas two dry powders in contact may take days. The central skill is a three-step translation that recurs in every calculation in this field, whatever the chemistry. First convert what you measured into moles of a substance, using either mass divided by molar mass or concentration multiplied by volume. Second, use the balanced chemical equation to convert moles of that substance into moles of the substance you care about, multiplying by the ratio of the stoichiometric coefficients. Third, convert those moles back into whatever the question asks for: a mass, a concentration, a volume of gas, a percentage purity. Almost every error made by students and by working analysts alike is a failure at one of those three steps, usually the second, and usually because the equation was not balanced or the ratio was inverted. Titration is the archetypal application. You react a solution of unknown concentration with measured portions of a solution whose concentration you know exactly, detect the moment when they have reacted in exactly the ratio the equation demands, and work backwards. The technique dates to the late eighteenth century — François-Antoine-Henri Descroizilles built the first burette around 1791, and Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac refined the method and coined the term titre in the 1820s for assaying silver and bleaching powder. Two centuries later, despite instruments that can detect single atoms, titration remains the reference method for water hardness, acid content in food, oxygen dissolved in rivers and the assay of countless pharmaceutical raw materials, because it is cheap, transparent, and traceable to a weighed mass of pure substance rather than to a calibration curve.

sections.heading: The Mole and Molar Mass
sections.body: The mole is simply a counting unit, like a dozen but vastly larger. Since the redefinition of the SI that took effect on 20 May 2019, one mole is defined as exactly 6.02214076 times ten to the twenty-third elementary entities. That number, the Avogadro constant, is now fixed by definition rather than measured, which means the mole is no longer tied to a physical sample of carbon-12. The entity must always be specified: a mole of oxygen atoms and a mole of oxygen molecules are different quantities of matter, differing by a factor of two in mass. Molar mass is the mass of one mole of a substance, in grams per mole. Numerically it equals the relative atomic or molecular mass, so carbon is 12.011 grams per mole and water is 18.015. The agreement is almost exact rather than perfectly exact under the new definitions — the molar mass constant is now 1.0000000 times ten to the minus three kilograms per mole only to within about one part in ten to the tenth — a discrepancy far below any laboratory measurement, so for all practical work you may still read molar masses straight off the periodic table and add them up. Computing a molar mass is arithmetic with care over the formula. Sodium carbonate, Na2CO3, is two sodiums at 22.990, one carbon at 12.011, and three oxygens at 15.999, giving 105.99 grams per mole. Hydrated salts must include the water: copper sulfate pentahydrate, CuSO4 times five H2O, is 63.55 plus 32.06 plus four oxygens at 15.999 plus five times 18.015, giving 249.68 grams per mole. Forgetting the waters of crystallisation is one of the most common and most expensive errors in preparing standards, because it produces a solution about forty per cent more concentrated than intended. The two conversions to memorise are trivially simple and endlessly used. Moles equal mass in grams divided by molar mass in grams per mole. Moles equal concentration in moles per litre multiplied by volume in litres. Because burettes and pipettes are graduated in millilitres, it is worth internalising the millilitre form as well: moles equal concentration in moles per litre times volume in millilitres, divided by one thousand. Equivalently, millimoles equal molarity times millilitres, which removes the factor of a thousand entirely and is how most experienced analysts actually work. A titre of 22.40 millilitres of 0.1000 molar sodium hydroxide is 2.240 millimoles of hydroxide; no decimal places were harmed in that calculation. Keep significant figures under control throughout. The result of a titration can be no more precise than its least precise input, which is almost always the burette reading, good to about four significant figures at best. Reporting a concentration to six figures because a calculator produced them is a claim about precision that the apparatus cannot support.

sections.heading: Concentration Units and When Each Is Used
sections.body: Concentration answers the question how much solute per how much solution, and there are at least six answers in routine use, each convenient for a different purpose. Confusing them silently is a classic source of order-of-magnitude errors. Molar concentration, or molarity, is moles of solute per litre of final solution, with the symbol c and units of mol per cubic decimetre, usually written as M in laboratory speech. It is the workhorse of solution stoichiometry because it converts directly to moles by multiplying by volume. Its one weakness is temperature dependence: solutions expand on warming, so a solution that is 1.000 molar at 20 degrees Celsius is about 0.998 molar at 30, a difference of two parts per thousand that matters in accurate work and not at all in a school laboratory. Molality is moles of solute per kilogram of solvent, symbol b, units mol per kilogram. Because it is defined by mass it does not vary with temperature, which is why it appears in colligative property calculations: freezing point depression, boiling point elevation and osmotic pressure. Note the difference in denominator — per kilogram of solvent, not of solution — which makes molality larger than molarity for concentrated aqueous solutions and about equal to it for dilute ones, since a litre of dilute aqueous solution contains close to a kilogram of water. Mass concentration is grams of solute per litre, and mass fraction is grams of solute per hundred grams of solution, usually written per cent w/w. Percentage strengths on commercial bottles are normally w/w: concentrated hydrochloric acid at 37 per cent w/w with a density of 1.18 grams per millilitre works out at about 12 molar. Percent w/v, grams per hundred millilitres, is common in biology and pharmacy: physiological saline at 0.9 per cent w/v is 9 grams of sodium chloride per litre, which is 0.154 molar. Parts per million and parts per billion are mass fractions in disguise; for dilute aqueous solutions, where a litre weighs a kilogram, one ppm equals one milligram per litre and one ppb equals one microgram per litre. Mole fraction, moles of one component divided by total moles of all components, is dimensionless and appears in Raoult's law and phase diagrams. Normality, equivalents of solute per litre, is an older unit that persists in industrial and clinical laboratories. One equivalent is the amount that supplies or consumes one mole of reacting units — protons in acid-base work, electrons in redox. Sulfuric acid at 1 molar is 2 normal because each molecule supplies two protons; potassium permanganate at 0.02 molar is 0.1 normal in acid solution because each ion accepts five electrons. Normality has the attraction that equal volumes of equal normalities react exactly, so the arithmetic collapses to N1V1 equals N2V2, but it is treacherous because the equivalence factor depends on the reaction, not on the substance, and permanganate has a different normality in neutral solution. Convert to molarity and use a balanced equation instead.

sections.heading: Preparing a Standard Solution
sections.body: A standard solution is one whose concentration is known accurately, and everything downstream depends on it. There are two ways to obtain one. A primary standard solution is made by weighing a pure, stable substance directly and dissolving it to a known volume; its concentration is known from first principles, limited only by the balance and the flask. A secondary standard solution is made up approximately and then its concentration determined by titration against a primary standard, a process called standardisation. Sodium hydroxide must always be standardised, because the solid absorbs both water and carbon dioxide from the air and a weighed pellet is never the mass of hydroxide you think. The volumetric flask is the key piece of apparatus. It is calibrated to contain a stated volume at a stated temperature, normally 20 degrees Celsius, when filled so that the bottom of the meniscus rests on the graduation line. A Class A 250 millilitre flask is certified to plus or minus 0.15 millilitres, about six parts in ten thousand. That precision is destroyed by two mistakes: making up to the mark while the solution is still warm, and failing to invert and mix, which leaves a denser layer at the bottom and gives every later pipetted portion a different concentration.
ingredients: An analytical balance reading to 0.1 mg, on a stable bench away from draughts and direct sunlight.
A primary standard solid of certified purity: potassium hydrogen phthalate (204.22 g/mol), anhydrous sodium carbonate (105.99), sodium oxalate (134.00) or potassium dichromate (294.18).
A drying oven and desiccator: most primary standards are dried to constant mass, typically two hours at 110 to 120 degrees Celsius, then cooled over silica gel.
A Class A volumetric flask of the required size, plus a beaker, stirring rod, wash bottle, funnel and teat pipette.
Distilled or deionised water; for trace work, water below 1 microsiemens per centimetre conductivity.
A labelled storage bottle: amber glass for light-sensitive solutions, polyethylene for alkalis, which etch glass over months.
steps: Calculate the mass needed: target concentration in moles per litre times flask volume in litres times molar mass. For 250.0 mL of 0.05000 M potassium dichromate that is 0.05000 by 0.2500 by 294.18, or 3.677 g.
Dry the solid if required and cool it in a desiccator to room temperature, since a warm solid sets up convection currents that make the balance read low.
Weigh by difference and record the actual mass, which need not equal the target; the true mass is what enters the calculation.
Dissolve completely in a beaker in about a third of the final volume of water. Never dissolve in the volumetric flask, whose narrow neck cannot be stirred.
Transfer quantitatively through a funnel, rinsing beaker, rod and funnel three times and adding every rinsing.
Let the flask reach room temperature, then add water to a centimetre below the graduation and complete dropwise until the meniscus base sits on the line at eye level.
Stopper and invert at least twenty times, then compute the true concentration as mass divided by molar mass divided by volume in litres: 3.681 g in 250.0 mL gives 0.05005 M.

sections.heading: Dilution and the Conservation of Moles
sections.body: Dilution is the most-used calculation in any laboratory and rests on one idea: adding solvent changes the volume but not the number of moles of solute already present. If moles before equal moles after, and moles equal concentration times volume, then the concentration before times the volume taken equals the concentration after times the final volume. This is the familiar relation written c1V1 equals c2V2, and because the same volume unit appears on both sides you may work entirely in millilitres without converting anything. A worked case: you need 500.0 millilitres of 0.100 molar hydrochloric acid and you have a 2.00 molar stock. Rearranging gives V1 equal to c2V2 divided by c1, that is 0.100 times 500.0 divided by 2.00, which is 25.0 millilitres. Pipette 25.0 millilitres of stock into a 500 millilitre volumetric flask containing some water, then make up to the mark. Note the order: for acids, and especially for concentrated sulfuric acid, always add acid to water rather than water to acid, because the heat of dilution is large — around 880 joules per gram for concentrated sulfuric — and adding water to acid can boil the surface layer and spit corrosive liquid. Serial dilution extends the idea when the required factor is too large for one step. To make a one-in-ten-thousand dilution you would need to pipette 0.10 millilitres into a litre, and a 0.10 millilitre measurement carries perhaps five per cent uncertainty. Doing it as four successive ten-fold dilutions, each 10.00 millilitres into a 100 millilitre flask, uses only measurements the glassware performs well, and the relative uncertainties add in quadrature rather than accumulating catastrophically. The overall dilution factor is the product of the individual factors. A subtlety worth stating plainly: volumes of solutions are not strictly additive. Mixing 50 millilitres of ethanol with 50 millilitres of water gives about 96 millilitres, not 100, because the molecules pack more efficiently together. For dilute aqueous solutions the effect is negligible, but it is the reason that volumetric flasks are used rather than measuring cylinders: you make up to a calibrated final volume rather than adding a calculated volume of solvent. Finally, mixing two solutions that do not react is handled the same way. Combine 200 millilitres of 0.150 molar sodium chloride with 300 millilitres of 0.250 molar sodium chloride. Total moles equal 0.200 times 0.150 plus 0.300 times 0.250, which is 0.0300 plus 0.0750, or 0.1050 moles, in 500 millilitres, giving 0.210 molar. If the two solutions share an ion but differ in the other, compute each ion separately: the sodium concentration and the chloride concentration may differ, and for ionic solutions it is always the individual ion concentrations, not the formula-unit concentration, that govern precipitation and conductivity.

sections.heading: Reacting Ratios in Solution
sections.body: The balanced equation is the exchange rate between substances, and it is the only place the chemistry enters an otherwise mechanical calculation. Getting it right is non-negotiable. Sodium hydroxide neutralises hydrochloric acid one to one, so equal moles react. Sodium hydroxide neutralises sulfuric acid two to one, because each sulfuric acid molecule supplies two protons: H2SO4 plus 2 NaOH gives Na2SO4 plus 2 H2O. A student who assumes one to one will report a sulfuric acid concentration exactly twice the truth, and the number will look entirely plausible. Ionic equations often make the ratio clearer than molecular ones. Strip out the spectator ions and any strong acid with any strong base is simply H plus plus OH minus giving H2O, one to one in protons and hydroxides. The complication is entirely about how many protons or hydroxides each formula unit delivers. Phosphoric acid, H3PO4, is triprotic and can be titrated to the first, second or in principle third equivalence point, giving apparent ratios of one, two or three to one depending on which indicator you chose — an excellent illustration that a titration measures the reaction you detected, not the reaction you intended. Precipitation and complexation follow the same discipline. Silver nitrate precipitates chloride one to one as AgCl, but precipitates chromate two to one as Ag2CrO4. EDTA forms one-to-one complexes with almost every metal ion regardless of the metal's charge, which is exactly why it is so useful analytically: the arithmetic never changes. Redox reactions must be balanced by electrons before any ratio can be read off, and this is where most errors occur, since the coefficients are rarely small whole numbers you could guess. Consider a full example. What volume of 0.2000 molar sodium hydroxide is needed to neutralise 25.00 millilitres of 0.1500 molar sulfuric acid? Step one, moles of acid: 0.1500 times 0.02500 equals 3.750 times ten to the minus three moles. Step two, the ratio: two hydroxides per acid, so 7.500 times ten to the minus three moles of hydroxide are required. Step three, volume: moles divided by concentration, that is 7.500 times ten to the minus three divided by 0.2000, which is 0.03750 litres, or 37.50 millilitres. Two habits prevent most mistakes. Write the balanced equation at the top of the working before touching a calculator, and carry units through every line so that a mismatch announces itself. If your answer comes out in moles per litre squared, you multiplied where you should have divided. And sanity-check the magnitude: a titre should normally land between about 10 and 40 millilitres on a 50 millilitre burette, so a calculated volume of 3 or 300 millilitres is a signal to recheck the ratio rather than to reach for a bigger burette.

sections.heading: Performing a Titration
sections.body: A titration adds a standard solution, the titrant, from a burette to a measured portion of the unknown, the analyte, until an indicator or an instrument signals that the reaction is complete. Two distinct moments must be kept apart in the mind. The equivalence point is the theoretical instant at which exactly the stoichiometric amount of titrant has been added; it is defined by the chemistry and cannot be seen. The end point is the observable event — a colour change, a potential jump — that you use as a proxy for it. The difference between the two is the titration error, and good method design makes it small enough to ignore. The apparatus imposes the achievable precision. A Class A 50 millilitre burette is graduated every 0.1 millilitre and can be read by interpolation to about 0.02 millilitres, with a certified tolerance of plus or minus 0.05. Since every titre involves an initial and a final reading, the reading uncertainty is roughly 0.03 millilitres combined. On a titre of 25 millilitres that is about one part in eight hundred; on a titre of 5 millilitres it is one part in a hundred and sixty. This is precisely why concentrations are chosen so that titres fall in the 15 to 40 millilitre range, and why a titration that consistently needs only 4 millilitres should be redesigned by diluting the titrant rather than accepted.
steps: Rinse the burette twice with small volumes of the titrant itself, and the pipette with the analyte, so that residual water cannot dilute either. Rinse the conical flask with water only, since added water changes volume but not moles.

Fill the burette above the zero mark, then run titrant through the tap until the tip is full and no air bubble remains; an unnoticed bubble that dislodges mid-titration adds its volume to the apparent titre.

Pipette an accurate aliquot of the analyte, commonly 25.00 mL, into a clean conical flask and add the indicator, typically two or three drops. More indicator is not better: the indicator itself consumes titrant.
Take the initial burette reading to two decimal places with the eye level with the meniscus, and place a white tile under the flask so the colour change is visible against a plain background.
Run a rough titration quickly to locate the end point to within about a millilitre, and record it but do not include it in the average.

For each accurate run, add titrant rapidly to about one millilitre before the expected end point, then dropwise, swirling continuously, washing the flask walls with a little distilled water so that no titrant is stranded above the liquid.

Stop at the first permanent colour change that persists for thirty seconds of swirling, and take the final reading. A half-drop can be delivered by touching the burette tip to the flask wall and rinsing it in.
Repeat until you have at least three concordant titres agreeing within 0.10 mL, and average only those, discarding any obvious outlier and recording that you did so.

sections.heading: The Acid-Base Calculation, Worked Through
sections.body: With a set of concordant titres in hand, the arithmetic is short. Suppose 25.00 millilitres of hydrochloric acid of unknown concentration required titres of 23.45, 23.40 and 23.45 millilitres of 0.1012 molar sodium hydroxide, using phenolphthalein. The mean titre is 23.43 millilitres. Moles of sodium hydroxide equal 0.1012 multiplied by 0.02343 litres, which is 2.371 times ten to the minus three moles. The equation NaOH plus HCl gives NaCl plus H2O is one to one, so the same number of moles of acid were present in the flask. Dividing by the aliquot volume, 2.371 times ten to the minus three divided by 0.02500, gives 0.09484 molar, sensibly quoted as 0.0948 molar to three significant figures, matching the four-figure precision of the inputs degraded by the subtraction. Change the acid to sulfuric and only the middle step changes. If the same aliquot and the same titre applied, moles of acid would be half the moles of base, 1.186 times ten to the minus three, giving 0.0474 molar. The lesson bears repeating because it is the single commonest source of a factor-of-two error in student work and in industrial quality control alike. Two further steps commonly follow. To report the result as a mass concentration, multiply by the molar mass: 0.0948 molar hydrochloric acid is 0.0948 times 36.46, or 3.46 grams per litre. To report a percentage purity of a solid, work backwards to the mass of analyte in the aliquot, scale up to the whole sample, and divide by the mass weighed. If 1.250 grams of impure sodium carbonate was dissolved in 250.0 millilitres, and a 25.00 millilitre aliquot needed 21.60 millilitres of 0.1000 molar hydrochloric acid using methyl orange, then moles of acid are 2.160 times ten to the minus three; the reaction Na2CO3 plus 2 HCl gives 2 NaCl plus H2O plus CO2 is one to two, so the aliquot held 1.080 times ten to the minus three moles of carbonate; the whole flask held ten times that, 1.080 times ten to the minus two moles; multiplying by 105.99 gives 1.145 grams; dividing by 1.250 gives 91.6 per cent purity. Notice the dilution factor of ten, arising because the aliquot is one tenth of the flask. Omitting it is the second commonest error, and it produces a purity of about nine per cent, which at least announces itself as absurd. The general habit that catches both errors is to state in words, before calculating, what each number physically is: this is the moles of acid delivered by the burette, this is the moles of carbonate in one tenth of the sample. A final check costs nothing and catches a great deal. Estimate the answer roughly before computing it: if the titre is a little smaller than the aliquot and the titrant is about a tenth molar in a one-to-one reaction, the analyte must also be near a tenth molar, so a computed answer of 0.948 or 0.00948 molar is a misplaced decimal rather than a discovery.

sections.heading: Titration Curves and What They Reveal
sections.body: Plotting the pH of the flask against the volume of titrant added produces a titration curve, and its shape encodes the chemistry of the acid and base involved. For a strong acid titrated with a strong base, the curve begins low and almost flat, because adding base to an excess of strong acid changes the logarithm of a large hydrogen ion concentration only slightly. Near the equivalence point the remaining acid is nearly exhausted, and each drop causes an enormous relative change; the pH leaps almost vertically, typically from about 3 to about 11 over a fraction of a millilitre. At the equivalence point the solution contains only a neutral salt and water, so the pH is exactly 7 at 25 degrees Celsius. Beyond it the curve flattens again in the alkaline region. Titrating a weak acid such as ethanoic acid with a strong base changes the picture in three diagnostic ways. The initial pH is higher, because a weak acid is only partly dissociated: 0.100 molar ethanoic acid, with an acid dissociation constant of 1.8 times ten to the minus five, has a pH near 2.9 rather than 1.0. The middle of the curve is a long, shallow buffer plateau where added base is consumed by converting acid into its conjugate base with little pH change. At the half-equivalence point, where exactly half the acid has been converted, the concentrations of acid and conjugate base are equal, and the Henderson-Hasselbalch relation — pH equals pKa plus the logarithm of the ratio of base to acid — reduces to pH equals pKa. Reading the pH at half the equivalence volume is therefore a direct measurement of pKa, which is one of the most elegant results in the subject. Third, the equivalence point is alkaline rather than neutral, because the salt formed contains a weakly basic anion that hydrolyses; for 0.1 molar ethanoate the equivalence pH is about 8.7. The vertical portion also shrinks. A strong-strong titration jumps through perhaps eight pH units; a weak acid of pKa 4.8 against a strong base jumps through perhaps three, from about 7 to 10. Titrating a weak acid with a weak base produces no sharp jump at all, which is why such titrations are avoided: there is no volume at which an indicator could change decisively. Polyprotic acids give a curve with one inflection per proton, provided the successive dissociation constants differ by a factor of about ten thousand or more. Phosphoric acid, with pKa values near 2.1, 7.2 and 12.3, shows two clear steps; the third is lost because it lies too close to the pH of water itself. Carbonate titrated with acid likewise shows two steps, at about pH 8.3 where carbonate becomes hydrogencarbonate and about pH 3.9 where hydrogencarbonate becomes carbonic acid, which is the basis of the classical determination of a carbonate-hydroxide mixture in a single titration.

sections.heading: Indicators and How to Choose One
sections.body: An acid-base indicator is itself a weak acid whose protonated and deprotonated forms differ in colour. Writing the indicator as HIn, the equilibrium HIn giving H plus plus In minus shifts with pH, and the eye perceives the transition over roughly the range pKa of the indicator plus or minus one pH unit, because a colour appears dominant when its form outnumbers the other by about ten to one. The practical consequence is that every indicator has a fixed working window, and the window must lie inside the vertical portion of the titration curve. Three indicators cover most laboratory work. Phenolphthalein, colourless below about pH 8.2 and pink above about 10.0, suits titrations whose equivalence point is alkaline: any weak acid against a strong base, and strong-strong titrations too, since their vertical section spans that range. Methyl orange, red below about pH 3.1 and yellow above about 4.4, suits titrations with an acidic equivalence point: a weak base such as ammonia or carbonate against a strong acid. Bromothymol blue changes from yellow to blue over about pH 6.0 to 7.6 and is the natural choice for a strong-strong titration where the equivalence point is exactly 7, though in practice the jump is so steep that either of the other two also works. Using phenolphthalein for ammonia against hydrochloric acid, whose equivalence point is near pH 5, would produce an end point far too early and an answer perhaps twenty per cent low. Several practical points follow. Use the smallest quantity of indicator that gives a visible change, usually two or three drops, because the indicator consumes titrant like any other weak acid; for accurate work an indicator blank can be determined by titrating the same volume of water plus indicator and subtracting. Choose the direction of the colour change to favour the eye: it is easier to detect the first appearance of a colour against colourless than the disappearance of one, which is why phenolphthalein titrations are conventionally run with the base in the burette. Note that phenolphthalein fades in strongly alkaline solution above about pH 13. Instrumental detection removes the indicator problem entirely. A pH electrode records the whole curve, and the equivalence point is located as the maximum of the first derivative or the zero-crossing of the second, which is far more objective than a human colour judgement and works for titrations too weak, too dilute or too coloured to see. Potentiometric titration with a suitable electrode extends the same logic to redox and to ion-selective determinations. Conductometric titration, plotting conductivity against volume, gives two straight lines whose intersection is the equivalence point, and is useful for very dilute or very weak systems where no sharp pH jump exists at all.

sections.heading: Primary Standards and Standardisation
sections.body: The accuracy of every titration ultimately traces back to a mass weighed on a balance, and the substance weighed must therefore be trustworthy. A primary standard is a substance that satisfies a demanding list of requirements: it is available in high purity, ideally better than 99.9 per cent; it is stable in air and does not absorb moisture or carbon dioxide; it does not decompose on drying; it dissolves readily; it reacts by a single known stoichiometry with no side reactions; and it has a reasonably high molar mass, so that the weighing error is a small fraction of the mass taken. That last criterion is often overlooked but matters: weighing 0.2 grams to plus or minus 0.2 milligrams is one part in a thousand, whereas weighing 0.02 grams to the same absolute precision is one part in a hundred. For acid-base work the standard primary standards are potassium hydrogen phthalate, molar mass 204.22, used to standardise bases, and anhydrous sodium carbonate, molar mass 105.99, used to standardise acids. Both are dried at around 110 to 120 degrees Celsius and cooled in a desiccator. Sodium carbonate is sometimes prepared by heating sodium hydrogencarbonate at 270 to 300 degrees Celsius, which drives off water and carbon dioxide to leave the pure carbonate. For redox work, potassium dichromate at 294.18 is the outstanding example, being stable, obtainable pure, and non-hygroscopic, while sodium oxalate at 134.00 serves to standardise permanganate. Potassium iodate and arsenic trioxide are used in iodometry. Many important reagents fail the test and must be standardised rather than weighed. Sodium hydroxide absorbs atmospheric carbon dioxide, forming carbonate that titrates differently depending on the indicator, which is the source of the classical carbonate error; solutions should be made from carbonate-free stock and protected with a soda-lime guard tube. Hydrochloric acid is a volatile liquid of variable concentration, though its constant-boiling azeotrope at 20.2 per cent can serve as a standard. Potassium permanganate slowly oxidises water and is catalysed by light and by manganese dioxide, so its solutions must be boiled, filtered through sintered glass rather than paper, stored in the dark and restandardised regularly. Sodium thiosulfate is attacked by bacteria and by dissolved carbon dioxide. Standardisation is simply a titration in which the unknown is your own reagent. Weigh an accurate mass of primary standard, dissolve it in a known volume or titrate it directly in the flask, and calculate backwards. Doing it in triplicate and averaging is standard practice, and the resulting concentration should be recorded on the bottle with the date, because most standardised solutions drift and should be rechecked weekly to monthly depending on the reagent. Certified reference materials, supplied with a stated purity and an uncertainty traceable to a national metrology institute, are the modern formalisation of the same idea, and are what a regulated laboratory will be asked to produce during an audit of its measurement traceability.

sections.heading: Back Titration and Indirect Determination
sections.body: Sometimes a direct titration is impossible. The analyte may be an insoluble solid that dissolves too slowly to give a sharp end point, such as calcium carbonate in a limestone chip or in an antacid tablet. It may be a volatile substance such as ammonia that would escape during a slow titration. It may react sluggishly, or there may be no suitable indicator for the direct reaction. The answer is a back titration: add a known excess of a standard reagent, allow it to react completely and at leisure, then titrate the unreacted excess with a second standard solution. The amount consumed by the analyte is the difference. The classical example is the assay of an antacid tablet. Crush a tablet of known mass and add 50.00 millilitres of 0.500 molar hydrochloric acid, an amount deliberately more than enough. Warm gently and swirl until effervescence ceases and no solid remains, which may take fifteen minutes. Then titrate the leftover acid with 0.200 molar sodium hydroxide using methyl orange, finding say 27.30 millilitres. The arithmetic runs in three lines. Total acid added is 0.500 times 0.05000, or 2.500 times ten to the minus two moles. Excess acid remaining is 0.200 times 0.02730, or 5.460 times ten to the minus three moles. Acid consumed by the tablet is the difference, 1.954 times ten to the minus two moles. If the active ingredient is calcium carbonate, reacting two acid to one carbonate, the tablet contained 9.77 times ten to the minus three moles, which at 100.09 grams per mole is 0.978 grams. Two cautions govern the method. First, the excess must genuinely be an excess and the reaction genuinely complete; an under-reacted sample gives a falsely low result and there is no warning sign. Run a preliminary trial to establish how much reagent and how much time are needed. Second, the answer is a difference between two measured quantities, so the uncertainties do not cancel — they combine, and the relative uncertainty of the difference is larger than that of either measurement. If the excess is small, the difference is well determined; if you add ten times more acid than needed, the titration measures mostly your own excess and the analyte disappears into the noise. Aim for an excess of roughly twenty to fifty per cent. Related indirect strategies include distilling ammonia from a digested sample into a known excess of acid, which is the basis of the Kjeldahl nitrogen determination introduced in 1883 and still used for protein content in food, and liberating iodine from an excess of iodide with an oxidising analyte, then titrating the iodine with thiosulfate. In each case the quantity actually measured at the burette is a proxy, and the chain of reasoning from proxy to analyte must be written out explicitly, because an unstated assumption in that chain is invisible in the final number.

sections.heading: Redox Titrations
sections.body: Redox titrations transfer electrons rather than protons, and the same three-step arithmetic applies once the equation is balanced by the half-reaction method. Balancing is the hard part: write each half reaction, balance atoms other than oxygen and hydrogen, balance oxygen with water, balance hydrogen with hydrogen ions, balance charge with electrons, then multiply the halves so that electrons cancel. Permanganate in acid is the standard example. The half reaction is MnO4 minus plus 8 H plus plus 5 electrons giving Mn 2 plus plus 4 H2O, so each permanganate ion accepts five electrons. Against iron two plus, which loses one electron each, the ratio is one to five: MnO4 minus plus 5 Fe 2 plus plus 8 H plus gives Mn 2 plus plus 5 Fe 3 plus plus 4 H2O. Permanganate is self-indicating: the deep purple ion is reduced to almost colourless manganese two plus, so the end point is the first faint permanent pink from a slight excess, visible at about two parts per hundred thousand. The titration must be run in sulfuric acid, never hydrochloric, because permanganate oxidises chloride to chlorine and gives a high result, and never nitric, which is itself an oxidant. Against oxalate the reaction is slow until warmed to about 60 degrees Celsius and is autocatalytic, accelerating once manganese two plus appears. Potassium dichromate accepts six electrons per ion — Cr2O7 2 minus plus 14 H plus plus 6 electrons giving 2 Cr 3 plus plus 7 H2O — is a true primary standard, and is not self-indicating, so an indicator such as sodium diphenylamine sulfonate or a potentiometric end point is used. It is the reagent behind the classical chemical oxygen demand test for wastewater, though its chromium content has driven replacement where possible. Iodometry is the most versatile family. An oxidising analyte is allowed to liberate iodine from an excess of potassium iodide, and the liberated iodine is then titrated with standard sodium thiosulfate: I2 plus 2 S2O3 2 minus gives 2 I minus plus S4O6 2 minus, a clean two to one reaction. The colour fades from brown to pale straw, at which point starch solution is added to give an intense blue-black complex that disappears sharply at the end point. Starch must be added late, because at high iodine concentrations it forms a complex that releases iodine only slowly and drags the end point. The Winkler method for dissolved oxygen in natural water, published in 1888, is an iodometric determination and remains a reference procedure; the iodometric assay of copper and of available chlorine in bleach are others. Direct iodimetry, titrating a reducing analyte with standard iodine solution, is used for vitamin C and for sulfur dioxide in wine. Other systems include cerium four, which is stable and clean but expensive, and bromate-bromine methods for phenols.

sections.heading: Complexometric and Precipitation Titrations
sections.body: Complexometric titration exploits the formation of a stable soluble complex between a metal ion and a ligand. The dominant reagent is ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid, universally called EDTA, introduced to analysis by Gerold Schwarzenbach in the 1940s. Its great convenience is that the fully deprotonated anion wraps around a metal ion through four carboxylate oxygens and two nitrogens, forming a one-to-one chelate with essentially every metal ion of charge two or higher, regardless of the metal's charge. The stoichiometry never changes, so moles of EDTA equal moles of metal, always. Because EDTA is a hexaprotic system, the concentration of the reactive fully deprotonated form depends strongly on pH, and the effective formation constant with it. Titrations are therefore run in a buffer: calcium and magnesium at pH 10 in ammonia buffer, many transition metals at pH 5 in acetate, and metals with very large formation constants such as iron three, bismuth and thorium in acid around pH 2 to 3, where calcium and magnesium do not interfere. Choosing pH is thus also the principal way of achieving selectivity, alongside masking agents such as cyanide for zinc and nickel or fluoride for aluminium. The classic application is water hardness, reported as milligrams of calcium carbonate per litre. A 100.0 millilitre sample buffered to pH 10 with Eriochrome Black T indicator turns wine red as the indicator binds magnesium; EDTA strips the metal away and the free indicator turns pure blue at the end point. If 12.40 millilitres of 0.01000 molar EDTA were used, that is 1.240 times ten to the minus four moles of metal in 100.0 millilitres; multiplying by the molar mass of calcium carbonate, 100.09, and scaling to a litre gives 124 milligrams per litre, moderately hard water. Precipitation titrations follow an insoluble product. The argentometric determination of chloride has three classical variants. Mohr's method titrates neutral chloride with silver nitrate using potassium chromate as indicator; silver chloride precipitates first, and once chloride is exhausted the brick-red silver chromate appears. It requires pH between about 6.5 and 10, since chromate is protonated in acid and silver oxide precipitates in strong alkali. Volhard's method is a back titration in nitric acid: add excess silver nitrate, then titrate the excess with thiocyanate using iron three as indicator, the end point being the blood-red iron thiocyanate complex. Volhard's back-titration route is preferred in acidic samples and for bromide and iodide, though with chloride the precipitate must be filtered off or coated with nitrobenzene, because silver chloride is more soluble than silver thiocyanate and would otherwise slowly redissolve and consume titrant. Fajans' method uses an adsorption indicator such as dichlorofluorescein, which adsorbs onto the precipitate surface and changes colour when the surface charge reverses at the equivalence point; it is fast and needs no back titration, but demands a finely divided precipitate and is upset by high electrolyte concentrations that cause coagulation.

sections.heading: Errors, Uncertainty, and Reporting
sections.body: A titration result is a number with an uncertainty, and stating the number alone is an incomplete report. Errors divide into two kinds that behave quite differently. Random errors scatter results either side of the truth, are reduced by repetition, and are quantified by the standard deviation of the replicate titres. Systematic errors shift every result the same way, are invisible in the scatter, and are found only by checking against a known sample or a second method. A precise but inaccurate result — three titres agreeing to 0.02 millilitres, all wrong by two per cent because the standard was mis-weighed — is the characteristic trap. Propagating the random uncertainty is straightforward for a chain of multiplications and divisions: the relative uncertainties add in quadrature, meaning you square each, add, and take the square root. A typical acid-base determination combines a pipette at plus or minus 0.03 in 25.00 millilitres, or 0.12 per cent; a burette titre at plus or minus 0.03 in 23.43, or 0.13 per cent; and a standard concentration known to perhaps 0.10 per cent. The combined relative uncertainty is the square root of 0.12 squared plus 0.13 squared plus 0.10 squared, about 0.20 per cent, so a result of 0.09484 molar carries an uncertainty near 0.0002 and should be quoted as 0.0948 plus or minus 0.0002 molar. Note that the largest single contributor dominates, so effort spent improving an already-good term is wasted. The systematic errors worth memorising are mostly avoidable. An air bubble in the burette tip that escapes during the run inflates the titre. Failing to rinse the burette with titrant dilutes it and inflates the titre. Rinsing the conical flask with the analyte instead of water adds extra analyte and inflates the titre; rinsing it with water is harmless, because water changes volume but not moles. Parallax on the meniscus can cost 0.05 millilitres per reading. Sodium hydroxide that has absorbed carbon dioxide reads differently with phenolphthalein and with methyl orange, the discrepancy itself being a diagnostic. Temperature affects glassware calibration by about 0.02 per cent per degree, negligible unless the room is far from 20 degrees Celsius. And an indicator used in excess consumes measurable titrant in a dilute determination. Report the mean of concordant titres, the number of replicates, the standard deviation or the uncertainty, and the method by which the standard was traced. Discard an outlier only with a stated reason or a stated test such as Dixon's Q, and record that you discarded it. A result presented without its replicates is a result that cannot be audited, and in any regulated setting that makes it worthless however carefully it was measured. Where the determination will be repeated over months, plot the results of a control sample on a chart with warning limits at two standard deviations and action limits at three; a drift that no single run would reveal becomes obvious across twenty.

sections.heading: When It Goes Wrong: Diagnosis and Limits
sections.body: Certain symptoms recur, and each has a short list of likely causes. If the end point flashes and then fades on swirling, you are near but not at the equivalence point and the local excess is being consumed; continue dropwise. If it fades permanently after a minute, suspect a slow reaction, absorption of atmospheric carbon dioxide by an alkaline solution, or an unstable indicator. If successive titres drift steadily upward or downward across a session, suspect evaporation from the burette, a leaking tap, or a titrant that is decomposing, as permanganate and thiosulfate both do. If the very first accurate titre disagrees with the rest, it is usually because the burette tip was not full at the start. If the result is systematically about double or half what was expected, the error is almost always the stoichiometric ratio: a diprotic acid treated as monoprotic, or a metal assumed to bind two EDTA. If it is out by a factor of ten, look for a missing dilution factor between an aliquot and a flask, or a decimal point in a molar mass. If it is out by a factor near 1.1 or 0.9, suspect a hydrated salt treated as anhydrous or a reagent that has taken up water. These magnitude signatures are worth learning because they identify the mistake far faster than rechecking the arithmetic line by line. Titration has genuine limits, and knowing them prevents misapplication. It needs a reaction that is fast, complete, of known and single stoichiometry, and detectable. Reactions with equilibrium constants below about ten to the sixth give no sharp break. Very dilute analytes, below roughly ten to the minus four molar, give end points too gradual to see, which is where instrumental detection or a different technique takes over. Coloured or turbid samples defeat visual indicators. Mixtures of similar species cannot be resolved: a titration of a river water sample measures total acidity, not which acids. And the technique is destructive and relatively slow at perhaps ten minutes per determination, so for large sample throughput automated potentiometric titrators, ion chromatography or spectroscopic methods are used instead. Where a result matters and cannot be checked directly, the professional response is to run a recovery experiment: take a sample of known composition, or spike a real sample with a known addition of analyte, and see whether the method returns what you put in. Recovery between 98 and 102 per cent is generally taken as evidence that no gross systematic error is present. Nothing else in the whole procedure provides that reassurance, and no amount of internal consistency among replicates substitutes for it, because a systematic error is by definition perfectly reproducible. If recovery falls outside that window, work through the chain in order — standard, glassware, stoichiometry, end point, interference — rather than adjusting the result, since a correction factor with no identified cause is simply the error written down in a more respectable form.

guides.safetyNote: Titration work involves corrosive and toxic reagents. Concentrated acids and alkalis cause severe burns; always add acid to water, never water to acid, and wear splash goggles, gloves and a lab coat. Chromium(VI) compounds such as potassium dichromate are carcinogenic, and cyanide masking agents release lethal hydrogen cyanide if acidified — never acidify a cyanide-containing solution. Never pipette by mouth. Work with volatile or gas-evolving reactions in a fume cupboard, and know where the eyewash station and spill kit are before you begin.

guides.title: Real Gases and the van der Waals Equation
guides.summary: How and why real gases depart from ideal behaviour, and a full account of the van der Waals equation: its two correction terms, the critical point, condensation, corresponding states, its modern descendants, and where each model fails.

sections.heading: Why Real Gases Refuse to Behave Ideally
sections.body:
Every introductory chemistry course teaches the ideal gas law, PV equals nRT, and every practising chemist,
engineer and meteorologist eventually discovers that it is a lie of convenience. It is an excellent lie: for
nitrogen at room temperature and one atmosphere it predicts the molar volume to within about one part in a
thousand, which is better than most laboratory measurements. But push a gas to two hundred atmospheres, or cool
it towards its boiling point, and the law fails not by a few percent but by factors of two or more. Worse, it
fails in a qualitative way. The ideal gas law says a gas can never condense. Compress it as hard as you like and
it simply gets denser, forever. Yet everyone knows that carbon dioxide in a fire extinguisher is liquid, that
propane in a barbecue cylinder sloshes, and that air can be liquefied and distilled to produce the oxygen in a
hospital cylinder. A law that cannot describe condensation is missing something structural, not merely something
numerical.

What it is missing is molecules. The ideal gas law is derived by assuming that gas particles are dimensionless
points that exert no force on one another except during instantaneous elastic collisions. Real molecules occupy
space and they attract each other. In 1873 a Dutch schoolteacher named Johannes Diderik van der Waals wrote a
doctoral thesis that patched both omissions with two extra terms and, in doing so, produced the first equation
of state capable of describing a gas and its liquid within one continuous mathematical framework. The equation
is not exact. It is quantitatively mediocre near the critical point and it is superseded in industrial practice
by more elaborate descendants. But it remains the single most instructive equation in physical chemistry,
because every term in it corresponds to a physical picture you can hold in your head, and because it predicted
the continuity of the liquid and gaseous states before anyone had a theory of intermolecular forces to explain
why such forces should exist.

The practical stakes are large. Natural gas pipelines are metered at pressures where ideal behaviour is out by
several percent, and a one percent metering error on a large pipeline is worth millions of currency units a
year. Ammonia synthesis runs at one hundred to two hundred and fifty atmospheres, where reactor design depends
on knowing real densities and fugacities. Refrigeration cycles, air separation plants, scuba gas blending,
carbon dioxide sequestration and the behaviour of gases inside a firearm cartridge all sit squarely in the
regime where the ideal law is inadequate. Understanding the corrections is therefore not an academic refinement
but the difference between a design that works and one that vents, freezes or explodes.

sections.heading: The Ideal Gas Law and the Assumptions Buried Inside It
sections.body:
The ideal gas law is usually written PV equals nRT, where P is pressure, V is volume, n is the amount of
substance in moles, T is absolute temperature in kelvin, and R is the universal gas constant, 8.314 joules per
mole per kelvin, or equivalently 0.08206 litre atmospheres per mole per kelvin. It was assembled historically
from three empirical relationships: Boyle's law of 1662, that pressure times volume is constant at fixed
temperature; Charles's law from the 1780s, that volume is proportional to absolute temperature at fixed
pressure; and Avogadro's hypothesis of 1811, that equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure
contain equal numbers of particles. Emil Clapeyron combined them in 1834.

The law can also be derived from first principles by the kinetic theory of gases, and that derivation is where
the assumptions become visible. Kinetic theory imagines a box containing N particles moving in straight lines,
bouncing elastically off the walls. Pressure is calculated as the rate of momentum transfer to the walls per
unit area. Carrying the algebra through gives PV equals one third N m times the mean square speed, and
identifying the mean kinetic energy with three halves kT yields PV equals NkT, where k is Boltzmann's constant,
1.381 times ten to the minus twenty-three joules per kelvin, and R equals k times Avogadro's number.

Three assumptions do the work. First, the particles have negligible volume compared with the container, so the
space available for a molecule to move in equals the full container volume. Second, they exert no forces on one
another between collisions, so their potential energy is zero and the internal energy depends only on
temperature. Third, collisions are perfectly elastic and take negligible time. Each assumption is a statement
that molecules are far apart relative to their own size and to the range of their mutual forces.

That condition is met when the gas is dilute and hot. At standard temperature and pressure, one mole of gas
occupies about 22.4 litres, while the molecules themselves occupy roughly 0.04 litres, less than two tenths of a
percent of the total. The mean spacing between molecules is around 3.3 nanometres, roughly ten molecular
diameters, and at that separation the attractive force between two nitrogen molecules is genuinely negligible
compared with their kinetic energy. Raise the pressure to two hundred atmospheres and the molar volume falls to
roughly a tenth of a litre; now the molecules themselves occupy something like a third of the space and are
close enough to attract one another continuously. The assumptions have not degraded gracefully, they have
collapsed. Everything that follows in the study of real gases is an attempt to write down what happens when they
do.

sections.heading: The Compressibility Factor: Measuring the Size of the Error
sections.body:
Before fixing the ideal gas law it helps to have a clean way of quantifying how badly it is failing. The
standard tool is the compressibility factor, written Z and defined as Z equals PV divided by nRT, or equivalently
PVm over RT where Vm is the molar volume. For a perfect gas Z is exactly one at all conditions. For a real gas Z
is a function of temperature and pressure, and its departure from unity is a direct, dimensionless measure of
non-ideality. If Z equals 0.85, the real gas occupies fifteen percent less volume than the ideal law predicts at
the same pressure and temperature. If Z equals 1.4, it occupies forty percent more.

Plotting Z against pressure for a fixed temperature produces a curve with a characteristic shape that repeats,
with variations, for almost every gas. Starting at zero pressure Z is exactly one, because in the limit of
infinite dilution every gas is ideal. As pressure rises Z first dips below one, reaches a minimum, then turns
around and climbs, crossing one again and rising steeply at high pressure. For nitrogen at 273 kelvin the
minimum is around Z equals 0.98 near 100 atmospheres; by 600 atmospheres Z has risen to about 1.4. For carbon
dioxide at 313 kelvin, closer to its critical temperature, the dip is far deeper, with Z falling to roughly 0.25
before recovering.

The two branches of the curve have distinct physical causes, and separating them is the key insight of the whole
subject. The initial dip below one means the gas is more compressible than ideal, which is what attraction
produces: molecules pulling on each other reduce the force with which they strike the walls, so the measured
pressure is lower than kinetic theory predicts, and the gas collapses to a smaller volume than expected. The
rise above one at high pressure means the gas has become less compressible than ideal, which is what finite
molecular size produces: once molecules are nearly touching, further compression must squeeze the molecules
themselves, and they resist fiercely.

Temperature governs which effect dominates. At high temperature, kinetic energy overwhelms the attractive
potential and the dip nearly vanishes; the curve rises monotonically from one. There exists for each gas a
particular temperature, called the Boyle temperature, at which the two effects cancel at low pressure so that Z
remains one over an unusually wide pressure range and the gas mimics ideality far beyond its normal limits. The
Boyle temperature is 346 kelvin for nitrogen, 714 kelvin for carbon dioxide, and only 22 kelvin for helium,
which is why helium behaves almost ideally at room temperature while carbon dioxide does not. Any successful
equation of state must reproduce this whole family of behaviours from a small number of constants.

sections.heading: Intermolecular Forces: The Physical Origin of Non-Ideality
sections.body:
The attraction that bends the compressibility curve downwards is real and has a name that honours the same man
as the equation: van der Waals forces. He postulated them from thermodynamic necessity in 1873; the quantum
mechanical explanation of the most universal of them did not arrive until Fritz London's work in 1930. There are
three distinct contributions, all of which fall off steeply with distance.

The first is the Keesom or dipole-dipole interaction, which acts between molecules that carry a permanent
separation of charge. Water, with a dipole moment of 1.85 debye, and hydrogen chloride, at 1.08 debye, attract
each other because tumbling molecules spend slightly more time in orientations where positive faces negative.
Averaged over all orientations at temperature T, the energy of this interaction varies as the fourth power of
the dipole moment divided by temperature and by the sixth power of separation. The second is the Debye or
induction interaction, in which a permanent dipole polarises a neighbouring molecule and then attracts the
dipole it has induced. The third, and the only one present in every substance without exception, is the London
dispersion interaction. Even in a perfectly symmetrical atom such as argon, the electron cloud fluctuates; at
any instant it has a transient dipole, which induces a correlated transient dipole in a neighbour, and the two
attract. Dispersion energy scales with the polarisability of the molecules and, crucially, also with the inverse
sixth power of separation.

That common inverse-sixth-power dependence is what makes a single correction term work so well. Whatever the
mechanistic mix, the long-range attractive potential between two neutral molecules goes as minus C divided by r
to the sixth, where C is a constant characteristic of the pair. At short range the behaviour is entirely
different: when electron clouds begin to overlap, the Pauli exclusion principle forces electrons into higher
orbitals and the energy rises almost vertically. This repulsion is often modelled as an inverse twelfth power,
giving the familiar Lennard-Jones potential, though an exponential is physically more accurate.

The result is a potential energy curve with a steep repulsive wall at short range, a minimum at an equilibrium
separation, and a long attractive tail. For argon the well depth is about 1.7 kilojoules per mole at a
separation of 0.38 nanometres; for nitrogen roughly 0.8 kilojoules per mole; for water, where hydrogen bonding
adds a much stronger and directional term, the effective well depth exceeds 20 kilojoules per mole. Compare
these with the average thermal energy, which at 298 kelvin is RT equals 2.48 kilojoules per mole. For argon the
well is comparable to thermal energy, so attraction matters but does not dominate; for water it is nearly ten
times thermal energy, which is why water is a liquid at room temperature while argon is a gas down to 87 kelvin.
The whole periodic pattern of boiling points follows from the relative sizes of these two numbers.

sections.heading: Van der Waals and the 1873 Thesis That Changed Physics
sections.body:
Johannes Diderik van der Waals was born in Leiden in 1837, the son of a carpenter. He had no classical education
and therefore, under Dutch law of the time, could not initially sit university examinations. He worked as a
schoolteacher and later as a school director, studying part time, until legal changes let him take his degree.
He was thirty-six when he defended his doctoral thesis at Leiden in June 1873, under the title Over de
Continuïteit van den Gas- en Vloeistoftoestand, On the Continuity of the Gaseous and Liquid States. James Clerk
Maxwell learned Dutch, by his own account, in order to read it, and reviewed it in Nature with the remark that
the name of van der Waals would soon be among the foremost in molecular science. Van der Waals received the
Nobel Prize in Physics in 1910 and died in 1923.

The intellectual context matters. In 1869 Thomas Andrews had published careful measurements on carbon dioxide
showing that above 31.1 degrees Celsius no amount of pressure would produce a liquid meniscus; the distinction
between liquid and gas simply vanished. Andrews called that temperature the critical point and argued that
liquid and gas were not two different states of matter but two regions of one continuous fluid state. Nobody
could explain it. The prevailing view still treated liquids and gases as fundamentally distinct, and the caloric
and molecular theories of the era offered no bridge.

Van der Waals's contribution was to take the kinetic theory seriously and ask what minimal modifications would
be required if molecules had size and attracted each other. He did not derive his terms rigorously from
statistical mechanics, which did not yet exist in usable form; he argued them semi-empirically, using Clausius's
virial theorem and physical reasoning. The result was an equation of state with two adjustable constants that
simultaneously described the gas at low density, the liquid at high density, the continuous transition between
them, and the existence and location of the critical point.

The prediction that made his reputation practically, rather than merely theoretically, was the law of
corresponding states, which he published in 1880. It implied that if you knew the critical temperature and
pressure of a substance you could estimate its behaviour everywhere, and by extension you could estimate the
conditions required to liquefy a gas you had never liquefied. James Dewar used this reasoning towards liquid
hydrogen, achieved in 1898, and Heike Kamerlingh Onnes, van der Waals's colleague at Leiden, used it explicitly
in designing the cascade apparatus that liquefied helium in 1908 at 4.2 kelvin. That achievement led directly to
Onnes's discovery of superconductivity three years later. A schoolteacher's equation about molecular size and
stickiness is thus an ancestor of an entire branch of low-temperature physics.

sections.heading: The Excluded Volume Correction: Where the Constant b Comes From
sections.body:
The first repair to the ideal gas law addresses the assumption that molecules are points. If each molecule
occupies a finite volume, then the space genuinely available for the centre of any given molecule to wander in
is less than the container volume. Van der Waals therefore replaced V with V minus nb, where b is a constant
with units of volume per mole, and the corrected equation for a purely repulsive gas reads P equals nRT divided
by the quantity V minus nb. Because the denominator is smaller, the predicted pressure is higher than ideal,
which is exactly the high-pressure behaviour observed when the compressibility factor climbs above one.

The value of b is not simply the volume of the molecules themselves, and the factor by which it differs is worth
working through because it is a common source of confusion. Model the molecules as hard spheres of diameter d.
Two such spheres cannot approach closer than centre-to-centre distance d, so around each molecule there is a
sphere of radius d, of volume four thirds pi d cubed, from which the centre of any other molecule is excluded.
That excluded volume is eight times the volume of one molecule, since a molecule of diameter d has volume four
thirds pi times d over two, all cubed. However, the excluded volume is shared between the pair, so the excluded
volume attributable to each molecule is four times its own volume. Multiplying by Avogadro's number gives b
equal to four times the actual molar volume of the molecules themselves.

Numerically this works out sensibly. For nitrogen b is 0.0387 litres per mole, implying a molecular volume of
about 0.0097 litres per mole, and from that a molecular diameter near 0.31 nanometres, which agrees well with
values from viscosity measurements and crystal structures. For helium, the smallest common gas, b is 0.0237
litres per mole; for the large and floppy molecule n-octane it is 0.237 litres per mole, ten times helium's
value, exactly as one would expect from size.

The correction also carries an important structural consequence: it puts a hard floor under the volume. As
pressure tends to infinity, V tends towards nb and no further. That is the equation's crude but essential
statement that matter is not infinitely compressible, and it is what allows the equation to describe a liquid at
all. It also, incidentally, gives a rough estimate of liquid density. If a substance's liquid molar volume were
simply b, liquid nitrogen would have a molar volume of 38.7 millilitres and hence a density of 0.72 grams per
millilitre; the true value is 0.81. Being within about eleven percent from a constant fitted to gas-phase data
is a striking success for such a simple picture, and the persistent underestimate reflects the fact that real
molecules are soft, not hard, spheres.

sections.heading: The Cohesion Pressure Correction and the Constant a
sections.body:
The second repair addresses attraction. A molecule in the bulk of a gas is pulled equally in all directions by
its neighbours, so the net force on it is zero and its motion is unaffected. A molecule about to strike the
container wall is in a different situation: it has neighbours behind it but none in front, so it experiences a
net inward pull that decelerates it slightly. It therefore hits the wall with less momentum than kinetic theory
assumes, and the measured pressure is lower than the pressure the same molecules would exert if they did not
attract each other.

Van der Waals wrote the size of that deficit as a term proportional to the square of the number density. The
reasoning is straightforward. The number of molecules in the surface layer available to be slowed is
proportional to the density, and the strength of the retarding pull on each one is proportional to the density
of the molecules behind it. Two proportionalities multiply, so the pressure deficit varies as density squared,
that is, as n squared over V squared. The proportionality constant is called a, and it has units of pressure
times volume squared per mole squared, conventionally litre squared atmospheres per mole squared.

The corrected relationship is therefore that the ideal kinetic pressure equals the measured pressure plus a n
squared over V squared. Combining this with the excluded volume gives the full van der Waals equation: the
quantity P plus a n squared over V squared, multiplied by the quantity V minus nb, equals nRT. In molar form,
with Vm the volume per mole, it reads P plus a over Vm squared, times Vm minus b, equals RT. Written explicitly
for pressure, P equals RT over the quantity Vm minus b, minus a over Vm squared. That form makes the competition
transparent: the first term is a repulsive contribution that diverges as Vm approaches b, the second is an
attractive contribution that subtracts from it, and the balance between them at any given temperature and
density determines everything the equation predicts.

The term a over Vm squared is often called the internal pressure or cohesion pressure, and it can be startlingly
large. For water vapour, with a equal to 5.54 litre squared atmospheres per mole squared, at a molar volume
equal to that of liquid water, roughly 0.018 litres per mole, the cohesion pressure is about seventeen thousand
atmospheres. That is not a fictional number: it is the internal tension that holds a liquid together and the
reason a column of water in a tree's xylem can be pulled to negative pressures without cavitating. For helium,
with a equal to 0.0346, the same calculation gives a cohesion pressure hundreds of times smaller, which is why
helium remains liquid only below 5.2 kelvin and never solidifies at atmospheric pressure at all. The constant a
is, in effect, a single number summarising how sticky a substance's molecules are.

sections.heading: What the Constants Mean Numerically Across Real Substances
sections.body:
The two constants are usually obtained by fitting to experimental critical data, and a table of them is a
compact summary of molecular character. Helium has a equal to 0.0346 litre squared atmospheres per mole squared
and b equal to 0.0238 litres per mole. Hydrogen: a of 0.2476, b of 0.0266. Nitrogen: 1.370 and 0.0387. Oxygen:
1.382 and 0.0319. Argon: 1.355 and 0.0320. Carbon dioxide: 3.658 and 0.0429. Ammonia: 4.225 and 0.0371. Water:
5.537 and 0.0305. Methane: 2.303 and 0.0431. Benzene: 18.82 and 0.1193. n-Octane: 37.88 and 0.2374.

Reading down the a column tells a clean story about intermolecular forces. Helium, a small closed-shell atom
with two electrons and very low polarisability, is the least sticky substance known. Hydrogen is barely better.
The diatomics nitrogen, oxygen and argon cluster near 1.4, reflecting similar polarisabilities. Carbon dioxide's
higher value comes from its larger electron cloud and substantial quadrupole moment. Ammonia and water break the
size trend entirely: water is a small molecule, smaller than carbon dioxide by the b column, yet it has the
highest a of any simple substance in the list, because hydrogen bonding adds an attraction of about 20
kilojoules per mole that dwarfs dispersion. Benzene and octane, by contrast, are sticky because they are large,
with many electrons and correspondingly high polarisability, and that is a pure dispersion effect.

The b column tracks molecular size almost monotonically, which is a useful sanity check on the physical
interpretation. Octane's b is ten times helium's, consistent with a molecule containing eight carbons and
eighteen hydrogens against a single small atom. Note that water's b of 0.0305 is smaller than nitrogen's,
correctly capturing the fact that a water molecule is genuinely compact.

Two warnings about these constants matter in practice. First, they are not universal physical constants of a
substance but fitting parameters, and the values you get depend on what data you fit to. Constants derived from
critical properties differ from those derived by fitting the low-pressure second virial coefficient, sometimes
by ten percent or more, and neither set is wrong. Always use a consistent source. Second, the units are a
recurring source of error. If a is quoted in litre squared atmospheres per mole squared, you must use volumes in
litres, pressures in atmospheres and R as 0.08206. In SI, a for nitrogen is 0.1370 pascal metre to the sixth per
mole squared and b is 3.87 times ten to the minus five cubic metres per mole, with R as 8.314. Mixing systems
produces answers wrong by many orders of magnitude, and this is by far the most common student and engineer
mistake with the equation. A useful habit is to carry units through the arithmetic explicitly rather than
plugging in bare numbers, and to check at the end that the attractive term a over Vm squared has come out in the
same pressure units as the repulsive term, since those two must be subtracted from one another.

sections.heading: Isotherms, the Critical Point and Predicting Critical Constants
sections.body:
The real power of the equation appears when you plot pressure against molar volume at constant temperature. At
high temperature the curve is a smooth monotonic decrease, close to the hyperbola of Boyle's law. As temperature
falls, the curve develops a shoulder, and below a particular temperature it acquires a genuine wiggle: pressure
falls, then rises, then falls again as volume increases. That wiggle is a mathematical maximum and minimum, and
between them lies a region where the equation predicts that increasing the volume increases the pressure, which
is mechanically impossible for a stable homogeneous fluid.

Between the smooth curves and the wiggly ones lies exactly one isotherm on which the maximum and minimum have
merged into a single horizontal inflection point. That is the critical isotherm, and the point itself is the
critical point. Mathematically it is defined by the simultaneous conditions that the first derivative of P with
respect to Vm at constant T is zero, and the second derivative is also zero. Applying both conditions to the van
der Waals equation gives a solvable pair of simultaneous equations, and the results are remarkably clean: the
critical molar volume equals 3b, the critical temperature equals 8a divided by 27Rb, and the critical pressure
equals a divided by 27b squared.

These can be inverted to obtain the constants from measured critical data, which is the standard route: a equals
27 R squared Tc squared divided by 64 Pc, and b equals R Tc divided by 8 Pc. For carbon dioxide, with Tc equal
to 304.2 kelvin and Pc equal to 72.9 atmospheres, this yields a of 3.61 and b of 0.0428, agreeing closely with
tabulated values.

Above the critical temperature the substance is a supercritical fluid, with the density of a liquid and the
diffusivity and zero surface tension of a gas, which is why supercritical carbon dioxide above 304 kelvin and 73
atmospheres is used to decaffeinate coffee: it penetrates plant material like a gas and dissolves like a
solvent.

The equation also makes a striking universal prediction. Combining the three critical expressions gives the
