critical compressibility factor Zc equals Pc Vc over R Tc equals three eighths, or 0.375, for every substance
without exception, since a and b cancel completely. This is testable and it is wrong, but wrong in an
illuminating way. Measured values are 0.292 for nitrogen, 0.274 for carbon dioxide, 0.291 for argon, 0.229 for
water and 0.302 for helium. Most simple substances cluster near 0.27 to 0.30, well below 0.375, so the equation
systematically overestimates the critical volume by roughly thirty percent. That the prediction is universal at
all is a genuine triumph; that its value is off by a fixed factor for nearly everything is the clearest single
signal that the equation is structurally too simple, and it is exactly this discrepancy that the later
Redlich-Kwong and Peng-Robinson equations were built to fix.

sections.heading: The Unstable Loop and the Maxwell Equal-Area Construction
sections.body:
Below the critical temperature the van der Waals isotherm predicts something physically impossible. Following
the curve from large volume inwards, pressure rises normally, then reaches a local maximum, then falls as the
volume continues to decrease, then reaches a local minimum, then rises steeply. The middle branch, between the
minimum and the maximum, has a positive slope of pressure with respect to volume. A fluid in that state would
respond to a tiny compression by dropping its own pressure, which would let the surroundings compress it
further, and so on without limit. Such a state is mechanically unstable and cannot exist. The condition for
mechanical stability is that the isothermal compressibility be positive, which requires the slope of P against
Vm to be negative everywhere.

What actually happens in the laboratory is condensation. Compress carbon dioxide at 20 degrees Celsius and the
pressure rises until it reaches 57 atmospheres, at which point a meniscus appears and further compression
proceeds at exactly constant pressure while gas converts to liquid, until all the vapour is gone and the
pressure climbs steeply again. The real isotherm has a flat horizontal segment where the theoretical one has a
loop.

James Clerk Maxwell showed in 1875 how to locate that flat segment from the theoretical curve, using an argument
from thermodynamics rather than fitting. Because the Gibbs free energies of coexisting liquid and vapour must be
equal at equilibrium, and because the change in Gibbs energy along an isotherm is the integral of Vm dP, the
horizontal line must be drawn at the pressure that makes the area enclosed between the line and the curve above
it exactly equal to the area enclosed between the line and the curve below it. This is the Maxwell equal-area
construction, and the pressure it identifies is the saturated vapour pressure at that temperature. The volumes
where the line meets the curve are the molar volumes of the saturated liquid and saturated vapour.

The portions of the loop between the equal-area endpoints and the local extrema are not meaningless. They
correspond to metastable states that genuinely occur: superheated liquid, which is liquid held above its boiling
point without boiling, and supercooled or supersaturated vapour, which is vapour compressed beyond its
condensation pressure without condensing. Both are real and both are consequential. Superheated water in a
microwave can flash to steam violently when disturbed. Supersaturated vapour is what makes a cloud chamber work
and what allows clouds to persist below the dew point in clean air. Only the truly unstable middle branch, where
the slope is positive, corresponds to nothing observable. The equation thus not only reproduces condensation, it
correctly separates the metastable from the impossible, which is more physics than anyone had a right to expect
from two fitted constants.

sections.heading: The Law of Corresponding States and Reduced Variables
sections.body:
In 1880 van der Waals extracted from his equation a result of far broader reach than the equation itself.
Suppose you measure every property in units of its own critical value: define the reduced temperature Tr as T
over Tc, the reduced pressure Pr as P over Pc, and the reduced volume Vr as Vm over Vc. Substituting the
critical expressions into the equation and simplifying causes both a and b to cancel entirely, leaving the
quantity Pr plus three over Vr squared, multiplied by the quantity three Vr minus one, equals eight Tr.

Nothing substance-specific survives. Every fluid obeying the van der Waals equation follows one identical curve
when plotted in reduced coordinates. This is the law of corresponding states, and its practical content is that
two different substances at the same reduced temperature and reduced pressure are in mechanically corresponding
conditions and will have the same compressibility factor. Nitrogen at 126 kelvin and argon at 151 kelvin are
both at Tr equal to one; they behave alike.

Remarkably, the law works considerably better than the equation that produced it. Plotting measured Z against Pr
for a dozen simple gases at fixed Tr produces curves that overlay within a few percent, far better agreement
than any of them shows with the van der Waals prediction individually. The reason is that the law only requires
the intermolecular potential to have the same shape for all substances, differing by a scale factor in energy
and one in distance. That is approximately true for spherical, non-polar molecules interacting by dispersion,
regardless of the details of the equation used.

Generalised compressibility charts, which plot Z against Pr for a family of Tr curves, were for most of the
twentieth century the standard engineering tool for estimating real gas properties without a computer, and they
remain useful for quick checks. Given a gas, look up Tc and Pc, compute Tr and Pr, read Z off the chart and
multiply the ideal molar volume by it.

The law fails for the substances whose forces are not simply scaled dispersion. Strongly polar and
hydrogen-bonding molecules, water and ammonia above all, deviate substantially, as do long chain molecules whose
shape makes their interaction orientation-dependent, and quantum fluids such as helium and hydrogen where
zero-point motion matters. Kenneth Pitzer's solution in 1955 was to add a third parameter, the acentric factor
omega, defined from the reduced vapour pressure at Tr equal to 0.7. It is zero for argon and the other spherical
noble gases by construction, 0.011 for nitrogen, 0.225 for carbon dioxide, 0.344 for water and 0.399 for
n-octane. Three-parameter corresponding states with omega gives accuracy of one to two percent for most
non-associating fluids and underpins the modern cubic equations used in industry.

sections.heading: Working Through the Equation: Two Numerical Examples
sections.body:
The equation is a cubic in molar volume, which makes solving for volume harder than solving for pressure. Two
concrete calculations show how it is done and how much difference it makes.

First, the easy direction. Suppose one mole of carbon dioxide is confined to 0.200 litres at 350 kelvin. The
ideal gas law gives P equals RT over Vm equals 0.08206 times 350 divided by 0.200, which is 143.6 atmospheres.
Now the van der Waals equation, with a equal to 3.658 and b equal to 0.0429. The repulsive term is RT over the
quantity Vm minus b, which is 28.72 divided by 0.1571, giving 182.8 atmospheres. The attractive term is a over
Vm squared, which is 3.658 divided by 0.0400, giving 91.5 atmospheres. The predicted pressure is 182.8 minus
91.5, or 91.3 atmospheres. The two answers differ by fifty-seven percent, and the true experimental value is
close to 92 atmospheres. At these conditions the ideal law is not approximately right, it is simply wrong, and
the corrections are individually enormous even though they partly cancel.

Second, the harder direction. Given pressure and temperature, expand the equation into standard cubic form: Vm
cubed, minus the quantity b plus RT over P times Vm squared, plus a over P times Vm, minus ab over P, equals
zero. Above the critical temperature this has one real root. Below it, in the two-phase region, it has three,
and the physical interpretation is that the largest root is the saturated vapour volume, the smallest is the
saturated liquid volume, and the middle root lies on the unstable branch and is discarded.

Solving by hand is best done by iteration rather than the cubic formula.
steps: Compute the ideal gas estimate first: Vm equals RT divided by P. This is the starting guess and, for a vapour, is usually within thirty percent of the answer.
Rearrange the equation into an iteration form that converges: Vm equals b plus RT divided by the quantity P plus a over Vm squared. Each pass uses the previous Vm on the right-hand side.
Substitute the current estimate into the right-hand side and compute a new Vm. For a vapour root this converges reliably, typically to four significant figures within five to eight passes.
Stop when successive values agree to the precision you need, usually when the change is under one part in ten thousand.
Check the answer by substituting back into the original equation and confirming that the computed pressure matches the target to within rounding error.

For a liquid root, this iteration will not converge, because the liquid branch is steep. Instead start from a guess just above b, around 1.1b, and use Newton's method on the cubic, or solve the cubic analytically with Cardano's formula and select the smallest positive real root.

Finally, sanity-check the physics: the answer must exceed b, and Z equals PVm over RT should fall in the range roughly 0.2 to 1.5 for ordinary conditions. A value outside that range almost always means mismatched units.

sections.heading: The Virial Expansion: The Rigorous Alternative
sections.body:
The van der Waals equation is a physically motivated guess. There exists a mathematically rigorous alternative,
derived without approximation from statistical mechanics, called the virial equation of state. It writes the
compressibility factor as a power series in density: Z equals one plus B over Vm plus C over Vm squared plus D
over Vm cubed and so on, where B, C and D are the second, third and fourth virial coefficients, each a function
of temperature alone. Heike Kamerlingh Onnes introduced the form empirically in 1901; the statistical mechanical
derivation, due to Joseph Mayer and others in the 1930s, gives each coefficient an exact meaning. The second
virial coefficient B is an integral over the interaction potential of a single pair of molecules, the third
involves genuine three-body configurations, and so on. The expansion is therefore an expansion in the number of
molecules interacting simultaneously, which is why it converges beautifully at low density and poorly at high
density, where many-body terms dominate.

The connection to van der Waals is direct and illuminating. Expand the van der Waals expression for Z as a
series in one over Vm. The result is Z equals one plus the quantity b minus a over RT, divided by Vm, plus b
squared over Vm squared, and so on. So the van der Waals equation predicts a second virial coefficient of B
equals b minus a over RT. That single expression captures the entire low-pressure story. At low temperature the
a over RT term dominates, B is negative, Z dips below one, and attraction rules. At high temperature the term
shrinks, B approaches b and becomes positive, and repulsion rules. B passes through zero at the Boyle
temperature, which the equation therefore predicts as T equals a over Rb. For nitrogen that gives 1.370 divided
by 0.08206 times 0.0387, or 431 kelvin, against the measured 346 kelvin: the right order and the right physics,
about twenty-five percent high.

Measured second virial coefficients are among the most reliable data in physical chemistry, obtained from
precise low-pressure density measurements, and they are the standard route to testing intermolecular potentials.
For nitrogen at 300 kelvin B is about minus 4.2 cubic centimetres per mole; for carbon dioxide at the same
temperature it is minus 123; for water vapour minus 1160, an extraordinary value reflecting hydrogen bonding.
For helium at 300 kelvin B is positive, about plus 12, because 300 kelvin is far above helium's Boyle
temperature.

The practical trade-off is clear. Truncating the virial series after B gives an equation that is accurate to
better than one percent up to about ten atmospheres for most gases and is theoretically clean, but it cannot
describe liquids and diverges from reality well before the critical density. The van der Waals equation is less
accurate where the virial series works, but it keeps working, qualitatively at least, in a regime where the
series has no meaning at all.

sections.heading: Modern Cubic Equations: Redlich-Kwong, Soave and Peng-Robinson
sections.body:
Industrial process simulation does not use the van der Waals equation, but it uses its direct descendants, and
they are recognisably the same animal. Otto Redlich and Joseph Kwong published the first important improvement
in 1949, keeping the excluded volume term unchanged but modifying the attractive term to a divided by the
product of the square root of temperature, Vm, and the quantity Vm plus b. The two changes were the explicit
temperature dependence and the different volume dependence, both introduced empirically because they fitted
data. The result reduced the predicted critical compressibility from 0.375 to a third, or 0.333, a genuine
improvement, and cut typical vapour-density errors from tens of percent to a few percent.

Giorgio Soave's 1972 modification, universally called SRK, replaced the crude inverse square-root temperature
dependence with a function alpha of reduced temperature and Pitzer's acentric factor omega. This mattered
enormously in practice because it made the equation reproduce vapour pressures accurately along the whole
saturation curve, which is the property that governs distillation, flash separation and phase envelopes. SRK
became the workhorse of the natural gas and hydrocarbon processing industries almost immediately.

Ding-Yu Peng and Donald Robinson published their equation in 1976 with a further modified volume dependence in
the attractive term, using the quantity Vm times Vm plus b, plus b times Vm minus b, in the denominator. This
lowered the predicted critical compressibility to 0.307, much closer to the observed 0.27 to 0.30 range for
hydrocarbons, and it substantially improved liquid density predictions, which had remained the weakest point of
SRK. Peng-Robinson is probably the single most widely used equation of state in the world today for petroleum,
gas processing and refrigeration work.

All of these share the essential structure van der Waals invented: a repulsive term with a hard volume floor
minus an attractive term that scales with the square of density. All are cubic in volume, which is not an
aesthetic preference but an engineering one, because a cubic can be solved analytically and fast, and a process
simulator may need to solve it millions of times. All extend to mixtures through mixing rules, most simply the
van der Waals one-fluid rules, in which the mixture a is a double sum over mole fractions of pairwise a values
adjusted by a binary interaction parameter, and the mixture b is a simple mole-fraction average.

Beyond the cubics lie fundamentally different approaches: the Benedict-Webb-Rubin equation with eight or more
constants, statistical associating fluid theory, or SAFT, which explicitly models molecules as chains of
segments with association sites and handles hydrogen bonding properly, and multiparameter reference equations
such as GERG-2008 for natural gas, which achieve accuracies near a tenth of a percent at the cost of dozens of
fitted terms and no interpretability at all.

sections.heading: Joule-Thomson Expansion and the Liquefaction of Gases
sections.body:
One of the most consequential predictions of a real-gas equation concerns what happens when a gas expands
through a valve or porous plug without exchanging heat or doing external work. For an ideal gas, whose internal
energy depends only on temperature, this throttling process produces no temperature change at all. For a real
gas it does, and the effect is the basis of almost all industrial refrigeration and gas liquefaction.

The physics is a competition between the same two terms. As the gas expands, molecules move further apart. Doing
so requires work against their mutual attraction, and that work comes out of the molecular kinetic energy, so
the gas cools. Simultaneously, the finite molecular volume means that expansion releases some of the energy
stored in repulsive near-contact, which warms the gas. Whichever effect dominates determines the sign of the
Joule-Thomson coefficient, defined as the change in temperature with pressure at constant enthalpy.

The van der Waals equation predicts, to leading order, that the coefficient is positive, meaning expansion
cools, when two a over RT exceeds b, and negative when it does not. Setting them equal gives the inversion
temperature, T equals 2a over Rb, which is exactly twice the predicted Boyle temperature. Above the inversion
temperature a gas warms on throttling; below it, it cools. For nitrogen the measured maximum inversion
temperature is 621 kelvin, comfortably above room temperature, so nitrogen and hence air cools when throttled,
which is why the Linde cycle works. For carbon dioxide it is around 1500 kelvin. But for hydrogen it is only 202
kelvin, and for helium a mere 40 kelvin. Throttle room-temperature hydrogen and it gets hotter, not colder, a
fact with direct safety implications for high-pressure hydrogen systems, where a leak can ignite partly for this
reason.

This is precisely why liquefying hydrogen and helium required pre-cooling rather than brute force. Carl von
Linde's 1895 air liquefaction process used regenerative counter-current heat exchange to cascade small
Joule-Thomson coolings into a large one, and it worked because air's inversion temperature is high. James Dewar
liquefied hydrogen in 1898 only after pre-cooling it below 202 kelvin with liquid air. Kamerlingh Onnes
liquefied helium in 1908 by pre-cooling with liquid hydrogen below helium's 40 kelvin inversion temperature, and
reached 4.2 kelvin. Every step of that chain was guided by corresponding-states reasoning derived from van der
Waals's work.

The same physics runs in reverse in everyday life. A carbon dioxide fire extinguisher discharges to a
frost-covered horn because throttled carbon dioxide cools sharply. A propane cylinder in use grows cold and may
frost over. A refrigerator's expansion valve is a Joule-Thomson device, and the choice of refrigerant is
partly a choice of a and b.

sections.heading: Failure Modes, Limits, and Choosing the Right Model
sections.body:
Knowing where the van der Waals equation breaks is more useful than knowing where it works, because the failures
are systematic and predictable. Near the critical point it is quantitatively poor: the predicted critical
compressibility of 0.375 is roughly thirty percent too high for most fluids, and the shape of the coexistence
curve is wrong in a deep way. Experimentally, the difference between liquid and vapour density near the critical
point vanishes as the temperature difference raised to a power of about 0.326; the van der Waals equation, like
every analytic equation of state, predicts an exponent of exactly one half. This is not a fitting failure but a
structural one, arising because mean-field theories average over fluctuations that become macroscopically large
near a critical point. Fixing it requires renormalisation group theory, work for which Kenneth Wilson received
the Nobel Prize in 1982.

Liquid densities are the second systematic weakness. Because b sets a hard floor at Vm equals b while real
liquids compress somewhat further, predicted saturated liquid densities are typically ten to twenty percent
wrong, and errors of that size propagate straight into pump sizing, vessel inventory and heat-exchanger duty. If
you need liquid density, use Peng-Robinson with a volume translation correction, or a dedicated correlation such
as Rackett.

Polar and hydrogen-bonding fluids are the third. A single constant a cannot represent a directional,
saturable, strongly temperature-dependent interaction. Water, ammonia, methanol, hydrogen fluoride and organic
acids all deviate badly, and acetic acid actually dimerises in the vapour phase, so its apparent molar mass
changes with pressure, something no equation with a fixed a and b can express. Use SAFT, or a dedicated
reference equation such as IAPWS-95 for water, which is accurate to parts per million and is the international
standard for steam plant.

Mixtures are the fourth. Simple mixing rules work acceptably for similar molecules, hydrocarbons with
hydrocarbons, but fail for asymmetric or polar mixtures, and a binary interaction parameter fitted to
experimental data is usually essential. Never trust a predicted phase envelope for an unfamiliar mixture without
some experimental anchor.

Practical guidance, then, runs roughly as follows. Below about ten atmospheres and well above the critical
temperature, use the ideal gas law and stop worrying; the error is under one percent. For moderate pressures and
simple gases, the truncated virial equation with a measured B is both accurate and defensible. For anything
involving hydrocarbons, phase equilibrium, or process design, use Peng-Robinson or SRK from a validated
thermodynamic package. For water and steam use IAPWS. For associating fluids use SAFT. Use the van der Waals
equation itself for teaching, for estimating critical constants when nothing else is available, and for building
intuition about which way an error will run.

Above all, sanity-check every result. Compute Z and ask whether it is plausible. Confirm units are consistent
throughout. Check the answer against a measured density if one exists at any nearby condition. An equation of
state is a model, and every model has a domain; the engineering skill is knowing which side of its boundary you
are standing on.

guides.title: The Gas Laws and the Ideal Gas Equation
guides.summary: How gases respond to pressure, temperature and quantity, from Boyle's and Charles's experiments to the ideal gas equation, the kinetic theory behind it, and the ways real gases depart from it. Includes worked calculations, units, and the practical and safety consequences.
guides.safetyNote: Compressed and liquefied gases store large amounts of energy. Never heat a sealed container, never throw aerosol cans or lighters into a fire, and never seal liquid nitrogen or dry ice into a closed vessel, since vaporisation expands the volume several hundred-fold and will burst it. Secure gas cylinders upright and fit the valve cap before moving them. Nitrogen, argon and helium asphyxiate silently: the breathing reflex responds to carbon dioxide, not to a lack of oxygen, so an oxygen-depleted confined space can cause collapse within one or two breaths and must never be entered without testing, monitoring and a standby person. When diving on compressed gas, never hold your breath while ascending; the gas in your lungs doubles in volume between ten metres and the surface and can rupture lung tissue in a few metres of ascent.

sections.heading: Why Gases Obey Simple Laws When Solids and Liquids Do Not
sections.body: There is something startling about the gas laws that is easy to miss when they are met as a set of formulas to memorise. Helium, nitrogen, carbon dioxide, ammonia and methane are wildly different substances. Their molecules differ in mass by a factor of eleven, in shape from single spheres to bent triatomics, and in chemical character from wholly inert to violently reactive. Yet at ordinary room conditions all of them obey the same equation, with the same numerical constant, to within a per cent or two. No such universal law exists for solids or liquids. Steel and ice and mercury each need their own measured coefficients for everything. Gases alone are described by a single relation that does not care what the substance is. The reason is emptiness. In a liquid or a solid the molecules are essentially in contact, and the properties of the bulk material are dominated by the specific forces between those particular molecules. In a gas at atmospheric pressure the molecules occupy roughly a thousandth of the volume of the container, and the average distance between neighbours is around ten molecular diameters. For the overwhelming majority of the time, each molecule is flying freely through empty space, far enough from its neighbours that their chemical identity barely matters. What produces pressure is not the molecules themselves but their momentum: they strike the walls and bounce. Under those conditions the only things that matter are how many molecules there are, how fast they are moving, and how much room they have. Everything specific to the chemistry drops out. That is why one equation covers them all. This insight arrived slowly and in pieces, largely through the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, as experimenters trapped air in tubes and measured what happened when they squeezed it or warmed it. The resulting empirical relations, named for Boyle, Charles, Gay-Lussac, Amontons and Avogadro, were each discovered independently and only later recognised as facets of one law. The unification into what is now written as the ideal gas equation is generally credited to the French engineer Benoît Paul Émile Clapeyron in 1834, with the universal constant given its modern role by Dmitri Mendeleev around 1874. The equation is also, importantly, an idealisation. Real gases deviate from it, mildly under everyday conditions and grossly near condensation or at high pressure. The deviations are not a failure of the theory but a map of exactly where the assumptions of emptiness and indifference break down, and they turn out to carry rich information about intermolecular forces. Understanding both the law and its limits is what separates plugging numbers into a formula from actually knowing what a gas is doing, which matters the moment a real cylinder, a real diver, or a real chemical plant is involved.

sections.heading: Pressure: What It Is, and the Regrettable Number of Units for It
sections.body: Pressure is force divided by the area the force acts on. In a gas, that force is the accumulated recoil of enormous numbers of molecules striking a surface and rebounding. Each individual impact is minute, but at atmospheric conditions a square centimetre of wall is struck roughly ten to the twenty-third times per second, and the sum is steady and smooth. Pressure is not a force pushing in a particular direction; in a gas at rest it acts equally in all directions at a given point, which is why a balloon inflates into a sphere rather than shooting off to one side. The SI unit is the pascal, defined as one newton per square metre, and named for Blaise Pascal. A pascal is a very small pressure; the weight of a sheet of paper resting flat on a desk is of that order. Because of this, the kilopascal and the bar, equal to exactly one hundred thousand pascals, are used in practice. Standard atmospheric pressure at sea level is defined as exactly 101,325 pascals, which is 101.325 kilopascals, 1.01325 bar, or about 14.696 pounds per square inch. It is also 760 millimetres of mercury, a unit inherited from Evangelista Torricelli's barometer of 1643, in which the atmosphere supports a column of mercury of that height in an evacuated tube. Mercury is used because its density of about 13.6 grams per cubic centimetre keeps the column to a manageable height; the same pressure would support a water column over ten metres tall. One millimetre of mercury is also called one torr, and the two are equal to within a part in seven million. A distinction that causes constant confusion in practical work is gauge pressure against absolute pressure. Most pressure gauges, including tyre gauges and the regulators on gas cylinders, read zero when open to the air, so they report the excess over atmospheric. Absolute pressure is what the gas laws require. A car tyre reading 32 psi on the gauge contains gas at about 46.7 psi absolute, and using 32 in a calculation will give a badly wrong answer. The convention is to write psig and psia, or bar gauge and bar absolute, and it is worth doing so explicitly. Two further points matter. Atmospheric pressure is not constant: it falls with altitude by roughly half for every 5.5 kilometres of ascent, so Denver at about 1,600 metres sits near 84 kilopascals, and it varies at sea level by a few per cent with weather. And in a fluid, pressure increases with depth by the density times gravitational acceleration times depth, which adds about one atmosphere for every 10.1 metres of seawater. That single fact governs the whole of diving physiology.

sections.heading: Temperature and Why Only the Absolute Scale Works
sections.body: Temperature in everyday life is a comparative notion measured against arbitrary reference points. The Celsius scale was built by assigning zero to the freezing point of water and one hundred to its boiling point at standard pressure; the Fahrenheit scale used a different pair of references entirely. Both are perfectly serviceable for weather and cooking, and both are useless inside the gas laws, for a reason that is worth understanding rather than merely obeying. The gas laws are proportionalities. Charles's relation says volume is proportional to temperature, meaning that doubling the temperature doubles the volume. On the Celsius scale that statement is nonsense: gas at 20 degrees does not have twice the volume of gas at 10 degrees, and gas at zero degrees does not have zero volume. Worse, the scale has negative numbers, so a ratio can be negative or undefined. A proportional law requires a scale whose zero is a genuine physical zero, not a convenient reference. That zero was found by extrapolation. If you measure the volume of a fixed quantity of gas at several temperatures and plot volume against temperature in Celsius, the points lie on a straight line, and every gas gives a line that, extended backwards, crosses zero volume at the same place: about minus 273.15 degrees Celsius. Different gases, different starting volumes, different pressures, and the extrapolated intercept is always the same. No gas actually reaches that point, because all of them liquefy first, but the convergence is unmistakable and it identifies a true absolute zero of temperature. Guillaume Amontons noticed the implication as early as 1702; William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, put it on a firm thermodynamic footing in 1848. The Kelvin scale therefore places zero at absolute zero and uses degree intervals the same size as Celsius degrees, so a conversion is simple addition: temperature in kelvin equals temperature in Celsius plus 273.15. Room temperature at 25 degrees Celsius is 298.15 K. The freezing point of water is 273.15 K. Note that the unit is written as a bare K with no degree symbol, a convention adopted in 1967. Since the 2019 revision of the SI, the kelvin is defined by fixing the Boltzmann constant at exactly 1.380649 times ten to the minus twenty-third joules per kelvin, which anchors temperature directly to energy rather than to any particular substance. In kinetic terms, absolute temperature is a direct measure of the average translational kinetic energy of the molecules: that energy equals three-halves of the Boltzmann constant times the absolute temperature, per molecule. At absolute zero that translational motion ceases, subject to the residual zero-point motion required by quantum mechanics. This is why the absolute scale is not a bookkeeping convenience but the physically meaningful one. Every gas-law calculation must use it, without exception, and forgetting to convert is comfortably the most common error students and practising engineers make.

sections.heading: Boyle's Law: Squeeze a Gas and It Pushes Back Proportionately
sections.body: Robert Boyle, working in Oxford with his assistant Robert Hooke, published in 1662 the relation that carries his name: for a fixed quantity of gas held at constant temperature, the pressure and the volume are inversely proportional. Double the pressure and the volume halves. The product of pressure and volume is a constant, so a gas at one pressure and volume moved to a new pressure has a new volume given by the first pressure times the first volume equals the second pressure times the second volume. The French physicist Edme Mariotte reported the same result independently around 1676, and in France the relation is still commonly called Mariotte's law. Boyle's apparatus was a glass tube bent into a J, sealed at the short end, with mercury poured into the long open arm. Air trapped in the short arm was compressed as more mercury was added, and Boyle measured the trapped column's length against the height difference of the mercury. His published table shows the product of pressure and volume holding constant to within a few per cent across a fourfold compression, which for seventeenth-century glassware is impressive work. Boyle himself described the result as the spring of the air, imagining the particles as coiled springs or wool fleeces resisting compression, an intuition that turns out to be wrong in mechanism but right in consequence. A worked example makes the arithmetic concrete. A scuba cylinder of internal volume 12 litres is filled to 200 bar absolute at constant temperature. Released into the open air at 1 bar, the same gas occupies 200 times 12 divided by 1, which is 2,400 litres. That number is why a modest steel bottle can supply a diver for the better part of an hour. Conversely, a 500-millilitre syringe of air at 1 bar, sealed and compressed to a volume of 100 millilitres, reaches 5 bar absolute, which is 4 bar gauge and quite hard to hold against with a thumb. The condition that temperature is constant deserves respect, because compressing a gas quickly warms it. Filling a scuba cylinder rapidly can raise its temperature by tens of degrees, and the pressure will fall noticeably as it cools back to ambient, which is why a cylinder filled hot reads short when cool. A bicycle pump barrel becomes warm for the same reason. Boyle's law applies to the isothermal case, where heat has time to leave; rapid compression is closer to adiabatic and follows a steeper relation. In kinetic terms the law is straightforward. Halving the volume puts the same number of molecules, moving at the same average speed, into half the space, so each wall receives twice as many impacts per second per unit area, and the pressure doubles. Nothing about the molecules themselves changed; only their crowding did.

sections.heading: The Temperature Laws: Charles, Gay-Lussac and Amontons
sections.body: Two further empirical relations complete the trio of two-variable laws, and both concern what heat does to a gas. The first, usually called Charles's law, states that at constant pressure the volume of a fixed quantity of gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature. Jacques Charles, a French balloonist and physicist, established it experimentally around 1787 but did not publish. Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac performed more careful measurements and published in 1802, generously crediting Charles for the earlier work. Gay-Lussac's own figure for the thermal expansion coefficient of air was about one two-hundred-and-sixty-sixth per degree; the accepted modern value is one part in 273.15 per degree, and the discrepancy is a fair measure of how hard careful thermometry was at the time. Written as a working relation, the first volume divided by the first absolute temperature equals the second volume divided by the second absolute temperature. A balloon of 2.00 litres at 20 degrees Celsius, which is 293.15 K, carried into a freezer at minus 18 degrees Celsius, or 255.15 K, shrinks to 2.00 times 255.15 divided by 293.15, about 1.74 litres, a visible thirteen per cent contraction. This is exactly the principle behind the hot air balloon: air at 20 degrees Celsius has a density near 1.204 kilograms per cubic metre, and heating it to 100 degrees Celsius at constant pressure expands it so that density falls to about 0.946, giving roughly 0.26 kilograms of lift per cubic metre of envelope. A 2,800 cubic metre sport balloon therefore generates something over 700 kilograms of gross lift. The second relation, variously called Gay-Lussac's law or Amontons's law, holds volume constant instead: the pressure of a fixed quantity of gas in a rigid container is directly proportional to its absolute temperature. Guillaume Amontons had the essential result around 1702, well before Gay-Lussac. The practical consequences are everywhere. Car tyre pressure rises as the tyres warm on a motorway: gas at 20 degrees Celsius and 2.4 bar absolute taken to 50 degrees Celsius reaches 2.4 times 323.15 divided by 293.15, about 2.65 bar absolute, a rise of roughly a quarter of a bar, which is why manufacturers specify cold inflation pressures. The same law is why a sealed aerosol can in a fire becomes a bomb, and why a gas cylinder left in direct sun on a hot day is genuinely dangerous rather than merely inadvisable. Both laws are kinetic consequences of temperature being molecular kinetic energy. Heating makes the molecules move faster, so each collision with the wall delivers more momentum and collisions happen more often. If the container can expand, it does so until the impacts per unit area fall back to match the external pressure. If it cannot, the pressure rises instead.

sections.heading: Avogadro's Law and the Molar Volume
sections.body: The three laws described so far all hold the amount of gas fixed. The missing piece was supplied by Amedeo Avogadro, an Italian lawyer turned physicist, who proposed in 1811 what was then a bold hypothesis: equal volumes of different gases, at the same temperature and pressure, contain equal numbers of molecules. Restated as a law, at fixed temperature and pressure the volume of a gas is directly proportional to the number of moles present, and the constant of proportionality is the same for every gas. The idea was resisted for half a century, largely because it required accepting that elemental gases such as hydrogen and oxygen exist as diatomic molecules rather than single atoms, which contradicted the chemical orthodoxy of the day. Avogadro died in 1856 without seeing his hypothesis accepted. It was rescued by his countryman Stanislao Cannizzaro, who presented the argument decisively at the Karlsruhe Congress of 1860 and in doing so resolved the chaos then surrounding atomic weights. The number of entities in a mole, now called the Avogadro constant, was fixed by definition in the 2019 revision of the SI at exactly 6.02214076 times ten to the twenty-third per mole. The immediate practical consequence is the molar volume: the space one mole of any gas occupies under stated conditions. Here a trap awaits the unwary, because the reference conditions have changed and textbooks disagree. The familiar figure of 22.4 litres per mole applies at 0 degrees Celsius and one atmosphere, which was the older definition of standard temperature and pressure. IUPAC revised the standard pressure to exactly 100 kilopascals, that is one bar, in 1982, and at 0 degrees Celsius and 1 bar the molar volume is 22.711 litres. Neither figure applies at room temperature. At 25 degrees Celsius and 1 bar, sometimes called standard ambient temperature and pressure, one mole occupies about 24.79 litres, and at 25 degrees Celsius and one atmosphere about 24.47 litres. Quoting 22.4 for a room-temperature problem is a routine error worth about ten per cent. The magnitude is worth pausing on. Twenty-four litres is a cube roughly 29 centimetres on a side. That volume holds six hundred thousand billion billion molecules, and yet it weighs only 28 grams if the gas is nitrogen or 2 grams if it is hydrogen. The emptiness is extreme. It is also why Avogadro's law is so useful for reaction stoichiometry involving gases: because volume tracks moles directly, the volume ratios in which gases combine are simply the whole-number coefficients of the balanced equation, a regularity Gay-Lussac had already observed experimentally in 1808 without being able to explain it. Two volumes of hydrogen combining with one volume of oxygen to give two volumes of water vapour is, on Avogadro's reading, simply the balanced equation restated in glassware, and no atomic weights need to be known to write it down.

sections.heading: Assembling the Combined and Ideal Gas Equations
sections.body: Four proportionalities have now been established. Volume varies inversely with pressure, directly with absolute temperature, and directly with the number of moles. Any quantity proportional to several others separately is proportional to their product, so volume is proportional to the number of moles times the absolute temperature divided by the pressure. Introducing a constant of proportionality and rearranging gives the ideal gas equation: pressure times volume equals the number of moles times the gas constant times the absolute temperature, conventionally written as PV equals nRT. Every earlier law is a special case obtained by holding variables fixed. Hold n and T constant and PV is a constant, which is Boyle. Hold n and P constant and V over T is a constant, which is Charles. Hold n and V constant and P over T is a constant, which is Gay-Lussac. Hold P and T constant and V over n is a constant, which is Avogadro. This is worth internalising because it means only one equation needs remembering; the rest are consequences that can be reconstructed in seconds. An intermediate form, the combined gas law, is often more convenient for change-of-state problems where the amount of gas does not alter. It states that the first pressure times the first volume divided by the first absolute temperature equals the second pressure times the second volume divided by the second absolute temperature. Because R and n appear on both sides and cancel, this form needs no gas constant at all and no absolute unit conversions beyond temperature, which removes a whole class of errors. Pressures may be in any unit provided both are the same, and likewise volumes; only temperature must be absolute. A worked example: a weather balloon is released at ground level holding 5.0 cubic metres of helium at 1.00 bar and 288 K. At 20 kilometres altitude the ambient pressure is about 5.5 kilopascals, that is 0.055 bar, and the temperature about 217 K. The new volume is 5.0 times one divided by 0.055 times 217 divided by 288, which comes to roughly 68 cubic metres. The balloon expands by more than a factor of thirteen, which is why such balloons are launched only partly inflated and slack, and why they eventually burst. The equation carries a name that should be read as a warning label. It describes an ideal gas, defined as one whose molecules have zero volume and exert no forces on one another except during instantaneous elastic collisions. No real gas satisfies this. The approximation is excellent for permanent gases near room temperature and around one atmosphere, typically accurate to better than one per cent, and it degrades progressively as pressure rises or as the temperature approaches the point where the gas would condense. Knowing where you sit relative to those limits is part of using the equation properly rather than mechanically.

sections.heading: The Gas Constant and the Discipline of Units
sections.body: The gas constant, written R, is the proportionality factor that makes the ideal gas equation numerically true. Since the 2019 redefinition of the SI it is an exact derived quantity, being the product of the Avogadro constant and the Boltzmann constant, both of which are now fixed by definition. Its value in SI units is 8.314462618 joules per mole per kelvin, and for nearly all work 8.314 is ample. That R has units of energy per mole per kelvin is not an accident of algebra but a physical statement. Pressure times volume has the dimensions of energy: a pascal is a newton per square metre, and multiplying by cubic metres gives newton-metres, which are joules. So the ideal gas equation says that the quantity PV, an energy, is proportional to the amount of substance and the temperature. R is the amount of energy per mole associated with each kelvin of temperature, and dividing it by the Avogadro constant gives the Boltzmann constant, the same quantity expressed per molecule rather than per mole. Because pressure and volume are measured in an unfortunate variety of units, R has an unfortunate variety of numerical values, and choosing the wrong one is the second most common error in gas calculations after forgetting to convert temperature. With pressure in pascals and volume in cubic metres, R is 8.314 joules per mole per kelvin. With pressure in kilopascals and volume in litres, it is again 8.314, in units of litre kilopascals per mole per kelvin, which is a genuine convenience since a litre kilopascal is a joule. With pressure in atmospheres and volume in litres, R is 0.082057 litre atmospheres per mole per kelvin. With pressure in torr and volume in litres, it is 62.364. With pressure in bar and volume in litres, it is 0.08314. In older thermochemical work R appears as 1.987 calories per mole per kelvin. The reliable defence is dimensional bookkeeping. Write every quantity with its unit attached, carry the units through the algebra as though they were symbols, and check that everything cancels to leave what you wanted. If moles per litre come out where kilograms per cubic metre were expected, the arithmetic has already told you something is wrong before any physical intuition is needed. Reserve a moment for a magnitude check too: one mole of gas at room conditions is about 24 litres, so if a calculation returns 240 litres for a mole, a factor of ten has gone astray. A related habit worth adopting is choosing the unit set at the start rather than converting midway. Working consistently in pascals, cubic metres and kelvin with R as 8.314 never fails, though the numbers are sometimes awkward. Working in kilopascals, litres and kelvin with the same 8.314 is usually the most comfortable compromise for laboratory-scale chemistry.

sections.heading: Kinetic Molecular Theory: Where the Laws Come From
sections.body: The gas laws were discovered empirically, but they are not merely empirical. They can be derived from a mechanical model of what a gas is, and that derivation, developed through the nineteenth century by Rudolf Clausius, James Clerk Maxwell and Ludwig Boltzmann, is one of the great achievements of physical science. It explains not only that the laws hold but why, and it predicts new results the empirical route could not reach. The model rests on five assumptions. A gas consists of a very large number of molecules in continuous random motion. The total volume of the molecules themselves is negligible compared with the volume of the container. The molecules exert no attractive or repulsive forces on each other except during collisions. Collisions between molecules and with the walls are perfectly elastic, meaning kinetic energy is conserved. And the average kinetic energy of the molecules is proportional to the absolute temperature, with the same constant of proportionality for every gas. From these, pressure follows by direct mechanics. Consider a molecule of mass m striking a wall perpendicularly at speed v and rebounding. Its momentum changes by twice m times v. Counting how many such impacts occur per second on a wall of given area, for molecules distributed randomly in direction, gives the result that pressure equals one third of the number density times the molecular mass times the mean square speed. Multiplying through by volume gives PV equal to one third of the total mass times the mean square speed, which is two thirds of the total translational kinetic energy. Setting that equal to nRT recovers the ideal gas law exactly, and identifies the average translational kinetic energy per molecule as three halves of the Boltzmann constant times the absolute temperature, or three halves of RT per mole. That identification is the theory's most important product. It means temperature is not a separate primitive property but a direct measure of molecular motion, and it means that at a given temperature every gas has the same average molecular kinetic energy regardless of molecular mass. Heavy molecules therefore move more slowly than light ones in exactly the way needed to keep the energy equal. The theory also yields the distribution of speeds, not just the average. Maxwell's speed distribution, published in 1860 and refined by Boltzmann, is a skewed curve: most molecules cluster around a typical speed, a few crawl, and a small high-energy tail runs far above the average. That tail is chemically decisive, since it contains the molecules energetic enough to react, and it is why reaction rates rise so steeply with temperature. Warming a gas broadens and flattens the distribution while shifting its peak to higher speed, and the fraction in the high-energy tail grows far faster than the average does.

sections.heading: Molecular Speeds, Diffusion and Graham's Law of Effusion
sections.body: Because average kinetic energy depends only on temperature while kinetic energy is one half the mass times the speed squared, molecular speed must depend on molar mass. Setting three halves RT equal to one half M times the mean square speed and solving gives the root-mean-square speed as the square root of three RT divided by the molar mass in kilograms per mole. The numbers surprise most people the first time. Nitrogen, with a molar mass of 0.028 kilograms per mole, at 298 K has a root-mean-square speed of the square root of three times 8.314 times 298 divided by 0.028, which is about 515 metres per second, roughly 1,850 kilometres per hour and comfortably faster than a passenger jet. Hydrogen, fourteen times lighter, moves at about 1,930 metres per second. Carbon dioxide, heavier at 0.044 kilograms per mole, manages about 411. The air in an ordinary room is a storm of particles moving at the speed of a rifle bullet. This raises an obvious puzzle. If molecules move that fast, why does an opened bottle of perfume take minutes rather than milliseconds to be smelled across a room? The answer is collisions. At atmospheric pressure a given molecule travels only about 68 nanometres between collisions, and undergoes something like seven billion collisions per second. Its net progress is therefore a random walk, not a straight flight, and net transport across a room is slow even though instantaneous speeds are enormous. This scrambling motion is diffusion, and its rate depends on pressure as well as molar mass. In a vacuum, or at very low pressure where collisions are rare, transport is fast and direct. Effusion is the related and cleaner case: the escape of gas through a hole small enough that molecules pass one at a time without colliding in the opening. Thomas Graham established experimentally in the 1840s that the rate of effusion is inversely proportional to the square root of the molar mass, which follows directly from the speed relation. The practical form compares two gases: the ratio of their effusion rates equals the square root of the inverse ratio of their molar masses. Helium, at 4 grams per mole, effuses out of a rubber balloon roughly 2.7 times faster than nitrogen at 28, which is why a helium balloon deflates in a day or two while an air-filled one lasts weeks. The most consequential application of Graham's law was uranium enrichment. Uranium hexafluoride made from uranium-235 has a molar mass near 349 grams per mole and from uranium-238 near 352, so the effusion rates differ by the square root of 352 over 349, a factor of only 1.0043. Achieving weapons-grade or even reactor-grade separation therefore required thousands of successive stages in vast gaseous-diffusion plants, the largest of which consumed a substantial fraction of a national electricity supply. That the technology worked at all rests entirely on a difference in the third decimal place of a square root.

sections.heading: Dalton's Law of Partial Pressures and Gas Mixtures
sections.body: Because an ideal gas is indifferent to the identity of its molecules, a mixture behaves as if each component were alone in the container. John Dalton stated the consequence in 1801: the total pressure exerted by a mixture of non-reacting gases equals the sum of the pressures each would exert if it occupied the container by itself. Those individual contributions are called partial pressures. The partial pressure of a component equals its mole fraction, that is its share of the total moles present, multiplied by the total pressure. Dry air at sea level, at a total pressure of 101.3 kilopascals, is about 78.1 per cent nitrogen, 20.9 per cent oxygen and 0.93 per cent argon by mole, so the partial pressure of oxygen is 0.209 times 101.3, about 21.2 kilopascals or 159 millimetres of mercury. That figure, not the percentage, is what physiology responds to. On the summit of Everest at roughly 33.7 kilopascals of total pressure, the air is still 20.9 per cent oxygen, but the oxygen partial pressure has fallen to about 7.0 kilopascals, which is why supplementary oxygen is needed even though the composition has not changed at all. Conversely a diver at 40 metres, at about 5 atmospheres absolute, breathing ordinary air, experiences an oxygen partial pressure near 1.05 atmospheres, which is above the sea-level value and approaching the range where oxygen becomes toxic. The generally accepted working limit for recreational diving is 1.4 atmospheres partial pressure of oxygen, with 1.6 as a contingency ceiling, because central-nervous-system oxygen toxicity can cause convulsions underwater. Nitrogen partial pressure at the same depth produces narcosis. Technical divers manage both by altering the mixture, adding helium to dilute nitrogen or reducing the oxygen fraction for deep work, and every one of those calculations is Dalton's law applied carefully. The most common laboratory encounter with partial pressures is collecting a gas over water. A gas bubbled into an inverted water-filled cylinder arrives saturated with water vapour, and the total pressure inside is the sum of the gas's partial pressure and the vapour pressure of water at that temperature. Water's vapour pressure is about 17.5 torr at 20 degrees Celsius and 23.8 torr at 25 degrees Celsius, values read from standard tables. To find the moles of the collected gas, subtract the water vapour pressure from the measured total pressure before applying the ideal gas equation. Skipping that correction overstates the yield by roughly two to three per cent at room temperature, and by far more if the collection is warm. A related quantity, Amagat's law of partial volumes, expresses the same physics in terms of volume fractions and is used more in engineering than in chemistry.

sections.heading: Working Gas Calculations Reliably
sections.body: Most errors in gas problems are procedural rather than conceptual, and a fixed routine eliminates nearly all of them. The routine below is worth following even when a problem looks trivial, because the failures are silent: a wrong answer from a Celsius temperature or a mismatched R looks entirely reasonable and carries no warning. Consider a worked case as the steps are followed. An automobile airbag must inflate to about 60 litres at 25 degrees Celsius and 1.10 bar absolute using the decomposition of sodium azide, which yields three moles of nitrogen for every two moles of azide. How much sodium azide is needed? Rearranging the ideal gas equation gives n equal to PV over RT: 110 kilopascals times 60 litres divided by 8.314 times 298.15, which is about 2.66 moles of nitrogen. Two thirds of that is 1.78 moles of sodium azide, and at 65.01 grams per mole that is about 115 grams, which is close to the quantity real driver-side inflators actually carry.
steps: Write down every quantity given, each with its unit, and identify explicitly which of pressure, volume, moles and temperature is the unknown.
Convert every temperature to kelvin by adding 273.15 to the Celsius value. Do this first and physically write the kelvin figure, rather than intending to remember it later.

Establish whether each pressure is gauge or absolute. If a reading came from a tyre gauge, a regulator or a manometer open to the atmosphere, add the local atmospheric pressure to convert it to absolute.

Decide whether the amount of gas is constant. If it is, use the combined gas law, which cancels R and n and avoids a whole class of unit errors; if moles change or are the unknown, use the full ideal gas equation.

Choose one consistent unit set before substituting anything, and select the matching value of the gas constant: 8.314 for kilopascals with litres, 8.314 for pascals with cubic metres, or 0.082057 for atmospheres with litres.

If the gas was collected over water or is otherwise a mixture, subtract the water vapour pressure at the stated temperature, or apply mole fractions, so that the pressure used is the partial pressure of the gas of interest.
Rearrange the equation algebraically to isolate the unknown before substituting numbers, so that the substitution is a single mechanical step with nothing left to rearrange under time pressure.
Substitute with units attached and carry them through the cancellation, confirming that the surviving units are those of the answer you want.

Check the magnitude against a known anchor: one mole occupies roughly 24 litres at room conditions and 22.4 litres at zero degrees Celsius and one atmosphere, so a molar volume far from these signals an error.
For stoichiometry, convert to moles first, apply the balanced equation's mole ratio, then convert back to whatever the question asked for, whether mass, volume or pressure.

Finally, ask whether ideal behaviour is a fair assumption at the stated conditions, and note the caveat explicitly if the pressure exceeds roughly ten bar or the temperature is near the substance's boiling point.

sections.heading: Where Ideality Fails: The Compressibility Factor
sections.body: The honest way to measure how far a real gas departs from the ideal is the compressibility factor, written Z and defined as the measured pressure times the molar volume divided by RT. For a perfectly ideal gas Z equals one at all conditions. For a real gas it does not, and the pattern of its deviation reveals the physics. Plot Z against pressure at room temperature for a typical gas such as nitrogen or methane and a characteristic shape appears. Starting at one at zero pressure, Z dips below one as pressure rises, reaches a minimum somewhere in the region of a few hundred bar, then climbs steeply and passes above one at high pressure. The dip and the climb have different causes. At moderate pressures the molecules are close enough often enough that their mutual attraction, the weak dispersion and dipole forces that the ideal model ignores, pulls them slightly together. A molecule about to strike the wall is tugged back by its neighbours, so it arrives with less momentum and the measured pressure is lower than the ideal equation predicts, making Z less than one. At very high pressures the molecules are packed close enough that their own finite size matters: the space actually available to move in is less than the container volume, effectively crowding them further and raising pressure above the ideal prediction, so Z exceeds one. Which effect wins depends on temperature. There is a temperature for each gas, called the Boyle temperature, at which the two influences cancel over a useful range of low pressures and the gas behaves almost ideally. For nitrogen it is around 327 K, close to room temperature, which is part of why air behaves so well. For carbon dioxide it is far higher, near 715 K, so carbon dioxide at room temperature shows attraction-dominated behaviour and deviates noticeably even at a few bar. For helium the Boyle temperature is about 23 K and for hydrogen about 110 K, both far below room temperature, which means these two gases have Z greater than one at essentially all pressures at ordinary temperatures: they are harder to compress than an ideal gas, not easier. The other boundary of ideality is the critical point. Every substance has a critical temperature above which no amount of pressure will liquefy it, because the distinction between liquid and gas ceases to exist. For carbon dioxide that temperature is 31.0 degrees Celsius at 73.8 bar; for nitrogen it is minus 147 degrees Celsius; for water 374 degrees Celsius at 220.6 bar. This has direct practical consequences. A propane cylinder, with a critical temperature near 97 degrees Celsius, holds liquid under about 8 bar at room temperature and its pressure depends on temperature alone, not on how full it is, which is why propane cylinders are weighed rather than gauged. A nitrogen cylinder at the same temperature holds only gas, and its pressure falls steadily as it empties. Near and below the critical temperature, the ideal gas equation is not approximately right; it is simply the wrong model.

sections.heading: The van der Waals Equation and Its Successors
sections.body: Johannes Diderik van der Waals, in his 1873 doctoral thesis at Leiden, proposed the first equation of state that captured both deviations with a physically motivated correction to each. He received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1910 for the work, and James Clerk Maxwell reportedly learned Dutch in order to read it. The reasoning is direct. The ideal equation assumes molecules have no volume, so the space available for motion is overstated; van der Waals subtracted a term proportional to the number of moles, writing the available volume as V minus n times b, where b is an excluded volume per mole roughly four times the actual volume the molecules themselves occupy. The ideal equation also assumes no attractions, so the measured pressure is understated; he added a correction proportional to the square of the concentration, since the strength of the pull depends both on how many molecules are near the wall and how many are pulling them back. The result is that pressure plus a times n squared over V squared, all multiplied by V minus n b, equals nRT. The two constants are fitted per substance and are tabulated widely. In units of litres squared bar per mole squared, a is 0.035 for helium, 1.37 for nitrogen, 3.64 for carbon dioxide and 5.54 for water, a sequence that tracks intermolecular attraction exactly as chemical intuition would predict. The excluded volume b, in litres per mole, runs from 0.024 for helium to 0.043 for carbon dioxide, tracking molecular size. A worked comparison shows the size of the correction. One mole of carbon dioxide confined to 1.00 litre at 300 K gives, from the ideal equation, a pressure of 0.08314 times 300 divided by 1.00, which is 24.9 bar. From van der Waals, the first term is 0.08314 times 300 divided by 1.00 minus 0.0427, which is 26.1 bar, and subtracting a divided by the molar volume squared, that is 3.64, gives 22.4 bar. The ideal figure is about eleven per cent too high, and at higher densities the discrepancy grows rapidly. The equation also predicts a critical point, which no ideal treatment can: the critical volume is three times b, the critical temperature is eight a divided by twenty-seven R b, and the critical compressibility comes out as three eighths, or 0.375, for every substance. Real gases cluster nearer 0.27 to 0.31, so the model is qualitatively right and quantitatively rough. Industrial work therefore uses refinements: the Redlich-Kwong equation of 1949, Soave's modification of 1972, and the Peng-Robinson equation of 1976, the last two being the workhorses of petroleum and chemical process simulation. The most flexible framework is the virial equation, which expresses Z as a power series in inverse molar volume with temperature-dependent coefficients, and whose second coefficient can be calculated directly from the intermolecular potential.

sections.heading: Gases in Practice: Breathing, Weather, Engines and Cylinders
sections.body: The gas laws are unusually visible in daily life once you know what to look for, and several of the applications are matters of life and death rather than curiosities. Breathing is Boyle's law made anatomical. The diaphragm contracts and flattens while the external intercostals lift the rib cage, increasing the volume of the thoracic cavity. Because the lungs are mechanically coupled to the chest wall through the pleural seal, their volume rises with it, and the pressure of the gas inside falls by only one or two millimetres of mercury below atmospheric. That tiny gradient is enough to draw in about half a litre of air in a resting breath. Exhalation at rest is mostly passive elastic recoil. The whole of ventilation is a pressure difference of less than a third of a per cent of atmospheric. Weather is largely the behaviour of a gas expanding and cooling. Air rising in the atmosphere moves into lower pressure and expands, and because the expansion is fast compared with heat transfer it is nearly adiabatic, so the parcel cools without losing heat to its surroundings. Dry air cools at close to 9.8 degrees Celsius per kilometre of ascent; once condensation begins, the latent heat released slows the rate to something nearer 5 or 6 degrees per kilometre. The difference between these rates and the actual temperature profile of the atmosphere determines whether a parcel keeps rising, which is precisely the difference between a clear afternoon and a thunderstorm. Internal combustion depends on the same physics. A four-stroke petrol engine draws in an air-fuel mixture, compresses it by a factor of roughly ten in volume, which raises both its pressure and, adiabatically, its temperature by several hundred degrees, then ignites it. Combustion converts a small volume of liquid fuel into a much larger number of moles of hot gas, and the resulting pressure drives the piston. Diesel engines use compression ratios near twenty so that the temperature rise alone ignites the fuel without a spark. Everyday pressure vessels are worth understanding concretely. A pressure cooker held at one bar above atmospheric raises the boiling point of water from 100 to about 121 degrees Celsius, which is why cooking times fall by half or more and why laboratory autoclaves sterilise at that same 121 degrees for fifteen to twenty minutes. An automobile airbag inflates in roughly 30 to 50 milliseconds by decomposing about 115 grams of sodium azide into some 2.7 moles of nitrogen, filling a 60-litre bag. A carbon dioxide fire extinguisher holds liquid, so it is checked by weight; a compressed-air cylinder holds gas, so it is checked by pressure. Recognising which of those two situations you are in is a genuinely useful piece of applied thermodynamics.

sections.heading: Common Errors, Limits and Real Hazards
sections.body: A short list of recurring mistakes accounts for the great majority of wrong answers. Using Celsius instead of kelvin is the most frequent by a wide margin, and it produces errors that can exceed a hundred per cent without looking absurd. Using a gauge pressure where absolute pressure is required is second, and is especially common in engineering contexts where every instrument reads gauge. Selecting a value of the gas constant that does not match the chosen units is third; the symptom is an answer wrong by a factor near 100 or 8.3 or 0.082, and recognising those factors is a quick diagnostic. Assuming a molar volume of 22.4 litres at room temperature is worth about a ten per cent error and is deeply entrenched. Forgetting to subtract water vapour pressure when a gas is collected over water costs another two or three per cent. Conceptual limits deserve equal attention. The ideal gas equation is a limiting law valid as pressure approaches zero, and applying it above roughly ten bar, or anywhere near the temperature at which the substance condenses, is a decision that should be made consciously and stated. It says nothing whatever about reaction rates, about how fast a gas will mix, or about liquids and solids. Molar volume is not a property of condensed phases and cannot be used for them. And the equation describes equilibrium states; it does not describe the transient behaviour during rapid compression or expansion, where the process is closer to adiabatic and temperature changes substantially. The physical hazards are real and specific. A compressed gas cylinder at 200 bar stores an enormous amount of energy; if the valve is snapped off, the cylinder becomes an uncontrolled rocket capable of penetrating masonry. Cylinders should be secured upright, capped when moved, and never subjected to heat, since pressure rises with absolute temperature and a cylinder at 20 degrees Celsius taken to 200 degrees Celsius in a fire sees its pressure rise by roughly sixty per cent before any relief device acts. Sealed containers holding liquid nitrogen or solid carbon dioxide are extremely dangerous because vaporisation multiplies the volume by several hundred times and will rupture almost any vessel. The most insidious hazard is inert gas asphyxiation. Nitrogen, argon, and helium are odourless and produce no warning sensation, and the human urge to breathe is driven by accumulating carbon dioxide rather than by lack of oxygen, so a person entering an oxygen-depleted confined space can lose consciousness within a breath or two without any sense of suffocation. Atmospheres below about 19.5 per cent oxygen are classed as oxygen deficient, and confined-space entry requires testing and monitoring rather than judgement. In diving, the corresponding absolute rule is never to hold the breath while ascending, because Boyle's law doubles the gas volume in the lungs on a rise from ten metres to the surface and lung rupture with arterial gas embolism can follow from a few metres of ascent.

guides.title: Kinetic Molecular Theory of Gases
guides.summary: How the observable behaviour of gases - pressure, temperature, diffusion, viscosity - follows from molecules in ceaseless random motion, with the derivations, the speed distributions, the real-gas corrections, and where the model breaks down.

sections.heading: The Central Idea and Why It Was Revolutionary
sections.body: The kinetic molecular theory holds that a gas is not a continuous fluid but an enormous swarm of tiny particles flying in every direction, colliding with one another and with the walls of whatever contains them, and that everything we can measure about a gas is a statistical summary of that motion. Pressure is not a mysterious tendency of gas to push outwards; it is the accumulated hammering of countless molecular impacts on a surface. Temperature is not a substance called caloric flowing between bodies; it is a measure of the average kinetic energy of that motion. Once those two identifications are made, the entire body of empirical gas laws collected across the seventeenth, eighteenth, and nineteenth centuries falls out as arithmetic. The numbers involved are worth confronting because they are the reason the theory feels counterintuitive. A single cubic centimetre of air at room temperature and ordinary atmospheric pressure contains roughly 2.5 times ten to the nineteenth molecules, that is twenty-five billion billion. Each nitrogen molecule in that sample is travelling at an average speed near 470 metres per second, considerably faster than a rifle bullet and comparable to the speed of sound, which is no coincidence since sound propagates by molecular collision. Each molecule collides with another roughly seven billion times every second, and travels only about 68 nanometres between collisions, a distance around 200 times its own diameter. The air in a quiet room is therefore an environment of extraordinary violence at the molecular scale, and its apparent stillness is entirely a matter of averaging. The historical fight over this picture was long and bitter. Daniel Bernoulli published essentially the correct derivation of pressure from molecular impacts in his Hydrodynamica of 1738 and was ignored for over a century. John Herapath in 1820 and John James Waterston in 1845 were both rejected by the Royal Society, Waterston's paper famously dismissed by a referee as nothing but nonsense and only published posthumously in 1892 after Lord Rayleigh rediscovered it. The theory was finally established through the work of Rudolf Clausius from 1857, James Clerk Maxwell from 1860, and Ludwig Boltzmann from the 1870s. Even then, prominent scientists including Ernst Mach and Wilhelm Ostwald rejected the physical reality of atoms into the early twentieth century, and Boltzmann's isolation in that dispute is often mentioned in connection with his suicide in 1906. The argument was settled the following year, when Albert Einstein's 1905 analysis of Brownian motion, confirmed experimentally by Jean Perrin in 1908, gave a direct measurement of molecular reality that no one could dispute. Perrin received the Nobel Prize in 1926 for it. What makes the theory worth studying today is not only that it is correct but that it is the clearest example in all of science of reduction actually working: a whole branch of empirical law, built by measurement over two centuries, dissolves into the mechanics of colliding particles, and nothing is left over.

sections.heading: The Postulates of the Ideal Gas Model
sections.body: The theory rests on a small number of explicit assumptions, and it is worth stating them precisely, because every failure of the ideal gas law is traceable to the violation of one of them. A model whose assumptions you can name is a model whose limits you can predict. First, a gas consists of a very large number of identical particles in continuous, random motion. Large is doing real work here: the results are statistical, so they are exact only in the limit of many particles, and a container holding twenty molecules would show wild pressure fluctuations that a container holding ten to the twenty-third does not. Second, the particles are point-like, meaning their own volume is negligible compared with the volume of the container. At standard conditions a mole of gas occupies 22.4 litres while the molecules themselves occupy roughly 0.03 litres of that, about one part in seven hundred, which is why the approximation is good at ordinary pressure and poor at high pressure. Third, the particles exert no forces on one another except during collisions. There is no attraction pulling them together and no repulsion pushing them apart between impacts, so a molecule travels in a perfectly straight line at constant velocity from one collision to the next. This is the assumption that fails first as a gas is cooled, since intermolecular attraction is what eventually condenses it into a liquid. Fourth, all collisions, both between particles and with the container walls, are perfectly elastic, meaning total kinetic energy is conserved. If collisions were inelastic the gas would steadily lose energy to heat, cool itself spontaneously, and eventually settle motionless at the bottom of the vessel, which is not observed. Fifth, the average kinetic energy of the particles is directly proportional to the absolute temperature in kelvin, and depends on nothing else, not on the identity of the gas nor on the pressure. This is less an assumption than a definition of temperature, and it carries the powerful consequence that a helium atom and a xenon atom at the same temperature have the same average kinetic energy, so the much heavier xenon must be moving much more slowly. Sixth, the particles obey Newton's laws of motion between collisions, and the duration of a collision is negligible compared with the time between collisions. Notice what is deliberately absent. No assumption is made about molecular shape, about rotation or vibration, or about quantum mechanics. Those omissions are exactly why the simple model gets pressure right and gets heat capacity partly wrong. A gas satisfying all six postulates is called an ideal gas, and no such thing exists. What exists are real gases that approximate one closely at low pressure and high temperature, which is precisely the regime in which molecules are far apart relative to their size and moving fast enough that weak attractions barely deflect them.

sections.heading: Deriving Pressure From Molecular Impacts
sections.body: The central derivation of the theory connects the microscopic and macroscopic worlds in about a page of algebra, and following it once is worth more than memorising any number of gas laws. Imagine a cubic box of side length L, containing N identical molecules each of mass m, and pick one molecule moving with velocity component u along the x direction. When it strikes the wall perpendicular to x and bounces back elastically, its x-momentum changes from mu to minus mu, so the momentum transferred to that wall is 2mu. The molecule must then cross the box and return before it can strike the same wall again, a round trip of distance 2L, which takes a time of 2L divided by u. The rate at which this one molecule delivers momentum to that wall is therefore 2mu divided by 2L over u, which simplifies neatly to m times u squared, divided by L. Force is rate of change of momentum, so that expression is the average force this molecule exerts. Summing over all N molecules and replacing the sum of their individual u squared values with N times the mean of u squared gives a total force of N m times the mean square x-velocity, divided by L. Pressure is force per unit area, and the wall has area L squared, so dividing gives pressure equal to N m times the mean square x-velocity divided by L cubed, and L cubed is simply the volume V. The final step invokes the randomness of the motion. Since no direction is special, the mean square velocities along x, y, and z must be equal, and together they sum to the mean square speed. Each is therefore one third of the mean square speed. Substituting gives the central result: pressure times volume equals one third of N m times the mean square speed. Rearranged, this reads PV equals two thirds of N times one half m times the mean square speed, and the quantity in the final bracket is precisely the average translational kinetic energy of a molecule. So PV equals two thirds of the total translational kinetic energy of the gas. Comparing this with the empirical ideal gas law PV equals N times Boltzmann's constant times T yields the identification that the average translational kinetic energy of a molecule equals three halves times Boltzmann's constant times the absolute temperature. Boltzmann's constant has the value 1.380649 times ten to the minus twenty-three joules per kelvin, fixed exactly by definition since the 2019 redefinition of the SI base units. That single equation is the bridge between a thermometer reading and molecular motion. Two sanity checks are worth making on this result. It contains no reference to the identity of the gas, which is Avogadro's law falling out unrequested. And the mass m appears only inside the kinetic energy term, so at a fixed temperature a heavier molecule must move proportionally slower, which is exactly what is observed.
